These findings indicate cross-study heterogeneity in coordinate-based AD network maps reflects seed definition and study-level confounders, not biology alone. Combining GROW-based seed reconstruction with confounder-adjusted population modeling may provide a robust framework for mapping disease-related brain networks and prioritizing candidate neuromodulation targets.

items.title: Robustness of a connectome model of the fly walking rhythm generator to modelling choices
items.abstract: Connectome-constrained models are increasingly used to attribute behaviour to wiring, but their conclusions rest on modelling choices that the connectome does not fix. We independently replicated the rate model of the Drosophila nerve cord in which descending neuron DNg100 drives a walking rhythm generator (Pugliese et al., 2026), and asked which of its conclusions survive defensible alternatives to eleven such choices. Changed one at a time, 19 of 20 alternatives left the rhythm intact, including transfer of the wiring to a second connectome. Changed jointly, the rhythm survived in only 20 of 48 model variants when the descending drive was set by rules that do not look at the rhythm. A post hoc sweep of the drive separated two causes. In 12 of the 28 failures a rhythm existed at another drive, in 11 of them a higher one: the published drive lies at the lower edge of the rhythmic range. The other failures concentrated where larger networks met two- or threefold heterogeneity of intrinsic parameters, an interaction that one-at-a-time tests cannot show. In the 31 variants with a rhythm at a common drive of the sweep, the two excitatory interneurons remained necessary (30 of 31) and the inhibitory interneuron dispensable (29 of 31). The rhythm stayed rare among degree-preserving rewired networks when their drive was swept as well, and left-right coupling in the model was weak. The operating point is a modelling choice in its own right, and what a connectome model "produces" should be reported across it.

items.title: Dynamic remodeling of hybrid BBB-fenestrated capillaries in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus
items.abstract: The hypothalamic arcuate nucleus (Arc) is a central regulator of metabolism. We show that capillaries with sparse fenestrae enable direct and rapid hormone transport into the Arc. Arc fenestrae are virtually absent during pregnancy and obesity, but reform postpartum and upon weight-loss. Fenestrated Arc endothelial cells display a unique hybrid BBB-permeable structural and molecular phenotype, which can be regulated by Wnt signaling. The Arc endothelium exhibits functional plasticity that may affect hypothalamic sensing of systemic metabolic signals.

items.title: Cross-Stream Self-Supervised Learning Inspired by Feature-Biased Visual Processing in the Brain
items.abstract: Humans and other animals develop rich visual representations without explicit object-category labels. Self-supervised learning (SSL) offers a computational framework for studying how such representations emerge from visual experience. Many contrastive SSL models, such as SimCLR, learn by being robust to augmented views of the same image, which may fail to preserve visual attributes such as color and orientation. Inspired by feature-specific visual processing streams in the brain, we propose BioCLR, an SSL framework that uses color- and orientation-biased networks to guide representation learning. We combine Bio-CLR with SimCLR into a BioCLR hybrid model, pretrain it on ImageNet-100, and evaluate it on this dataset and four transfer datasets. In frozen linear evaluation, the BioCLR hybrid outperforms SimCLR across all datasets and mitigates negative transfer on a handwritten-character dataset. In limited-label fine-tuning, it outperforms SimCLR in most transfer conditions. Compared with the AugSelf and RotNet hybrids, which incorporate color and orientation information into SimCLR in other ways, the BioCLR hybrid shows the best overall performance, particularly in limited-label fine-tuning. Ablation analyses suggest that orientation guidance helps more than color guidance on these datasets, and that combining both generally improves frozen linear evaluation performance. Together, these findings suggest that incorporating feature-specific information into SSL can improve representation quality and model adaptability, and that the learning mechanism used to incorporate this information matters. For neuroscience, these results suggest that specialized visual streams in the brain may provide learning signals that guide visual representation learning without explicit supervision. For machine learning, they imply that principles of feature-biased processing in visual cortex may improve SSL.

items.title: Ion-channel transcript loss and variable firing in SCA1 Purkinje cells: a modelling test
items.abstract: In spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1), Purkinje cells fire with more variable interspike intervals before they degenerate, and reduced ion-channel expression is a proposed cause. We asked whether their channel transcript changes, applied as conductance changes, could produce this firing. We analysed public single-nucleus RNA-seq from male and female Atxn1 154Q/2Q knock-in and wild-type mice (24 discovery mice, 5-30 weeks; six held-out, 12 weeks). Knock-in Purkinje nuclei showed a reproducible transcriptional shift from 5 weeks. Transcripts of five channels, Kv3.3, BK, Kv4.3, Cav2.1 and Cav3.1, were reduced by 12 weeks (28-41 % at 18 weeks) and also lower, though not significantly for any single transcript, in ATXN1[82Q] Purkinje nuclei. We scaled the five conductances by these ratios in a published Purkinje cell model (130 parameter sets). The simulated neurons fired at 1.9 times the wild-type rate, outside the range recorded in knock-in Purkinje cells, and at 1.14 times in a second model. Scaling only Kv3.3, BK, Kv4.3 and Cav3.1, with Cav2.1 left at its wild-type value, brought both models close to the wild-type rate. With BK and Cav3.1 set from published staining, the afterhyperpolarization and depolarization-block threshold moved towards knock-in values, but by less. Dividing the five transcript ratios by the smaller knock-in membrane area (0.80 of wild type) also brought the median firing rate into the recorded range. Among versions whose median firing rate was in the recorded range, the median over parameter sets of the KI/WT ratio of the interspike-interval coefficient of variation was at most 1.57, whereas the recorded ratios of the group means were 1.8 and 2.9. In some versions, pauses in a few simulated neurons raised the ratio of the mean coefficients of variation. In these models, transcript changes alone did not reproduce the firing. Measuring spontaneous firing, Cav2.1 current density and membrane capacitance in the same knock-in and wild-type Purkinje cells, matched for age and lobule, would show whether Cav2.1 current falls less than its transcript, whether the cells are smaller, or both. Significance StatementIn spinocerebellar ataxia type 1 (SCA1), Purkinje cells fire with more variable interspike intervals before they degenerate. Five ion-channel transcripts are lower in SCA1 knock-in Purkinje cells and, though not significantly for any single transcript, in a second SCA1 model. We asked whether these lower transcripts, taken as smaller conductances, explain the firing. In a Purkinje cell model, reducing all five conductances made the simulated neurons fire almost twice as fast as wild type, unlike knock-in Purkinje cells. Keeping Cav2.1 at its wild-type value, or correcting for the smaller knock-in membrane, brought the median firing rate close to that of knock-in cells, but the median increase in the variability of the interspike interval stayed below the recorded increase. Measuring spontaneous firing, Cav2.1 current density and membrane capacitance in the same knock-in and wild-type Purkinje cells, matched for age and lobule, would show whether Cav2.1 current falls less than its transcript, whether the cells are smaller, or both.

items.title: An expanded GRAB sensor palette for multiplexed imaging of purinergic dynamics in vivo
items.corresponding_institution: Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China.; College of Advanced Ag
items.abstract: Extracellular ATP and adenosine operate as tightly coupled purinergic signals, yet tracking both molecules simultaneously in vivo has been limited by the performance and spectral range of existing sensors. We describe an expanded set of genetically encoded GPCR-Activation-Based (GRAB) sensors for ATP and adenosine that together support multiplexed imaging of purinergic signaling in the intact brain. Systematic optimization of receptor scaffolds, membrane trafficking, and fluorophore coupling yielded next-generation green sensors (Ado2h, Ado2m, ATP2h, ATP2l) and spectrally separated red variants (rAdo1h, rATP1h), each combining high ligand specificity, genetically targetable expression, sub-second kinetics, and minimal engagement of endogenous GPCR pathways. This combination allows minimally invasive, dual-color imaging of purinergic activity in vivo. Using multiplexed fiber photometry and two-photon imaging, we tracked ATP and adenosine concurrently across several behavioral and pathological settings. ATP release preceded extracellular adenosine accumulation during sleep-wake transitions and neuronal activation, a pattern consistent with extracellular ATP hydrolysis as a substantial contributor to in vivo adenosine signaling. During epileptic seizures, paired imaging of extracellular ATP with extracellular adenosine, and of extracellular with intracellular adenosine, indicated distinct spatiotemporal dynamics across cellular compartments. This expanded sensor set offers a platform for multiplexed purinergic imaging and for probing ATP-adenosine coupling across physiological and pathological brain states.

items.title: Behaviorally driven increased glutamatergic activity from lateral entorhinal cortex to hippocampus supports object and spatial memory recall
items.corresponding_institution: New York University Grossman School of Medicine
items.abstract: Interactions between the entorhinal cortex (EC) and hippocampal area CA1 are vital for episodic memory formation, but their role in recall is less clear. Canonically, spatial processing -- the "where" of an experience -- is attributed to the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC), whereas the lateral entorhinal cortex (LEC) processes the "what": non-spatial sensory cues and objects. Though these inputs are anatomically segregated in CA1, multimodal memory processing requires integrating spatial and contextual information, and recent work suggests greater MEC-LEC crosstalk than previously thought. Global LEC silencing via lesions, or combined suppression of glutamatergic and GABAergic LEC neurons, impairs associational goal-oriented learning and multi-object-cued encoding. However, the role of LEC glutamatergic projections specifically to CA1 during recall in freely moving spatial behaviors, and their contribution to synaptic plasticity, remains unclear. We used fiber photometry to record LEC axonal calcium dynamics in CA1 during novel object recognition and Barnes maze tasks, and ex vivo electrophysiology with LEC optogenetic activation. LEC activity increased during recall in both tasks, especially as animals learned spatial cues, peaking at late training stages of the Barnes maze. Local chemogenetic silencing of LEC inputs in CA1 after learning impaired recall. Ex vivo, temporally precise optogenetic activation of LEC input paired with CA3 intrahippocampal inputs was sufficient to induce long-term potentiation of both pathways in CA1 pyramidal neurons. These results suggest that LEC glutamatergic input to CA1 is dynamically modulated by experience to support recall during both object recognition and spatial navigation, with a functional role in synaptic plasticity.

items.title: Dynamic Weight Signatures as a Novel Biomarker of Motor Dysfunction in Mouse Models
items.corresponding_institution: National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences
items.abstract: Motor dysfunction is typically assessed through clinical examination and manual scoring, with gait analysis and accelerometry providing objective measures of subtle abnormalities. The observable 4-6 Hz resting tremor of Parkinsons disease highlights the importance of capturing motor fluctuations at relevant timescales. Using a high-precision industrial weighing module, we tested whether high-frequency weight recordings of freely moving mice could provide a simple, noninvasive means of detecting disease-associated motor abnormalities. Aging MitoPark mice spend more time in non-ambulatory states and exhibit less stable locomotion than healthy controls; however, bradykinesia and shaking can be mitigated by intraperitoneal levodopa. Here we demonstrate that irregular motor activity and tremor-like movements are quantifiable via weight frequency analyses, which permit detection of early symptoms and post-levodopa motor control restoration. This non-invasive approach is less data-intensive than video-based analyses, adaptable for home-cage monitoring, and potentially translatable for clinical or home use for detection of subclinical motor dysfunction.

items.title: One More Night: Investigating the Stability of Verbal Overnight Memory Consolidation and Sources of Variability
items.corresponding_institution: Brain and Mind Centre, The University of Sydney
items.abstract: Sleep-Dependent Memory Consolidation (SDMC) plays a vital role in facilitating the retention of newly learnt information. However, retesting in the literature is scarce and thus little is known regarding the daily stability of the SDMC process. The present study investigated whether overnight memory consolidation performance is stable (reflecting a trait) or variable (reflecting a state) across two nights using a novel word-pair smartphone application. Furthermore, the study examined the influence of subjective sleep quality and motivation on overnight consolidation performance, and whether these associations remained consistent across nights. Young healthy adults (N = 52) completed a validated word-pair task via a smartphone application over two nights and completed subjective sleep and motivation questionnaires. Results indicated overnight consolidation performance was not stable across nights, despite same-day and next-day recall exhibiting significant stability. Subjective sleep and motivation scores were not associated with performance, although these associations remained consistent across nights. However, worse PSQI scores were associated with lower next-day recall. After considering semantically related and unrelated word-pairs, both same-day and next-day recall performance exhibited significant stability for unrelated word-pairs only. These findings question the reliance on single-night SDMC protocols, and future research should examine modifiable factors that underlie SDMC variability across nights.

items.title: Structural Landscape of MHC Complexes through Fold Mining
authors: Nazare, P. G. B. d. S.
items.corresponding_institution: Brazilian Biosciences National Laboratory (LNBio), Brazilian Center for Research in Energy and Materials (CNPEM)
items.abstract: Major histocompatibility complex (MHC) proteins share a characteristic structural platform formed by two -helices positioned above a {beta}-sheet (1-2 domain), which can accommodate ligands and provide an exposed surface for recognition by protein binding partners. This interaction system is best characterized for classical MHC-I molecules presenting peptides to T-cell receptors (TCRs), one of the most extensively studied mechanisms of immune recognition. However, non-classical MHC and MHC-like proteins reveal that the 1-2 platform is considerably more versatile, supporting a remarkably diverse range of biological functions. Related architectures are also exploited by pathogens, further expanding the diversity of molecular interactions associated with this fold. Yet how this functional diversity relates to structural variation within the shared 1-2 platform and to the diverse modes of recognition employed by natural and engineered binding partners has not been systematically examined across the broader MHC fold. Here, we systematically mapped MHC 1-2-like domains across experimentally determined structures in the Protein Data Bank and predicted structures in the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database using Foldseek, and compiled their natural and engineered binding partners. Our comparative analyses revealed substantial heterogeneity across multiple structural layers, including 1-2 geometry, ligand-binding cavity architecture, and the physicochemical properties and spatial conservation of exposed recognition surfaces, despite the overall conservation of the fold. We further characterized a diverse repertoire of natural and engineered binding partners, revealing distinct structural architectures, interface compositions, and recognition geometries. Together, these findings provide an integrated structural landscape connecting the diversity of the MHC fold with the multiple modes of molecular recognition it supports, offering a comparative framework for understanding these interactions and guiding the engineering of novel MHC-targeting proteins.

items.title: Forecasting Human Sleep Dynamics with a Latent-State Framework
items.corresponding_institution: National Engineering Research Center of Neuromodulation, School of Aerospace Engineering, Tsinghua University
items.abstract: Sleep is essential for health, and forecasting its evolution could clarify its temporal organization and guide intervention timing. We developed a representation-forecasting model using electroencephalography from 5,419 participants. From 30-minute histories, 10-minute forecasts achieved 90.71% four-class accuracy in the 10% of windows with lowest predicted risk and averaged 72.11% overall. Direction-specific encoder feature axes had spectral correlates. Forecast changes under fixed-strength perturbations along these axes can quantify window-specific sensitivity varying with observed transition destination and bout timing. Physiological validation linked greater simulated perturbation sensitivity to stronger observed sleep-state responses following acoustic stimulation and respiratory events. Clinical profiling linked older age and higher apnoea-hypopnoea index to stronger modeled Wake-directed and weaker N3-directed responses. These results demonstrated that sleep-state forecasting could quantify dynamics, prioritize candidate intervention windows, and help interpret post-intervention changes.

items.title: Local sleep in wake is widespread across the rat cortex and tracks sleep need
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Psychiatry, University of Wisconsin - Madison
items.abstract: During non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep, cortical neurons alternate between ON periods of firing and OFF periods of silence, the latter accounting for the slow waves of the EEG. Converging evidence indicates that OFF periods can also occur locally during extended wake ("local sleep"), at a behavioral cost, but whether this phenomenon is ubiquitous across the cortex, whether some areas are more resilient than others, and whether it can also provide any benefit, remain open questions. Here we recorded from 11 cortical areas (and claustrum) in 15 rats using high-density Neuropixels probes and detected OFF periods with a novel method that captures spatially restricted and irregularly shaped events mischaracterized or missed by traditional methods. We found OFF periods during extended wake in every region tested, with no evidence that any area is spared. Over the course of sleep deprivation, OFF periods became more frequent, longer, larger, and quieter, and their features correlated with delta power on a per-event basis in both wake and NREM sleep, consistent with the notion that they reflect accumulating sleep need. The extent to which OFF periods overlapped across areas also increased across sleep deprivation. Finally, the rate of medium and large OFF periods during sleep deprivation was negatively correlated with their rebound in subsequent recovery sleep, consistent with the possibility that local sleep in wake partially discharges sleep need before the animal falls asleep. Statement of SignificanceProlonged wakefulness drives small groups of cortical neurons into brief sleep-like states even as the animal remains awake and behaving. This "local sleep" in wake is thought to underlie the errors and slowed responses of sleep deprivation, but how widespread it is, and whether it helps, remains unclear. Using high-density recordings across many cortical regions in the rat and a novel detection method sensitive to small, irregular events, we show that local sleep is not confined to a few vulnerable areas but occurs throughout the cortex, growing with accumulating sleep need. We also find that these neuronal lapses may begin to relieve that need before sleep takes over, suggesting that they may represent an early, piecemeal form of recovery.

items.title: Inferred interactions transform values into lattice-patterned choice attractors in orbitofrontal cortex
items.abstract: Economic decisions require transforming option values into choices, a process involving the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), but the circuit mechanism remains unclear. We recorded OFC activity in monkeys performing a juice-choice task, fitted graphical Ising models to spike data, and simulated the inferred networks. Offer inputs shifted the networks toward attractor states favoring the choice representation supported by relative value. Targeted ablations revealed a core functional backbone for this transformation, linking offer-value and choice-tuned populations, alongside amplification by broader network interactions and complementary contributions from positive- and negative-encoding pathways. Mean interactions between tuning groups captured the average transformation, while finer interaction structure shaped its network-specific implementation. At single-neuron resolution, the transformation was expressed through a recurring response motif coupling activation and suppression in a spatial lattice. Together, these results reveal how inferred OFC interactions transform offer values into choice-selective attractor states and shape the lattice-patterned neuronal recruitment characterizing this transformation.

items.title: From cellular synaptic input profiles to population-level respiratory circuitry
items.abstract: Breathing depends on coordinated activity among brainstem neurons. Their discharge patterns show when populations are active but do not specify the synaptic inputs that generate these patterns. Assuming that respiratory pattern generation involves a small number of interacting populations distinguished by discharge timing and excitatory or inhibitory output, we used synaptic conductances as readouts of their convergent activity. We reconstructed excitatory and inhibitory conductances from our previously described in situ rat brainstem-spinal cord recording archive (168 recordings, 150 neurons). We represented candidate presynaptic activity by five independently recorded population discharge patterns, assuming that phase-dependent inputs originated within these populations. We fitted each conductance time course as a nonnegative weighted sum of these patterns and tested whether candidate inputs could be omitted from the population mean, using variation across cells. Post-inspiratory inhibition was supported in all three inspiratory populations. Ramp-inspiratory neurons also showed augmenting-expiratory inhibition, and pre-inspiratory/inspiratory neurons showed augmenting-expiratory excitation. Excitation increased during the active phases of ramp-inspiratory and augmenting-expiratory neurons. Both expiratory populations showed inspiratory excitation alongside their prominent inspiratory inhibition. The inferred circuit retained major inhibitory interactions of the transection-based three-phase architecture and included additional excitatory inputs suggested by the earlier analysis. We distinguished some individual inspiratory discharge patterns but could not resolve other assignments. Source assignments depended on conductance reconstruction and how well the activity patterns represented presynaptic timing. These findings support excitatory interactions across populations with distinct discharge phases and suggest a contribution of late-expiratory excitation to recruitment of the next inspiration. Key pointsO_LIRespiratory discharge patterns show when neurons are active but not the synaptic interactions generating these patterns. Our recent work reconstructed previously unavailable excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs in respiratory neurons (Molkov et al., 2025). C_LIO_LIWe reconstructed inputs in a larger sample from the same archive and combined them with published population activity to identify candidate input sources for each receiving population and reconstruct a circuit. C_LIO_LIThe inferred circuit retained major inhibitory interactions of the three-phase architecture proposed to explain brainstem transection experiments. It included excitatory and inhibitory subpopulations with post-inspiratory and augmenting-expiratory discharge, with additional excitation during active and silent phases of receiving neurons. C_LIO_LISome inputs could be assigned to individual inspiratory discharge patterns, assuming representative activity patterns; overlapping activity left other assignments unresolved. C_LIO_LIExcitatory inputs link populations active in different phases. Rising late-expiratory excitation together with declining inhibition provides a candidate mechanism for recruitment of the next inspiration. C_LI

items.title: Evidence supporting resting-state power spectrum exponent as a non-invasive measure of neural-circuit excitation:inhibition balance in children with and without autism
items.corresponding_institution: Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and University of Pennsylvania
items.abstract: IntroductionAn ongoing neural circuit excitation (E) and inhibition (I) imbalance is thought to be a major contributor to clinical conditions such as autism, schizophrenia, and epilepsy. Current methods for directly measuring E:I dynamics require invasive procedures that are difficult to perform in non-human animals and nearly impossible in humans. A non-invasive measure of E:I balance is of great interest as a diagnostic as well as therapeutic marker, and as a means of studying relevant pathological and intervention mechanisms. Scientists have recently developed a computational model to show that, using resting-state (RS) MEG or EEG recordings, the E:I balance can be estimated from the power law exponent (slope) of the electrophysiological power spectrum. In their model, the RS power spectrum exponent is hypothesized to reflect the integration of synaptic currents in the brain, an index of E:I balance driven largely by excitatory (glutamate, Glu) and inhibitory (gamma-aminobutyric acid, GABA) neurotransmitter levels. Glu and GABA are the principal excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters in the brain, together shaping the balance between neural circuit excitation and inhibition. The present study shows that parietal-occipital neurochemistry as a predictor of the parietal-occipital RS exponent is driven by inhibitory neurotransmitter levels in typically developing (TD) children but not in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). MethodsMidline parietal-occipital RS power spectra (MEG) and Glu and GABA+ concentration (MRS) were obtained from 129 children (TD N = 84, ASD N = 45) 10.2 to 17.9 years old, with follow-up measures in a subset of the children providing 148 MEG and MRS datasets. Analyses focused on RS neural function and Glu and GABA+ concentration in parietal-occipital cortex. Resultst-tests showed no group differences between the parietal-occipital exponent, Glu, GABA+, or Glu/GABA+ ratio measures (ps > 0.21). In the full sample, older age was marginally associated with a lower exponent (p = 0.07), and older age associated with lower Glu concentration (p 0.05). There was no main effect of Glu or Glu x Group interaction with the exponent (ps > 0.14). Simple effect analyses of group interactions for GABA+ (p < 0.05) and ratio (p<0.05) showed a GABA+ and exponent association for TD (p = 0.01) but not ASD (p = 0.40) and a ratio and exponent association for TD (p = 0.01) but not ASD (p = 0.83). DiscussionThe brain chemistry and RS exponent associations suggest that a simple method for estimating E:I ratio reduces a major hurdle in understanding a currently difficult-to-measure, yet fundamental aspect of neural computation that has been proposed as central to clinical conditions such as ASD, epilepsy, and schizophrenia. Present findings indicate that the contribution of local brain chemistry to neural-circuit E:I balance differs for older children with and without ASD, with GABA inhibition presenting the more promising contributor to the E:I balance in TD children. Findings have the potential for high impact, including identifying neural markers for use in tracking treatment response.

items.title: Closed-loop control of sensorimotor aperiodic neural dynamics can manipulate excitatory-inhibitory balance in humans
items.corresponding_institution: Faculty of Science and Technology, Keio University
items.abstract: A ubiquitous property of physical and biological systems is scale-free dynamics in which spectral power decreases as a function of frequency, showing a 1/f spectral slope. The 1/f slope of neural power spectra has been proposed as a marker of cortical excitation-inhibition (E/I) balance, based on pharmacological experiments and computational models of synaptic activity in cortical networks. However, whether or not the spectral slope in the human population recordings, influenced by biophysical or experimental factors, can be utilized as an index of cortical E/I is debatable. Here, we show that this slope can be volitionally modulated and that its modulation is accompanied by changes in motor cortical activity reflecting E/I balance. To this end, we used a closed-loop paradigm in which real-time changes in the sensorimotor 1/f slope during neurofeedback trigger transcranial magnetic stimulation to probe intracortical circuits in the primary motor cortex. We found lower facilitatory effects in the steeper 1/f state than in both the flatter state and at rest, despite no significant between-state differences in 1/f-adjusted band power. These findings establish the physiological relevance of 1/f modulation with cortical states and support the contribution of intracortical E/I-related processes to the aperiodic dynamics.

items.title: Lifespan Remodeling of Cerebral Biomechanical Network Organization Reveals Coordinated Maturation and Aging-Related Convergence
items.abstract: Brain biomechanical connectivity (BC) captures shared regional viscoelastic properties that may support functional interactions. Although functional and structural brain networks are well characterized, the systems-level organization of brain biomechanics remains unknown. Using in-vivo magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) and community detection, we established BC and its network organization across the mouse lifespan, spanning seven stages from early adolescence (4 weeks) to old age (72 weeks). BC was benchmarked against established functional and structural connectivity, revealing shared connectivity features. Biomechanical network organization showed increasing segregation during adolescence, peaking in late adolescence, followed by progressive reintegration with aging. Biomechanical network dynamics defined by the pace of age-related change showed coordinated maturation during adolescence, regionally differentiated trajectories throughout adulthood, and partial reconvergence in aging. These findings establish a lifespan framework for cerebral biomechanical connectivity in mice and reveal age-dependent systems-level network reorganization that may underlie critical windows of brain maturation, aging, and disease vulnerability.

items.title: Prethalamus integrates neocortical and hypothalamic input to promote courage
items.corresponding_institution: Hospital del Mar Research Institute Barcelona
items.abstract: Courage, the ability to act despite potential danger, is essential for adaptive behavior, yet the circuit mechanisms that balance caution and risk-taking under threat are not fully understood. Here we identify the ventral lateral geniculate nucleus (vLGN), an inhibitory prethalamic structure, as a key node in this process. High vLGN activity predicts courageous behavior, such as leaving a shelter to enter a potentially threatening environment, and optogenetic activation of vLGN neurons promotes risk-taking under diverse aversive conditions. Inputs to vLGN from retrosplenial cortex (RSC) and ventromedial hypothalamus (VMH) modulate this behavior in opposing directions: RSC input promotes leaving safety, while VMH input suppresses it. These inputs target largely distinct vLGN populations that interact to integrate these opposing drives: a hypothalamic signal promoting defensive caution and a neocortical signal promoting action despite potential threat.

items.title: ProteoBridge Connects Proteomics Quantification Outputs to Reusable Analysis Workflows
items.corresponding_institution: Functional Genomics Center Zurich, ETH Zurich and University of Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland
items.abstract: Quantification tools for bottom-up label-free proteomics, including DIA-NN, Spectronaut, MaxQuant, and FragPipe, use different table layouts, column headers, modification notations, and parameter files. Downstream applications maintain separate readers for these outputs. ProteoBridge lets an application request the same quantity, such as unnormalized ion intensity, across reports from different quantification tools. JSON parsing rules describe each tools tables, and software-specific parameter parsers read the settings. The rules currently cover 14 tools and are tested on public inputs. A shared parser organizes the reported quantities into one level for each feature type the tool reports (fragments, ions, peptidoforms, peptides, or proteins) and writes the result as AnnData/MuData, Parquet, or DuckDB. A JSON summary records the structure, provenance, and conversion warnings, such as unmapped modifications. Applications can use the apb-catalog API in Python, R, or TypeScript to map the requested quantity to the field that holds it for each tool and version. Researchers can supply a sample table to add the experimental design and a FASTA database to check peptide sequences. ProteoBridge can serve as a common interface for reading quantification results across tools and versions.

items.title: Paternal transmission of the APPPS1 transgene is associated with increased amyloid pathology and a small Thy1.2-APP methylation difference
items.abstract: Maternal transmission of the APP transgene lowers amyloid burden in 5xFAD mice. We examined whether APPPS1-21 shows a similar parent-of-origin association and whether Thy1.2 methylation contributes. F1 offspring inheriting the transgene from the mother had less A{beta}42, fewer plaques, less gliosis, and less human APP at intermediate ages. The A{beta}42 difference was not detected in the F2 cohort at 100 days. Non-transgenic off-spring of APPPS1 mothers did not differ in glial counts, and serum anti-A{beta} antibody levels were not higher at 40 days. In an exploratory methylation analysis of 32 brains, parent-of-origin-associated differences were sex-specific and enriched on chromosome X, not chromosome 2. The Thy1.2-APP cassette showed an approximately three-percentage-point paternal increase; the PSEN1 cassette did not. These findings establish an association with parental transmission but do not show that methylation causes the pathology differences. HIGHLIGHTSO_LIMaternal transmission is associated with lower amyloid pathology C_LIO_LIThe amyloid-beta 42 difference was not detected in the second generation C_LIO_LIAmyloid precursor protein cassette methylation is higher with paternal transmission C_LIO_LIThe methylation difference does not establish a causal mechanism C_LI IN BRIEFWe report lower amyloid pathology after F0 maternal APPPS1 transmission to F1. The A{beta}42 difference was not detected in the F2 cohort. The small Thy1.2-APP methylation difference does not establish a causal mechanism.

items.title: Top-down prefrontal connectivity accompanies perceptual breakthrough after interocular suppression
items.abstract: The role of the prefrontal cortex (PFC) in the emergence of visual stimuli into conscious awareness remains contested. Additionally, whether top-down prefrontal connectivity is shaped by prior expectations during this process is not well understood. To address these questions, we applied dynamic causal modelling (DCM) to an EEG dataset during breaking continuous flash suppression (bCFS), which offers tight control over when a stimulus breaks into conscious perception. Our network comprised bilateral PFC, primary visual cortex, fusiform gyrus and motor cortex. Because perceptual breakthrough precedes behavioural report, we used a temporally resolved classifier to empirically define each participants moment of perceptual breakthrough (M = 1250ms, SD = 100ms). DCMs were then inverted over this time window up until each individuals breakthrough point. Parametric empirical Bayes revealed that top-down connectivity from the PFC to all regions was necessary to explain the observed neural dynamics (posterior probability [pp] > 0.99), though evidence that this top-down influence was modulated by expectation was inconclusive (pp = 0.74). Together, these findings suggest that top-down PFC connectivity accompanies perceptual breakthrough in bCFS, but it remains unclear whether this is modulated by expectation.

items.title: Resource-State Modulation of Prefrontal Value Processing during Earning-Spending Decision Making
items.corresponding_institution: Center for Excellence in Brain Science and Intelligence Technology, Institute of Neuroscience, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shanghai, 200031, China
items.abstract: Money mediates earning and spending, and accumulated monetary holdings constitute both a basic form of wealth and an external resource state that shapes economic decisions. Unlike internal physiological states such as hunger or satiety, external resources persist outside the body, can be acquired or depleted through choice, and preserve access to future consumption. Although money and wealth are human constructs, balancing resource acquisition and consumption may rely on evolutionarily conserved neural computations. Here we investigated these computations using an earning-spending task, in which rhesus monkeys chose between earning virtual tokens and spending accumulated tokens for water, with holdings carrying across trials. As holdings varied, monkeys shifted between earning and spending choices. A state-dependent utility model explained this shift through opposing changes in the relative values of earning and spending. We recorded single-unit activities from the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). Neuronal populations across all three regions represented current holdings, while ACC and OFC updated these representations after earning and spending outcomes. Crucially, resource state modulated value coding and reshaped the geometry of earning- and spending-value representations across all three regions. OFC exhibited a broader spectrum of signals spanning option value, chosen value, and good-based choice, whereas DLPFC representations were weighted more strongly toward action-based choice. Together, these findings identify distributed prefrontal mechanisms that represent, update, and use an external resource state to guide valuation and choice, extending neural accounts of state-dependent valuation beyond internal physiological conditions and suggesting an evolutionarily conserved foundation for balancing resource acquisition and consumption.

items.title: Expression of human-specific SRGAP2C increases representational capacity in mice
items.abstract: The brain of modern humans has evolved remarkable computational abilities enabling higher cognitive functions. Recent progress in evolutionary genomics and experimental neuroscience has identified several human-specific genetic modifiers of brain development that underlie the emergence of human-specific traits of cortical circuit connectivity and function. The human-specific gene SRGAP2C emerged by partial duplication of the ancestral gene SRGAP2A, which encodes a postsynaptic protein regulating synaptic development. SRGAP2C inhibits all known functions of SRGAP2A and its expression in mouse cortical pyramidal neurons leads to neotenic synaptic maturation, increased cortico-cortical connectivity, increased reliability of sensory coding by cortical layer 2/3 PNs, and improved learning of a sensory discrimination task. However, it remains unclear whether SRGAP2C expression in the mouse cortex is sufficient to produce changes in cognition. To test this idea, we trained adult wild-type (WT) and SRGAP2C mice on a Go-NoGo task that involves learning to associate a whisker stimulus with the presence of a water reward. SRGAP2C mice displayed a licking strategy that accelerated the learning of stimulus-reward associations at the cost of punishment timeouts compared to WT mice. The licking strategy was selective to the task, not driven by a general increase in consumptive behavior, and it accelerated the information that SRGAP2C mice gathered in early learning. SRGAP2C mice also displayed more structured behavior later in training and were, overall, better information channels than their WT counterparts. A computational model confirmed that SRGAP2C mice learning strategy increases representational capacity. Our results reveal that expression of human-specific gene SRGAP2C in cortical circuits is sufficient to increase the cognitive abilities of mice by optimizing the use of sensory information to guide action. The human-specific gene SRGAP2C might have contributed to the emergence of distinct functional cortical circuit features underlying our unique learning abilities and flexible decision-making.

items.title: The IFN-γ Paradox: Mechanistic Modeling Uncouples Cytokine Abundance from Influenza Pathogenesis
items.corresponding_institution: University of Tennessee Health Science Center
items.abstract: IFN-{gamma} has both pathogenic and protective roles during influenza infection, yet its value as a biomarker remains unclear because both increased and decreased levels associate with greater severity. To resolve this, we developed a mechanistic mathematical model of IFN-{gamma} and IFN-{gamma}-producing cell kinetics. The model was calibrated using murine data and validated against immune perturbation experiments, murine transcriptomics, human influenza challenge, and critically ill patient data. Personalizing the model with human challenge data quantified interindividual heterogeneity and generating cohorts of virtual patients with varying degrees of severity predicted unmeasured dynamics and was validated with transcriptomic and proteomic data from critically ill patients. Although severe disease was associated with greater receptor-mediated IFN-{gamma} uptake despite comparable production in non-ICU and ICU patients, early innate IFN-{gamma} signaling was a stronger determinant. These findings explain divergent IFN-{gamma} responses and establish a mechanistic framework for interpreting cytokine measurements.

items.title: NAD(P)H-FLIM reveals spatial and temporal epithelial metabolic heterogeneity in live intestinal organoids
items.abstract: Metabolism contributes globally to energy production at cell and tissue levels, but its cell-specific metabolic states also support tissue function and architecture. Conventionally used bulk metabolic flux assays however provide only the average readouts across cell populations, while fixed-sample and destructive spatial analysis methods result in endpoint. NAD(P)H fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) enables label-free, spatially resolved imaging of the individual cells and their responses to metabolic perturbations, directly probing dynamics of catabolic and anabolic metabolic pathways. The application of FLIM methodology to the intact living three-dimensional tissues such as stem cell-derived organoids, linking the cellular NAD(P)H dynamics to cell identity and mitochondrial function remains challenging. Here, we combined NAD(P)H-FLIM with lineage reporters, fluorescent probes and pharmacological perturbations in live mouse small intestinal organoids. Optimised acquisition and guided differentiation revealed drastic effects of the culture growth medium and crypt-villus axis on the intercellular gradient of NAD(P)H and mitochondrial polarisation. Further, guided organoids differentiation and marker-based analyses identified enterocytes as the principal population with highest NAD(P)H intensity and long lifetimes. Enterocyte-confined high NAD(P)H correlated with higher cell-specific ATP, contrasting with higher crypt/stem cell niche-associated mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) that persisted after apical efflux inhibition. Compared to the crypt-based cells, NAD(P)H in villus mitochondria-specific and high ATP enterocyte regions was also more sensitive to oligomycin, suggesting OxPhos as their main energy production mechanism. These findings indicate greater proton-gradient utilisation for ATP synthesis potentially contributing to the lower MMP in enterocytes, whereas higher ROS levels were revealed in crypt. Altogether, integrating epithelial lineage assignment with complementary detection of MMP, ROS and ATP provide better insight in interpretation of NAD(P)H-FLIM applied in a broader context of regional cell metabolic heterogeneity, supporting future epithelial dynamic metabolic studies visualizing intestinal regeneration and disease progression.

items.title: A long-lived human gastric tissue model defines regulators of lineage maturation
items.abstract: The gastric epithelium maintains barrier function against food-borne pathogens and executes metabolic activities through specialized cell types. The niche signals and gene-regulatory networks governing gastric specification remain poorly understood, partly due to the lack of mature human in vitro models. Here we develop long-lived engineered gastric epithelia that recapitulate gland-pit topography and, upon extended culture, give rise to all known gastric epithelial lineages including rare enteroendocrine and tuft cell subtypes. We use niche and genetic perturbations on EGE to explore patterning, cell differentiation, and gene regulation in the stomach. We establish a role for Neuregulin-1 in foveolar cell maturation, discover a novel FOXI1-regulated population resembling ionocytes and generate a roadmap of gastric enteroendocrine cell differentiation. This work establishes a physiological model that provides insights into the regulation of lineage maturation and can be employed to investigate broad aspects of gastric homeostasis and disease.

items.title: A sequence context-unbiased approach to enable precise inference of mutational processes in cancer.
items.abstract: Mutational signatures are recurring patterns of somatic mutations observed in cancer genomes, resulting from the activity of endogenous and exogenous mutagenic processes. Their investigation has significantly advanced our understanding of cancer etiology, informing prevention strategies and supporting clinical stratification. Although analytical approaches facilitate the identification of mutational signatures, their biological interpretation can be challenging, as some signatures may reflect methodological artifacts rather than distinct underlying mutational processes. Conventional mutational signatures inference frameworks generally assume that mutational opportunities are uniformly distributed across the genome and comparable across cancer types. However, mutable DNA motifs are not evenly distributed throughout the genome and their accessibility to DNA repair machinery is influenced by local chromatin states. To address these limitations, we developed SEQUENCE (SEQuence context Ubiased InferENCE of mutational signaturEs), a method that accounts for the heterogeneous nucleotide composition by generating weighted mutation catalogues, in which each mutation is adjusted for the local availability of its respective sequence context. By using SEQUENCE-generated mutation matrices as input for SigProfilerExtractor, a conventional framework for mutational signature extraction, we demonstrate that our approach mitigates biases arising from cell-type specific and locally varying mutational rates across the genome. Furthermore, the latent local information encoded in the weights enables the disentanglement of co-occurring mutational processes targeting the same sequence context and refines the mutational spectra of previously described mutational signatures. Mutational signatures characterised by relatively flat mutational spectra are notoriously difficult to extract. Here, using clinically relevant mutational signatures, we demonstrate that SEQUENCE can improve patient stratification according to their response to adjuvant chemotherapy. Together, these findings highlight sequence context unbiased mutational signature inference as a promising new framework for revisiting current reference signatures, providing deeper insight into their underlying origins and facilitating their translation into cancer prevention and clinical application.

items.title: Genomic insertion sequence populations of an ancient chemosynthetic symbiont
items.abstract: Genetic isolation as a consequence of host restriction of bacterial symbionts can lead to reductive genome evolution resulting in small, functionally streamlined genomes that are biased toward high AT contents. Frequently, reductive genome evolution leads to the loss of transposable elements, which are one of the major initial drivers of symbiont genome evolution through massive expansion events following initial host restriction. Under specific circumstances, where host-restricted bacteria continue to experience genetic mixing, transposable elements are retained in and, in some cases, introduced to symbiont genomes, even in ancient symbioses. Very little is known about these transposable element populations, regarding density, diversity, and activity as well as their influence on symbiont evolution and physiology. Here, we explored genomic population dynamics of insertion sequence (IS) elements, a type of transposable element, in 647 genomes of the chemosynthetic Gammaproteobacteria symbiont Candidatus Thiosymbion from three distantly related marine invertebrate hosts. We observed host-group specific patterns of genomic properties, likely reflective of symbiont genome evolution driven by varying degrees of genetic isolation due to differences in symbiont localization (ecto- to endosymbiont). We found that Thiosymbion genomes had highly diverse and dynamic IS populations, which varied by both symbiont localization and symbiont lineage with instances of clade-specific gain, loss, and expansion of certain IS families. Combined, our results suggest that variable IS expansion in Thiosymbion likely contributes to high intraspecific variability in genome structure.

items.title: GinsengMind: An evidence-grounded AI research agent for integrative molecular research in Panax ginseng
items.corresponding_institution: China Academy of Chinese Medical Sciences
items.abstract: Panax ginseng C. A. Meyer is one of the most extensively studied medicinal plants, with substantial pharmaceutical and economic importance owing to its diverse bioactive constituents, particularly ginsenosides. Despite considerable advances in ginseng molecular research, the fragmentation of genomic, transcriptomic, protein structural, and biochemical information remains a major challenge for investigating gene function and specialized metabolism. Here, we developed GinsengMind (https://ginsengai.nrc.ac.cn), an evidence-grounded AI research agent that integrates species-specific molecular knowledge with large language model (LLM)-guided tool orchestration and structured retrieval-augmented generation. Built upon the telomere-to-telomere reference genome of P. ginseng, GinsengMind integrates 77,266 genes, 154,754 transcripts, and 77,266 protein records. Comprehensive functional annotation using Swiss-Prot, eggNOG, and InterProScan covered 97.00% of the 76,947 quality-controlled proteins. The platform further incorporates 71,046 ESMFold-predicted protein structures, 7,263,004 gene expression records across 94 RNA-seq samples, and 4,813 bibliographic records. Six specialized research tools enable autonomous evidence retrieval and source-linked scientific interpretation through natural-language interaction. To evaluate its performance, we established GinsengBench, comprising 50 curated questions across six research categories. In a blinded evaluation by three experts, GinsengMind achieved a mean weighted composite score of 96.18 across ten core questions, substantially exceeding GLM-5.3 without database access (23.24; mean paired difference, 72.94; 95% confidence interval, 65.19-79.87). Across five shared questions, GinsengMind outperformed nine general-purpose LLMs on average and achieved a score (96.56) close to that of GLM-5.3 supplied with predefined evidence packages (96.88), highlighting the importance of domain-specific knowledge and autonomous evidence retrieval. A case study of the ginsenoside biosynthetic enzyme PgUGT94Q2 further illustrates how integrated molecular evidence can reveal unresolved biological relationships and identify priorities for subsequent experimental investigation. Beyond conventional database querying, GinsengMind provides a foundation for exploring potential biological associations, prioritizing candidate biosynthetic genes, and formulating experimentally testable hypotheses. We anticipate that GinsengMind will facilitate research on medicinal plant specialized metabolism, natural product biosynthesis, enzyme discovery and engineering, and synthetic biology, while offering an adaptable framework for developing domain-specialized AI research agents across other medicinal plants and scientific disciplines.

items.title: Measuring and reducing segmentation-driven cell-type labeling errors in imaging spatial transcriptomics
items.abstract: Imaging spatial transcriptomics labels each segmented cell from transcripts that include some of its neighbors RNA. We labeled each cell from its nucleus and its whole mask at equal depth, with two nuclear halves as a null. Whole-cell counts drew small, RNA-poor cells toward their larger neighbors labels. On three platforms, relative to nuclear labels at equal depth, T and NK cells lost 23-53% of their labels in six datasets of five tissues and 4-9% in renal cell carcinoma; this label-only measure matched same-cell protein markers in five donors and, where it differed, understated the loss. In gut, labels alone placed the loss at 58% of T cells among epithelial cells, compared with 24% in the lamina propria. The error lowered immune contact counts mainly by removing T cells; random relabeling, a common robustness test, raised them. Nuclear labels, where nuclei held enough counts, recovered many lost T cells. Imaged nuclei also carried some neighbor RNA and isolated nuclei carried none, indicating that these losses are lower bounds.

items.title: Multimodal profiling resolves the functional and spatial organization of colorectal cancer liver metastases
items.corresponding_institution: Aix Marseille Univ, INSERM U1068, CNRS, Institut Paoli-Calmettes, CRCM, Predictive Oncology laboratory, Label Ligue contre le cancer, Marseilles, France
items.abstract: BackgroundColorectal cancer (CRC) is the second leading cause of cancer-related mortality, largely because of liver metastases (LM). Despite advances in perioperative treatment and surgery, recurrence after resection of CRC liver metastases (CRC-LM) remains common. The cellular complexity of treatment-exposed CRC-LM and the interactions among malignant, stromal, immune, vascular and liver-resident populations remain incompletely understood, limiting the identification of biological vulnerabilities associated with disease progression and recurrence. MethodsWe used single-nuclei RNA sequencing (snRNAseq) to characterize the cellular composition and transcriptional states of nine chemotherapy-treated CRC-LM specimens. Single-nucleus profiles were integrated with spatial transcriptomic and protein-based analyses to define the functional and spatial organization of the metastatic ecosystem. We further compared tumors from patients with early versus no or later relapse and investigated candidate cell-cell interactions associated with recurrence-related cellular states. ResultsSingle-nucleus profiling recovered malignant epithelial tumor cells, fibroblasts, immune cells, endothelial cells and liver resident epithelial populations across samples and revealed substantial functional heterogeneity within each compartment. Malignant epithelial cells occupied interconnected stem-like, proliferative, differentiated and invasive states, whereas stromal, immune and vascular populations exhibited distinct transcriptional programs organized within specific tissue niches. Comparative analysis identified a fibroblast subtype enriched in early-relapse metastases, which was reproducibly identified in independent LM-CRC single-cell datasets. This population showed features consistent with a role in tumor dissemination and appeared to actively shape the metastatic microenvironment. ConclusionOur study provides an integrated single-nucleus and spatial characterization of the cellular organization of chemotherapy-treated CRC-LM. It reveals functionally specialized multicellular niches and identifies a fibroblast state associated with early relapse and epithelial and endothelial plasticity.

items.title: Optogenetic Kindling Model Reveals Functional Synaptopathy as a Driver of Temporal Lobe Epilepsy and Associated Comorbidities
items.abstract: Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) is one of the most prevalent and pharmaco-resistant forms of focal epilepsy in adults. The precise cellular and network mechanisms underlying TLE progression remain elusive. Animal models are essential for studying molecular and cellular mechanisms of TLE; however, widely used models largely rely on acute seizure induction and fail to recapitulate the gradual, progressive course of human TLE. Here, we present an optogenetic kindling mouse model of TLE, in which repeated stimulation induces a progressive increase in seizure susceptibility. This mouse model exhibits prominent TLE phenotypes, including robust hippocampal epileptiform activity, behavioral seizures, emotional changes, reactive astrogliosis, and impaired hippocampal learning and memory. Moreover, hippocampal synaptic analyses of this model revealed altered synaptic transmission and plasticity, without structural changes in excitatory or inhibitory synapses or overt cell death. These findings demonstrate that progressive epileptogenesis, synaptic dysfunction and TLE-associated phenotypes can develop independently of structural remodeling or overt cell death. This model provides a platform for investigating the synaptic mechanisms underlying TLE-associated synaptopathy.

items.title: Aiolos is specifically altered in schizophrenia, is expressed in hippocampal neurons and regulates structural synaptic plasticity through complement-mediated mechanisms
items.abstract: Aiolos (Ikzf3), a member of the Ikzf family, has been primarily characterized in the immune system, whereas other Ikzf family members have reported roles in the brain and have been implicated in schizophrenia. However, the potential role of Aiolos in the brain remains broadly unexplored. Combining human samples, translational and gain and loss of function mouse models we characterized Aiolos expression in the brain and investigated its potential involvement in schizophrenia. Here we show that Aiolos expression varies across brain regions and developmental stages, stabilizing in principal neurons during adulthood. Moreover, we identified that Aiolos is dysregulated in peripheral immune cells and in the hippocampus of patients with schizophrenia. Modeling the impact of those dysregulations in mice induced behavioral phenotypes relevant to the positive, negative and cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia. Finally, we found that mimicking Aiolos hippocampal dysregulation in mice generated increased complement protein abundance, accompanied by microglia-associated loss of synaptic material. Our results suggest that Aiolos may regulate complement-mediated synaptic elimination with potential implications for schizophrenia.

items.title: Gaze and Pupil Patterns in ADHD and ASD during Naturalistic Viewing
items.abstract: BackgroundAutism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) frequently co-occur, and both are associated with atypical attention and arousal. Whether these associations arise from shared or distinct processes remains unclear because the conditions are rarely modeled jointly and attention and arousal are rarely measured simultaneously. MethodsWe analyzed eye-tracking data (gaze position and pupil size) collected during naturalistic video viewing from 2,421 youth (aged 5-22) in the Healthy Brain Network. ASD, ADHD-Inattentive, and ADHD-Hyperactive diagnostic statuses were modeled jointly alongside age and sex. ResultsAtypical gaze trajectories were uniquely associated with ASD. Basic oculomotor control and orienting after scene cuts and to faces were typical, but autistic participants maintained gaze consistently farther from typical viewing locations and spent less time looking at characters, faces, and mouths. Pupil fluctuations were atypical in both ASD and ADHD-Hyperactivity via distinct routes: reduced pupil synchrony in ASD was largely explained by gaze allocation, whereas in ADHD-Hyperactivity it was gaze-independent and accompanied by faster pupil fluctuations. ConclusionsASD and ADHD show dissociable signatures during natural viewing: ASD differs in what is looked at rather than when, whereas ADHD-Hyperactivity is characterized by faster-fluctuating arousal.

items.title: PICALM deficiency exacerbates amyloid pathology in murine and nematode Alzheimers disease models
items.abstract: Alzheimers disease (AD), characterized by the accumulation of amyloid {beta}-peptide (A{beta}) plaques, is a progressive age-related neurodegenerative disorder affecting more than 35 million people worldwide. The risk of developing AD is significantly influenced by genetic factors. Deciphering their molecular functions has substantially advanced our understanding of the pathogenic mechanisms underlying AD. The PICALM gene represents a highly validated AD risk factor, and the encoded endocytic adaptor CALM is critical for endothelial A{beta} clearance and microglial A{beta} phagocytosis. However, it remains controversial how neuronally expressed CALM modulates AD pathogenesis. We find that loss of neuronal CALM accelerates A{beta} plaque formation and impairs neurotransmission in an AD mouse model, revealing a protective role for neuronal CALM. These phenotypes are accompanied by an elevated surface level of the endolysosomal SNARE protein VAMP8, consistent with a role for CALM in promoting the turnover of aggregated proteins via the autophagy/lysosome pathway. Moreover, loss of CALM promotes A{beta} aggregation in a C. elegans model expressing fluorescently labelled A{beta}, while neuron-specific overexpression of CALM decreases A{beta} aggregation. Finally, we demonstrate that the ANTH domain of CALM displays chaperone-like activity by inhibiting A{beta} aggregation in vitro. Our combined data suggest that neuronal CALM might counteract AD progression by suppressing A{beta} aggregation and by safeguarding endolysosomal SNARE trafficking.

items.title: Dissociation of Reward Incentive and Motivational Drive by Distinct Neural Circuits in Mice
items.abstract: The generation of reward incentive value and maintenance of motivational drive are distinct processes in reward-related behavior. However, how neural circuits differentially process these components remains poorly understood. Although intracranial self-stimulation (ICSS) paradigms have been utilized to identify reward-related circuits, ICSS measures may conflate reinitiated actions attributed to learned incentive value with ongoing motivated behavior sustained by concurrent stimulation. Here, we reveal a dissociation between these processes by optogenetically stimulating fibers in the stria terminalis bundle projecting to the medial nucleus accumbens (STBmNAc) and those in the medial forebrain bundle originating from the lateral NAc (MFBlNAc). We found that STBmNAc stimulation facilitated the reinitiation of ICSS actions, whereas MFBlNAc stimulation sustained ongoing ICSS behavior. Moreover, shortening the stimulation duration in STBmNAc mice increased the likelihood of subsequent re-engagement of stimulation-seeking. Additionally, STBmNAc stimulation, but not MFBlNAc stimulation, could substitute for primary rewards and support the acquisition of sensory cue-dependent operant behavior. Together, our findings suggest that STBmNAc activation promotes reward-anticipatory behavior by conferring reward incentive value, whereas MFBlNAc activation sustains ongoing behavior by maintaining motivational drive. Thus, reward-related behavior may not be governed by a unitary motivational system but may involve anatomically and functionally distinct neural components.

items.title: A Comparative Metagenomic Analysis of the Viral Diversity in Faecal Samples from Malnourished and Non-malnourished Children with Gastroenteritis Admitted at Victoria Mxenge Hospital in Durban, KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa
items.abstract: Viral gastroenteritis and malnutrition remain major health burdens among children under five in South Africa. Malnourished children are particularly vulnerable to prolonged enteric viral infections, yet their gut virome remains poorly characterised in South Africa. This study compared gut virome diversity among malnourished and non-malnourished children with gastroenteritis, and children without gastroenteritis and malnutrition (healthy controls). This retrospective laboratory-based continuation study analysed 69 faecal samples from age-matched children aged 0- 36 months at Victoria Mxenge Hospital across three cohorts: malnourished children with gastroenteritis, non-malnourished children with gastroenteritis, and healthy controls. Viral metagenomic sequencing was performed using Illumina NextSeq 2000, followed by bioinformatic analyses. Virome profiling identified 39 viral families, 71 genera, and 243 species. Of the total sequenced reads, 60.4% were classified comprising 91.0% mapped to bacteria, 6.4% to viruses, and 2.6% to human host and other microorganisms. Eukaryotic viral reads were highest among non-malnourished children with gastroenteritis (37.2%), followed by healthy controls (32.3%) and malnourished children with gastroenteritis (30.5%). Detected enteric viral families included, Sedoreoviridae, Caliciviridae, Picornaviridae, Astroviridae, and Adenoviridae, with Sedoreoviridae being predominant. Multiple co-detections of enteric viruses were observed. Significant cohorts differences occurred in viral diversity (p = 0.0038) and abundance (p = 0.0001), but not in evenness (p = 0.146) and richness (p = 0.0896). This study revealed differences in faecal virome composition across cohorts and provides baseline genomic data for viral surveillance. The findings highlight the importance of vaccination, nutritional and preventive strategies to curb infant mortality associated with gastroenteritis and malnutrition in South Africa.

items.title: RFoldSearch enables fast RNA structure search beyond sequence similarity
items.abstract: The rapid growth of predicted RNA structure databases demands fast and sensitive structural search methods. Sequence-based approaches lose sensitivity for divergent homologues, whereas exhaustive coordinate alignment is computationally expensive. Analogous to Foldseeks 3Di representation, we introduce RFoldSearch and 3Dr, a learned 80-state structural alphabet encoding local RNA tertiary environments. RFoldSearch combines indexed prefiltering, structure-aware token alignment and optional coordinate-based reranking. On held-out RNAsolo 2.0 queries, RFoldSearch retained 81-89% of the family-level sensitivity of exhaustive coordinate aligners and outperformed RiboSeek (RS-20) and BLASTN. On a single CPU core, RFoldSearch searched 531,888 predicted structures in 0.31 s per query, 20-fold faster than RiboSeek with its RS-20 alphabet while using 7.7-fold less peak memory. Searches of predicted-structure databases demonstrated its ability to recover structurally similar RNAs with limited detectable sequence similarity, complementing profile-based sequence search. Recurrent 3Dr words captured conserved local RNA geometries, including fragments corresponding to known RNA 3D motifs. RFoldSearch is available as open-source software, a web server and a REST API.

items.title: kRISP-meR: A Reference-free Guide-RNA Design Tool for CRISPR/Cas9
items.corresponding_institution: Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology
items.abstract: Designing specific guide RNAs for CRISPR/Cas9 typically relies on reference genomes, which limits the applicability in non-model organisms and fails to account for individual-specific genomic variations. To address this, we present a reference-free method for single-guide RNA (sgRNA) design that operates directly on raw sequencing reads, implemented in a tool called kRISP-meR. Instead of relying on whole genome assembly, kRISP-meR models the k-mer frequency spectrum of the sequencing data using an Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm and uses a probabilistic model to calculate the expected number of cuts for candidate gRNAs by estimating genomic copy numbers. Results on datasets from three different organisms show that the expected cuts estimated by kRISP-meR from reads agree closely with those computed from reference assemblies. Furthermore, analysis of human and rice sequencing data reveals that kRISP-meR successfully detects and filters candidate gRNAs within repetitive genomic regions with high off-target risk, highlighting its importance for gRNA design when references are unavailable or incomplete.

items.title: A systematic benchmark evaluation of algorithms for 3D tissue alignment and registration with spatial omics
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Biostatistics, Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, Baltimore, MD, USA
items.abstract: Recent advances in spatial omics have enabled tissue atlases spanning serial sections, donors, and experimental technologies. Aligning these datasets is essential for comparing spatial organization, reconstructing three-dimensional tissue architecture, and registering sections to a common coordinate framework. However, systematic comparisons of alignment accuracy, computational efficiency, and usability remain limited. Here, we benchmarked 15 tissue alignment and registration algorithms using experimental and simulated spatial transcriptomics datasets across pairwise alignment, three-dimensional reconstruction, cross-resolution alignment, and atlas registration tasks. We assessed spatial-domain and cell-type correspondence, spatial gene-expression similarity, computational scalability, and usability. Simulated datasets with known spatial coordinates additionally enabled direct evaluation of geometric accuracy and reconstruction stability. No single method performed best across all settings: performance depended on the task, spatial resolution, and tissue characteristics, and strong pairwise alignment did not necessarily translate into reliable three-dimensional reconstruction. Evaluation metrics captured complementary aspects of alignment quality, highlighting the importance of using multiple criteria for comprehensive assessment. These findings provide practical guidance for method selection and identify priorities for improving the accuracy, scalability, and accessibility of spatial omics alignment.

items.title: The ear receives only weak parametric information about saccade directions
items.abstract: Eye movement-related eardrum oscillations (EMREOs) are acoustic signals recorded in the ear canal induced by saccades, whose amplitude and time course relate to the saccade vector. While horizontal saccades evoke robust, and largely opposing EMREO signals in the two ears, the reliability and informational content of vertical EMREOs has remained more elusive. Here, we analyzed bilateral EMREOs in human participants performing visually guided horizontal and vertical saccades. Consistent with previous work, horizontal saccades induced stereotyped, opposing waveforms across ears. In contrast, vertical EMREOs exhibited distinct temporal profiles between upward and downward directions, weaker signal modulation, and substantially higher inter-individual variability, particularly for downward saccades. To quantify the parametric information carried by single-trial bilateral EMREOs about the saccade vector, we applied multivariate classification and reconstruction analyses. The cardinal saccade direction was classified above chance, with significantly higher accuracy for horizontal than vertical saccades. Similarly, the reconstruction recovered horizontal saccade components more accurately than vertical ones, yet severely underestimated saccade amplitudes with high variability. These findings demonstrate that EMREOs carry reliable categorical saccade information, but primarily along the horizontal axis, and provide only weak and noisy parametric estimates of the full two-dimensional saccade vector. They also suggest that EMREOs may be particularly driven by the differential engagement of oculomotor neuromuscular pathways across the two sides of the brainstem.

items.title: A signature of deep credit assignment in the human Orbitofrontal cortex
items.abstract: Humans are remarkably efficient at learning from limited experience because they can generalize quickly. Doing so, however, requires first learning about the latent structures that govern outcomes. The dominant theoretical framework to understand this interactive cycle between learning task representations and generalisation is deep learning, which updates parameters throughout multi-layered neural networks using deep credit assignment. Yet, whether the brain uses a similar "deep" approach to learning is unclear. Here, we derive and test a prediction that uniquely characterizes deep credit assignment, namely, that a single learning experience should trigger immediate, structured representation changes that are non-local (i.e. generalize beyond the observed experience), and adapt as learning proceeds. Using fMRI (N=51) and neural network simulations, we tested whether feedback on a limited set of items induces structured changes in the representations of other, non-feedbacked items during a partially-observable reinforcement learning task. We find that with sufficient learning, feedback on a small set of trials begins to induce rapid, context-dependent shifts in non-local orbitofrontal cortex representations that extend beyond experienced items and predict concurrent improvements in behavioral generalization. The neural findings and their link to behaviour were mirrored by representation learning dynamics in performance-matched recurrent neural networks, trained using gradient descent on the same curricula as participants. These findings reveal fast, non-local dynamics of representation learning that support generalization and are shared across humans and distributed deep networks.

items.title: Multi-omic cardiac adaptation to exercise training identifies adaptive and disease-opposing signatures: findings from MoTrPAC
authors: Writing Group for the MoTrPAC Study Group,
items.last_author: Writing Group for the MoTrPAC Study Group,
items.abstract: BackgroundEndurance exercise reduces cardiovascular disease risk, but how this protection is mediated at the molecular level remains incompletely understood. MethodsUsing multi-omic data from MoTrPAC, we integrated 13,790 selected molecular features across eight cardiac omic layers from 50 female and male rats undergoing 1-8 weeks of endurance training, as well as sedentary controls. Multi-omic temporal programs were defined using MOFA/MEFISTO and compared to physiological adaptation, human cardiac disease signatures, causal cardiomyopathy genes, and cross-tissue responses. ResultsSeven temporal programs of coordinated molecular responses were identified across cardiac omic layers. Transient metabolic responses showed sex-dependent timing and generally preceded sustained structural changes with limited correspondence to skeletal muscle, while complement proteins declined with training. Among these, a sustained program was associated with improvement of VO2max and accounted for 38 of 50 significant overlaps with human cardiac disease signatures, frequently with opposing molecular responses, including reduced Fn1 and increased Klhl40 transcript and protein abundance by 8 weeks. To provide mechanistic context, we examined 112 genes causally linked to inherited cardiac disease, finding significant training-associated changes in 72 genes at the transcript level and 57 at the protein level. Notably, FLNC, BAG3, and PKP2 protein abundance increased, contrasting with reduced-dosage mechanisms in their respective cardiomyopathies. Conversely, disease-aligned and disease-opposing chaperone responses suggested coordinated protein quality-control mechanisms that may contribute to exercise-mediated cardioprotection. ConclusionsEndurance training induces coordinated, time-dependent molecular responses across cardiac pathways implicated in human disease, including both disease-opposing changes in known causal genes and disease-concordant stress responses. Clinical implicationsO_ST_ABSWhat is new?C_ST_ABSO_LIEndurance training induces distinct cardiac temporal programs, including a sustained multi-omic response associated with improved cardiorespiratory fitness, while transient metabolic responses generally precede progressive structural remodeling. C_LIO_LIFemale and male hearts engaged broadly shared metabolic pathways with sex-specific timing of mitochondrial protein and post-translational responses. C_LIO_LISustained programs account for most overlaps with human cardiac disease signatures, frequently with opposing molecular responses; increased FLNC and BAG3 further suggest potential compensation for reduced-product cardiomyopathy mechanisms. C_LI What are the clinical implications?O_LIEndurance training induces molecular responses that significantly overlap with cardiovascular disease signatures.
