Both disease-opposing and disease-aligned regulation may help distinguish potentially protective adaptations from pathological remodeling. C_LIO_LITraining upregulates several causal cardiomyopathy genes implicated in haploinsufficiency, suggesting potential compensation for reduced gene dosage across distinct genetic disease contexts. C_LIO_LIFemale and male hearts have distinct temporal responses in excitation-contraction coupling, metabolism, and cytoprotection, highlighting potential sex-specific mechanisms of cardiac adaptation. C_LI

items.title: Social Behavior in Mice Relies on a Capacity to Phosphorylate the Serotonin Transporter
items.abstract: The biogenic amine 5-hydroxytryptamine (serotonin, 5-HT) regulates social behavior across the animal kingdom. Although drugs that promote 5-HT transporter (SERT)-mediated 5-HT efflux within the nucleus accumbens (NAc) enhance sociability, the extent to which endogenous mechanisms regulating SERT contribute to normal social behavior is unknown. Prior in vitro studies have shown that SERT trafficking and activity are controlled by transporter phosphorylation, with the Thr276 site required for rapid, protein kinase G (PKG)-dependent increases in SERT function. Using SERT Ala276 knock-in mice, we demonstrate that sex-specific social behaviors rely on the capacity to phosphorylate SERT at Thr276. Whereas WT males and females exhibited social preference and sustained interactions with juvenile mice, these behaviors were selectively diminished in Ala276 females. In contrast, Ala276 males exhibited preserved sociability but increased retreat behavior in the tube dominance test. Dorsal and ventral brain slice biotinylation studies revealed sex-independent, PKG-induced increases in striatal SERT surface expression that were abolished in Ala276 mice. In the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN), PKG activation failed to elevate SERT surface expression in either sex. Extracellular 5-HT responses in the NAc recorded via in vivo fiber photometry during repeated, but not initial, social interactions were absent in Ala276 females but not males. Ex vivo patch clamp recordings from DRN slices uncovered reduced excitability of 5-HT neurons from female Ala276 mice compared with WT controls, an effect reversed by blockade of 5-HT1A autoreceptors, consistent with tonic activation of these receptors in mutants. Supporting this idea, systemic administration of the 5-HT1A partial agonist buspirone restored sociability in Ala276 females and social dominance in Ala276 males, while elevating extracellular NAc 5-HT responses in Ala276 females. Our findings support a model in which sustained social behavior requires the capacity to phosphorylate SERT at Thr276 to limit somatodendritic 5-HT1A autoreceptor-mediated inhibition and support serotonergic signaling.

items.title: Quantal release through the fusion pore
items.abstract: Exocytosis of neurotransmitters and peptides begins with the formation of a fusion pore that connects the vesicle lumen to the extracellular space. Release is completed when vesicles undergo full fusion. Here we show that full quanta of serotonin are released through a slowly closing fusion pore without full vesicle fusion. Amperometric recordings of serotonin release from dense-core vesicles in the axons of isolated Retzius neurons of the leech contained a subset of small release currents with a long biexponential decay. These slow-closure currents reflected the release of 90,262 {+/-} 8,829 molecules, a number similar to full-fusion quanta and 54% larger than that of kiss-and-run events. The reconstructed dynamics of fusion pores show that slow-closure pores narrow rapidly after the peak and then close slowly or remain open. By contrast, kiss-and-run pores closed while vesicles still contained a large fraction of their serotonin content. Forces influencing pore kinetics were analyzed from pore velocity. The velocity decay of slow-closure pores developed a rapid undershoot characteristic of near-critical or underdamped relaxation. By contrast, in kiss-and-run pores, velocity decayed exponentially and turned negative during closure, consistent with an overdamped relaxation. Analysis of pore velocity revealed that slow-closure pores initiate rapid closure under a stiff force coupled to the pore diameter. Another force then arrests closure at a residual diameter of 1-2 nm that membrane tension alone cannot sustain. This allows release of the full serotonin quantum. Impact statementRelease of the entire transmitter content of a vesicle, the quantum, is usually associated with the opening of a fusion pore followed by full vesicle fusion. Here we show that a full serotonin quantum can be released without full fusion, through pores that close rapidly to a residual diameter and then close slowly or stay open.

items.title: Relative distance change rather than absolute distance drives auditory alerting
items.abstract: The function of hearing as an early warning system relies partly on detecting the distance and motion of an object based on sound. Approaching - or looming - objects activate the human alerting system, but it is debated whether sounds in the immediate vicinity of the body achieve the same irrespective of the direction of motion and of sound intensity. We addressed this question by examining distance perception of and phasic alertness states evoked by virtual sonic motion into and within peripersonal and extrapersonal space, at high and low intensities, in normal-hearing adults. Based on distance ratings, target detection promptness, and electroencephalography (EEG), we found that looming auditory objects increase phasic alertness and auditory sensory gain, and we also observed a general tendency to perceive sound offsets as closer to the body than onsets. However, we did not find evidence that auditory objects moving at a constant distance within peripersonal space affect alerting over and above the influence of intensity. We suggest that the auditory looming bias is not amplified further by preferential processing of auditory information near the body, and that the early warning function of hearing emphasizes the direction of motion over distance.

items.title: Dopamine shifts striatal ramping dynamics
items.abstract: Diseases that disrupt dopamine impair cognition; however, it is unknown how dopamine affects neuronal networks that instantiate cognitive processing. We studied this problem in the dorsomedial striatum during interval timing, an elementary cognitive task requiring working memory and attention to estimate an interval of several seconds. Interval timing requires medium spiny neurons (MSNs) that ramp up or down over temporal intervals. While these neurons receive prominent dopaminergic input from the substantia nigra, it is unknown how dopamine modulates MSN activity during interval timing. Here, we report four new findings. First, ramping activity of MSN ensembles predicts interval timing behavior. Second, dopamine dynamics predict timing behavior and preferentially predict the slope of MSN ensembles that ramp down; these relationships are not observed during tasks without temporal control such as Pavlovian conditioning. Third, inactivating substantia nigra dopamine disrupts timing as well as MSNs that ramp down, but not those that ramp up. Fourth, a drift-diffusion model perturbing down-ramping accurately predicted interval timing behavior in mice with dopamine inhibition and in humans with Parkinson's disease. Together, these results reveal how dopamine shapes striatal ramping dynamics and suggest that disrupting dopamine can alter specific trajectories of cognitive computations. These data are relevant for understanding the cognitive striatum and for generating new markers and therapeutic strategies for human striatal and dopaminergic diseases.

items.title: DualBranchEEG: A Dual-Branch CNN BiLSTM Network with Temporal Attention and Spectral Features for Three Class EEG Seizure Classification
items.abstract: Automated seizure detection from electroencephalography (EEG) is a key step toward closed-loop brain-computer interface (BCI) systems and clinical decision support. We present DualBranchEEG, a dual-branch network that fuses (i) a temporal branch--a three-block 1-D convolutional encoder, a two-layer bidirectional LSTM and an additive attention layer--operating on the raw z-scored waveform, with (ii) a spectral branch--an MLP on log-power spectral density (PSD) features from Welch's method. We evaluate three-class classification (normal, interictal, ictal) on the Bonn University EEG dataset (500 single-channel recordings, 173.61 Hz) using a single stratified 70/15/15 split (seed 42). We position this work as a transparent reference implementation and exploratory comparison, not as evidence of superiority. A CNN-BiLSTM baseline (728,387 parameters; last-time-step readout, no attention, no augmentation) attains 96.00% test accuracy (72/75) and a macro AUC-ROC of 0.9795; five-fold stratified cross-validation of this baseline gives 98.40 {+/-} 1.52% accuracy and 0.9952 {+/-} 0.0071 AUC-ROC. The full DualBranchEEG (823,556 parameters) attains the same 96.00% test accuracy, macro F1 of 0.9543 and macro AUC-ROC of 0.9952. In the ablation, CNN-only, BiLSTM-only and CNN+BiLSTM+attention variants each reach 94.67%, and the full model is one test recording better; with only 75 test recordings these differences lie within sampling uncertainty (95% Wilson interval for 96.00%: 88.9-98.6%). Band-power differences between all class pairs are significant in all five canonical EEG bands. Grad-CAM, t-SNE and attention visualisations are reported as qualitative diagnostics only. We document all known methodological limitations, including PSD standardisation fitted on all 500 recordings and Welch's default 50% segment overlap.

items.title: Causal dissociation of occipital and mid-fusiform contributions to human visual experience
items.corresponding_institution: Sorbonne Universite, Institut du Cerveau - Paris Brain Institute - ICM, Inserm, CNRS, APHP, Pitié-Salpêtrière Hospital, 47 Bd de l’Hôpital, 75013 Paris, France
items.abstract: Visual experiences can arise without corresponding retinal input, as in imagery, dreams, and hallucinations. Influential models of visual mental imagery propose that mental images acquire their visual quality in early visual cortex. Direct intracranial electrical cortical stimulation (DIECS) causally probes which cortical sites can evoke visual experiences, and of what kind. We examined de novo visual experiences evoked by stimulation in three patients undergoing stereo-EEG monitoring for drug-resistant epilepsy and localized the effective contact pairs using the Julich-Brain cytoarchitectonic atlas. Among the sampled sites, stimulation of occipital and adjacent intraparietal cortex and of the posterior fusiform area FG1 elicited simple or intermediate phenomena, including flashes, colored spots, and elementary shapes. By contrast, only stimulation of sites in or adjacent to the mid-fusiform areas FG3 and FG4 elicited complex images of people, scenes, and objects. These findings provide cytoarchitectonically localized causal evidence that stimulation of right mid-fusiform cortex can trigger complex visual experiences, possibly through distributed networks. They also identify the mid-fusiform gyrus as a promising causal node for complex visual content, and are compatible with lesion and neuroimaging evidence challenging the necessity of early visual cortex for visual imagery.

items.title: Human hematopoietic development during the first year of life and its remodeling by neonatal Bacillus Calmette-Guerin vaccination
items.abstract: Hematopoiesis and immune development are well defined in adults but remain poorly understood in early life, despite the neonatal period being critical for immune maturation. We map hematopoietic and immune programs across the first year of human life using single-nucleus epigenomic and transcriptomic profiling of circulating hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (cHSPCs), including Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) vaccinated infants to illustrate a controlled immune challenge. BCG-naive infants displayed heightened myeloid activation through 3 months of age, followed by an interferon-enriched HSPC program at 13 months. BCG vaccination induced earlier interferon responses in HSPCs and dampened inflammatory programs in myeloid cells. These findings define the landscape of early-life human hematopoiesis and provide mechanistic insight into the heterologous protection associated with neonatal BCG vaccination.

items.title: A novel engineered T7 RNA polymerase produces therapeutic mRNA without inflammatory dsRNA byproducts
items.corresponding_institution: Genentech, South San Francisco, CA 94080, USA
items.abstract: The therapeutic application of in vitro transcribed (IVT) messenger RNA (mRNA) is constrained by double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) impurities generated by wild-type (WT) T7 RNA polymerase (RNAP). These impurities trigger innate immune responses via RIG-I and MDA5, suppressing protein translation. Conventional polymerase engineering often trades dsRNA reduction for lower transcription processivity. Here, we report engineered T7 RNAP variants that limit this trade-off. Physicochemical profiling identified variant G3, which suppresses high-molecular-weight aggregates and 3'-loopback hairpins while preserving full catalytic yield, high capping efficiency, and sequence processivity. In primary dendritic cells, N1-methylpseudouridine (N1psU)-modified mRNA produced by G3 yielded up to a three-fold increase in protein expression compared to WT T7, without inducing CD86 maturation. Systemic in vivo delivery in mice confirmed superior therapeutic expression and completely abrogated pro-inflammatory cytokine release. Functional knockouts confirmed that G3-transcribed mRNA evades cytosolic RIG-I/MDA5-mediated translational suppression by selectively eliminating inflammatory dsRNA byproducts. Together, G3 offers a superior, scalable manufacturing solution for advanced mRNA therapeutics.

items.title: Physiological Culture Modulates the Cargo and Wound-Healing Potential of MSC Extracellular Vesicles
items.abstract: This study demonstrates that animal-free 3D culture and long-term hypoxic conditioning modulate mesenchymal stromal cell-derived extracellular vesicle (MSC-EV) production and cargo composition without compromising MSC identity. Mimicking the in vivo microenvironment through hypoxic 3D culture increased MSC-EV yield and altered EV molecular composition, highlighting the potential of culture engineering as a strategy to optimise MSC-EV manufacturing. While 3D culture exerted the greatest effect on both cellular and MSC-EV proteomes, increasing protein abundance and complexity associated with translational and peptide biosynthesis pathways, hypoxic conditioning further enhanced the functional activity of 3D-derived MSC-EVs in an in vitro wound-healing model. These findings suggest that even subtle alterations in MSC-EV cargo can influence biological activity. Collectively, our results demonstrate that culture configuration and oxygen tension are important process variables that affect MSC-EV yield, composition, and functionality. This work highlights the importance of integrating physiologically relevant culture conditions into MSC-EV production strategies and provides insights for the development of scalable and clinically translatable MSC-EV therapeutics for wound healing and regenerative medicine.

items.title: Cell type specific Rab Munc13-4 coupling defines divergent exosome fusion mechanisms and post-docking fusion pore opening
items.abstract: Munc13-4 operates as an intracellular Ca2+ sensor for regulated secretion in both immune and cancer cells. Its capacity to physically engage multiple Rab GTPases and SNARE proteins places it at the center of membrane reorganization upon intracellular Ca2+ elevation. Here, we define the mode of action of Munc13-4 during Ca2+ evoked exosome secretion in RBL-2H3 mast cells. We show that Munc13-4 coupling to Rab27a is essential to retain Munc13-4 on secretory membranes for exosome release in mast cells, contrasting with cancer cells where the Munc13-4 Rab11 axis predominates. Using simultaneous epifluorescence and total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy validated by high pressure freezing electron microscopy, fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), and staged acute inhibition with Bexin 1, we demonstrate that Munc13-4 acts at the terminal post-docking stage of multivesicular body (MVB) exocytosis: acute Munc13-4 inhibition after vacuole formation leaves PM contact intact but abolishes fusion pore opening and destabilizes nascent pores. Moreover, depleting Rab27a while elevating Rab11 redirects Munc13-4 onto Rab11+ compartments in mast cells, recapitulating the cancer-cell phenotype. Together, our findings support a rapid-exchange, abundance weighted Rab partitioning model that tempers cellular Ca2+ responsiveness and governs cell type specific exosome fusion pathways, providing a mechanistic rationale for context selective modulation of pathological exosome release.

items.title: Population-scale measurement of human centromere array length variation from short-read sequencing
items.abstract: Alpha-satellite higher-order repeat (HOR) arrays at human centromeres vary several-fold in length across individuals and have been linked to kinetochore function and chromosome missegregation. However, their repetitive megabase-scale architecture has largely restricted length measurement to a few hundred long-read derived genome assemblies, leaving short-read cohorts uncharacterized. Here we introduce cenlen, an alignment-free method that estimates active centromeric array lengths across all 24 human chromosomes directly from short-read or long-read CRAM files. To estimate array lengths, we first identify $k$-mers that are common within a query chromosome's centromere array but rare across other chromosomes. For acrocentric and other repeat-sharing families lacking private k-mers, cenlen instead models shared k-mer mixtures against assembled pangenome reference profiles using non-negative linear deconvolution. Across 61 genomes that were not used for training, cenlen estimates agreed closely with assembled array lengths (median relative error 2.4%), outperforming existing short-read estimators. We further optimized sequence retrieval and targeted k-mer counting, reducing CPU time 313-fold relative to existing methods. We applied cenlen to 2,557 individuals across genetic ancestries from the 1000 Genomes Project. Most variation in array length occurred within populations, but arrays on chr21, chr7 and chr16 differed between superpopulations more than the average common SNV. Finally, we found that array lengths were associated with molecular phenotypes, including splicing of MED14 in chromosome X. Overall, cenlen makes it possible to test associations between centromere array length variation and human traits in large sequencing cohorts.

items.title: Genomic conformation reflects epigenetic programming rather than gene expression
items.abstract: Genome function is regulated temporally and tissue-specifically through coordinated interplay between epigenetic modifications and genomic elements, however, the extent to which chromatin conformation shapes or is shaped by epigenetic programming and transcriptional activity in vivo, remains largely unresolved. Through analysis of the well-characterised Dlk1-Dio3 imprinted domain, we have identified tissue and parent-of-origin specific conformations and taken a genetic approach to determine the hierarchical relationships between conformation, epigenetic state and transcription. Parental-origin specific topological domains identified in fetal brain are dependent on the germline-derived imprinting control region. In the absence of specific CTCF binding at a secondary imprinting control element, the parental origin-specific CTCF-mediated conformation can be disrupted without a change to domain-wide imprinting, transcription or epigenetic state. These findings indicate that, in this developmental context, conformation can be decoupled from transcription and that each can be independently governed by a hierarchy of epigenetically controlled regulatory features initiated in the germline.

items.title: A Framework for Identifying Determinants of Epigenomic State: Decoding Variable CTCF Occupancy and Contact Frequency
items.abstract: CTCF binding is essential for delineating topologically associated domains, constraining enhancer-promoter interactions, and controlling gene expression. Many CTCF peaks are bound in all cell-types, but the mechanisms regulating cell-type-specific CTCF occupancy are not fully understood. Here, we present a general framework to comprehensively discover factors driving variable epigenomic state and TF occupancy. We apply this framework to CTCF ChIP-seq binding across hundreds of cell/tissues, and we identify five distinct mechanisms regulating CTCF occupancy. In addition to known mechanisms of DNA methylation and cell-type-specific TF co-binding, we find that the largest set of variable-occupancy sites is modulated by CTCF expression levels. Variable peaks have weaker-affinity, and their occupancy is modulated by either higher CTCF levels or flanking TFs. We evaluate the predictive power on CTCF occupancy in held-out samples. Finally, we show that variable CTCF binding predicts differential contact frequency, chromatin loop structure, and upregulation of gene expression.

items.title: BPQ_RNA: A Thermodynamically Informed, Hybrid Quantum-Classical Framework for RNA 2D Structure Prediction Including Chemical Modifications
items.abstract: Predicting RNA secondary (2D) structural folds remains a Nondeterministic Polynomial-time (NP)-hard challenge. Existing quantum approaches predominantly rely on coarse-grained heuristics or classical stem pre-estimation, shifting core thermodynamic computations outside the quantum workflow and limiting localized structural precision. Here, we present a Base-Pair QUBO framework for RNA (BPQ_RNA), a hybrid pipeline that directly maps experimental Nearest Neighbor Database (NNDB)-derived free energies onto a gate-based quantum framework strictly at the base-pair level. This eliminates pre-assembly constraints and integrates chemical modifications with zero additional qubit overhead. Executed on a GPU-accelerated simulator with classical maturation for multi-body loops, BPQ_RNA resolves biological ground states within a 5-22 qubit footprint. Finally, we analyze a Variational Convergence Bound, demonstrate how uniform randomized multi-start initialization and multi-replica sampling aids navigation of rugged energy landscapes, and outline future directions for scaling to more complex RNA 2D folds and expanded modification libraries.

items.title: Learning Protein Structure Representations through Joint-Embedding Prediction
items.corresponding_institution: College of Pharmacy, Seoul National University, 1 Gwanak-ro, Gwanak-gu, Seoul 08826, Republic of Korea
items.abstract: Motivation: Protein structure representations are often learned by reconstructing coordinates, yet reconstruction quality does not necessarily track performance on biological prediction tasks. We therefore investigate whether joint-embedding prediction can capture information useful for biological prediction while retaining recoverable backbone geometry. Results: We introduce PS-JEPA, a self-supervised model that learns protein structure representations by predicting masked residue embeddings from visible backbone context. The encoder combines geometric graph encoding with bidirectional Mamba and is pretrained without a coordinate-reconstruction objective. On StructTokenBench, frozen PS-JEPA representations achieve a mean remote-homology macro F1 (x100) of 72.24, compared with 67.12 for GearNet-Edge, the strongest baseline for this category, while remaining competitive in functional and flexibility prediction. A separately trained decoder reconstructs backbones from these frozen representations, achieving a mean C RMSD of 1.61 [A] on 309 external test chains filtered to exclude sequence matches to training and reference data. In an exploratory test of unconditional generation, a learned latent prior with the same decoder yields 62 of 384 backbones (16.15%) that meet the computational designability criterion. Together, these results show that joint-embedding prediction can learn representations that support both biological prediction and backbone reconstruction. Availability and Implementation: https://github.com/ahexlwang/PS-JEPA

items.title: GRACE: Discrete Biological Sequence Optimization with Gradient-Resolved Adaptive Constrained Exploration
items.abstract: Machine learning increasingly enables biological sequence redesign for therapeutic and biotechnological applications by optimizing sequences for desired properties. However, improving one property can compromise another: for example, increasing enzyme activity may reduce stability, while enhancing regulatory DNA activity may diminish cell-type specificity. We formulate sequence redesign as a constrained optimization problem guided by learned predictive models, where a reference sequence is mutated to improve a predicted target property while keeping predicted auxiliary properties within specified tolerances of their reference values. To solve this problem, we introduce GRACE (Gradient-Resolved Adaptive Constrained Exploration), a method that optimizes discrete biological sequences using gradients from property predictors via a straight-through estimator. GRACE combines two complementary mechanisms: null-space projection, which removes target-gradient components that interfere with active constraints, and an augmented Lagrangian mechanism, which encourages feasibility after constraint violations. We evaluate GRACE across fourteen diverse tasks, including six protein optimization tasks (spanning activity, stability, and solubility), five DNA tasks (spanning cell-type-specific enhancer activity, heat-shock-responsive promoters, and tissue-selective splicing), and three RNA design tasks (spanning translation efficiency, RNA folding, and toehold-switch function). Across these tasks, GRACE consistently achieves larger improvements in predicted target properties than discrete and continuous baselines while satisfying predicted auxiliary constraints. Together, these results establish GRACE as a general framework for machine-learning-guided biological sequence redesign under competing property constraints.

items.title: scXOrGAN: A Generative Framework for Cross-Organ Single-Cell Transcriptomic Translation
items.corresponding_institution: Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology
items.abstract: Gene expression profiles of organs provide important insights into their health and disease states. However, while some organs can be sampled only through invasive procedures, others, such as blood, are readily accessible. Existing methods for predicting gene expression in one organ from another typically work with bulk or averaged profiles, obscuring cell specific differences. Translation at single-cell resolution is more challenging, because individual cells in the source and target organs lack direct correspondence. Here, we present scXOrGAN, a generative model that translates single-cell transcriptomes between two organs of the same individual using data that are unpaired at the cell level. scXOrGAN combines two variational autoencoders that share a latent space with cycle consistency, adversarial training and distribution matching. Across three organ pairs (ileum to rectum, blood to bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) in COVID-19, and blood to heart in heart failure), the generated gene expressions closely matched the real target cell profiles of held-out donors and preserved cell-to-cell variation. Notably, generated BALF macrophages exhibit expression of COVID-19-associated genes that are nearly absent in source blood cells, while generated cardiac fibroblasts express genes upregulated in heart failure.

items.title: A BMP-to-GREM1 cancer-associated fibroblast switch at the colorectal cancer invasive front, revealed by histology-anchored spatial transcriptomics
items.abstract: Which fibroblast state signals to tumour cells at the colorectal cancer invasive front, and from what distance, has not been resolved in human tissue, and spatial transcriptomics obscures the answer whenever tumour regions are defined from the expression being analysed and RNA is assigned to the wrong, neighbouring cell. We introduce a histology-anchored framework that segments cells from H&E (OmiCoreSeg), maps the tumour from H&E alone (OmiCoreTumorDetector; area under the ROC curve 0.91 against pathologist annotation) and returns RNA to the cell that made it (OmiCoreCloud). In three untreated stage II-IV colorectal adenocarcinomas profiled by Visium HD, Xenium and single-cell RNA-seq, with pre-registered tests carried to held-out patients, platforms and four bulk cohorts (1,319 patients), RNA spill reached only adjacent cells (8-12 um), stromal programmes varied over 400 um, and expression-defined tumour regions overstated immune exclusion three- to fivefold. Across the H&E border, cancer-associated fibroblasts switch from a BMP4/5-producing, telocyte-like state in the tumour bed to a GREM1-producing palisade with TGF-beta/SMAD3 and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) activity at the front (6/6 validation sections); adjacent tumour cells lose the BMP target ID1 (held-out odds ratio 0.47) and SMAD5 activity. No ligand-receptor pair was enriched at cell contact (0 of 1,233), whereas myeloid IL-1 and lymphoid LT coupled to fibroblast programmes at niche scale. A GREM1-fibroblast score was associated with shorter survival (hazard ratio 1.23), and unlike the mouse and organoid GREM1-ISLR model the human axis is one-sided. These maps nominate GREM1 neutralisation and IL-1 blockade as front-targeted therapeutic hypotheses and provide a spatial reference of the human colorectal cancer front.

items.title: Cost-information trade-offs partially rationalize the feed-forward loop census
items.abstract: Gene transcription regulatory networks let cells encode an internal representation of their environment as patterns of protein expression. Among the thirteen connected directed subgraphs on three nodes, the feed-forward loop (FFL) is the one consistently over-represented in transcriptional networks relative to randomizations that preserve the node degrees, yet its eight structural variants occur very unequally: in Escherichia coli and Saccharomyces cerevisiae the C1 and I1 variants dominate and the other six are rare. We ask whether the trade-off between cost and information in these architectures can rationalize this asymmetry. Each variant is treated as a noisy channel from the environment to the output expression level, with a channel capacity obtained from the Lyapunov equation of the linearized chemical Langevin dynamics and a protein burden from the mean of the regulated proteins at steady state. The analytical capacity agrees with mutual information estimated from Gillespie simulations across families, gates, and Hill coefficients. We compare the eight variants on the Pareto frontier of the cost-information plane under four information measures and ten promoter logics. Two results follow. First, only C1, C3, I1, and I3 are ever Pareto winners within their family, while C2, C4, I2, and I4 never win, consistent with their rarity; C1 robustly dominates the coherent family, in agreement with the census. Second, no measure separates I1 from I3 by more than a few percentage points, and the measures disagree on which is ahead, so cost and information treat the two as nearly equivalent. In the census, by contrast, I1 outnumbers I3 by 21:1 in S. cerevisiae. Cost and information thus account for the exclusion of four variants and for the dominance of C1, but not for the dominance of I1, whose separation from I3 may require a measure of response timing, which our measures of the environmental level do not probe.

items.title: Chinese hamster tissue and CHO cell transcriptomes reveal immortalization signatures and the factors driving lineage divergence
items.abstract: Chinese Hamster Ovary (CHO) cells dominate biotherapeutic manufacturing but still have a few limitations in post-translational modifications such as N-glycan branching, O-glycan core extension and inefficient protein folding/processing. It is yet unclear whether these CHO-specific traits reflect general Chinese hamster biology or arise specifically from cell line immortalization. We assembled a uniformly processed transcriptome compendium of 350 RNA-seq samples from 24 studies, integrating nine native Chinese hamster tissues with four CHO lineages (CHO-K1, CHO-S, CHO-DG44, CHO-DXB11). While CHO cells retain core proliferative and biosynthetic machinery when compared to Hamster tissues, it has undergone coordinated and selective loss of tissue-specific functions, and thus establishing these are immortalization-driven traits rather than general hamster-biology origin. Focused analysis of CHO cell lines further revealed that parental lineage and culture media as the dominant drivers of observed transcriptional heterogeneity where the cell identity is responsible for transcriptome variation in a higher proportion of genes. By integrating genome copy number or alternate promoter usage with gene expression data, we observed that while gene copy number variations contributions are almost negligible, alternate promoter usage governs the variation in about 20% of genes that showed cell line specific patterns while 60% had a buffering effect, indicating that additional, yet to be characterized regulatory layers drive CHO cell heterogeneity. Together, these findings establish a genomic and regulatory framework for understanding CHO lineage divergence, with direct implications for rational cell line selection and engineering in biotherapeutic manufacturing.

items.title: Brain rhythms during Instagram Reels viewing and subsequent performance on sustained attention and working memory: an EEG study
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Psychology, School of Behavioral Sciences, University of Social Welfare and Rehabilitation Sciences, Tehran, Iran
items.abstract: What does even a short scrolling 'snack' do to the brain? Short-form video feeds such as Instagram Reels have been rapidly becoming a near-universal phenomenon, used widely by people around the world, especially young adults. However, this is a very recent development, and yet their immediate effects on brain activity, attention, and working memory remain unclear. In a counterbalanced, within-subject experiment, we examined whether 10 minutes of Instagram Reels altered electroencephalographic (EEG) activity, cognitive performance, and subjective fatigue. Thirty university students completed three testing blocks separated by two counterbalanced interventions selected from viewing Reels on their own accounts, viewing a silent sequence of neutral images on their phones, or resting with eyes closed. EEG was recorded using 65 electrodes during interventions and subsequent sustained-attention (SART) and working-memory (N-back) tasks. Compared with neutral images, Reels viewing was associated with higher posterior relative theta power and a lower posterior alpha-to-theta ratio. During the subsequent N-back, frontal relative alpha was higher after Reels than after neutral images. Fatigue increased more after Reels than after rest. One of four planned contrasts in the cleaned sample was significant. Brief Reels viewing was associated with differences in EEG activity compared with viewing neutral images, while no significant differences in attention or working-memory performance were detected after correction for multiple comparisons.

items.title: Optimisation of femtosecond dispersion compensation at the sample using side-view two-photon fluorescence imaging
items.abstract: Efficient two-photon absorption depends on compensating the dispersion of the whole excitation path. Building on established fluorescence-based adjustment, we describe a practical procedure that uses side-view images of fluorescence in a dye cuvette, independently of the microscope's scanning and detection, with reference records, stability warnings and open analysis software. For a 1045 nm laser, maxima lay between 21 and 24 screw turns in 11 of 13 sweeps. For a 920 nm laser, fluorescence maxima at the sample differed by 1.63 kfs^2 on average from autocorrelation minima before the scan optics. The recordings also show limitations from signal instability and proximity to clipping. The procedure targets two-photon microscopes for in vivo imaging, such as of neuronal activity, where tissue heating limits the usable power; it may also apply to photostimulation and polymerisation paths.

items.title: Acute Effects of Prolonged Intermittent Theta Burst Stimulation on Cortical Excitability: A Randomized Crossover TMS-EEG Study
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Rehabilitation Sciences, The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, Hong Kong, China
items.abstract: Background: prolonged intermittent theta burst stimulation (piTBS), as used in Stanford Neuromodulation Therapy (SNT), achieves antidepressant efficacy, yet its acute single-session mechanisms remain elusive. EEG can capture online oscillatory dynamics during piTBS and pre- to post-stimulation changes in TMS-evoked cortical reactivity. Methods: in a randomized, sham-controlled crossover trial, 40 healthy males completed two visits ( [≥]7-day washout), receiving active or sham piTBS over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Inter-train EEG power was analyzed across three blocks of 20 trains in 37 participants. Pre- and post-stimulation measures of TMS-evoked potentials (TEPs), working memory and sustained attention were analyzed in all 40 participants. Results: left frontal theta power followed different trajectories across blocks during active and sham piTBS (conditionxblock interaction, p = .014). During active piTBS, theta power was below baseline in blocks 1 and 2 and increased significantly from block 2 to block 3. Across conditions, alpha power was lower in blocks 2 and 3 than in block 1. Direct comparison of pre-to-post TEP changes between active and sham piTBS identified no significant clusters in the N45, P60, N100 and P180 component windows. Exploratory analyses within active piTBS identified a decrease in frontal N100 cluster amplitude and an increase in posterior N100 cluster amplitude. Neither behavioral outcome showed condition-dependent changes. Conclusion: a single session of active piTBS modulated left frontal theta power between stimulation trains. Whether this early response is associated with cumulative plasticity or antidepressant outcomes following SNT warrants further investigation.

items.title: Scale-dependent predictability of microscopic brain structure from MRI using paired PS-OCT
items.corresponding_institution: Nanjing University of Posts and Telecommunications
items.abstract: Cortical layering, fascicle geometry and tissue texture of the mouse brain lie in the mesoscopic range. That range sits below the hundred-micrometre sampling of a whole-brain magnetic resonance (MR) volume and above the micrometre structure of individual fibre bundles. Polarization-sensitive optical coherence tomography (PS-OCT) reaches into it, and MRI does not. Super-resolution models can enlarge an MR volume to any grid, but the grid size does not decide what the volume contains. We take PS-OCT at 10 um isotropic sampling as the target and ask whether a 100 um MRI volume still carries information about each target band. At each candidate magnification we ask whether the source still determines something about the target band. Two readouts on a shared band index answer it. The bands come from an isotropic spherical-shell decomposition. The energy readout predicts a log-RMS energy envelope, which needs no unobservable phase, and a structural-tensor comparison separates geometric from intensity guidance, with the absolute cosine read against an analytic level of 0.50. On nine paired mouse brains the two readouts do not weaken together. The median absolute cosine falls from 0.864 at 1x to 0.661 at 4x and to 0.518 at 10x, while the R-squared of the energy envelope decays from 0.627 to 0.438 at 4x and to 0.175 at 10x. The two readouts part company at 4x, a target voxel of 25 um, the last of the six candidates at which both conditions hold. Each candidate interrogates a different physical scale. The curves therefore cannot carry a claim about a special frequency, and we report the boundary as the output of a procedure and not as a constant. Two further effects pull the readouts in opposite ways. One is intrinsic to the envelope kernel and accounts for part of the accelerated decay beyond 4x. The other comes from the smoothing applied to the reference before it is scored.

items.title: Focused Ultrasound Neuromodulation: Disentangling Neural Signals from Mechanical Artifacts
items.abstract: Transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS) can noninvasively modulate neural activity in the human brain (Blackmore et al., 2019; Fomenko et al., 2018; Legon et al., 2014), and EEG, with millisecond resolution, is well suited to track the timing of cortical engagement. In humans, tFUS aimed at primary visual cortex (V1) has been reported to evoke phosphenes, with EEG peaks (N55, P100) during sonication (Lee et al., 2016). Ultrasound can also activate cortex indirectly through the auditory pathway (Sato et al., 2018), although airborne sound from the transducer can be masked (Braun et al., 2020; Liang et al., 2023). Whether the N55 and P100 peaks reflect neuronal activation or artifacts (i.e., non-neuronal signals produced by the ultrasound itself) is unclear. We set out to ask whether EEG decoding could detect neural engagement during tFUS to V1 in eight participants receiving 150 or 300-ms pulses or sham. Decoding of tFUS versus sham reached as much as 93% for exactly the duration of each pulse (cluster p = .004 and .008), with no later cluster significant. But the same pulse-locked step appeared on all channels, scaled with drive, and was also recorded from a foam head and a forehead piezo pickup, identifying it as mechanical. Decoding during sonication must therefore be interpreted as a mechanical artifact rather than cortical engagement. EEG peaks observed within a pulse cannot on their own be taken as evidence of neural engagement. EEG studies of tFUS will need controls that reproduce the vibration without focusing on the brain, such as an active sham.

items.title: Conditional feature importance with error control for machine-learning-based biomarker discovery in Alzheimer's disease
authors: for the Swedish BioFINDER study group,
for the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative,
items.last_author: for the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative,
items.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is characterized by complex biology captured by proteomics, transcriptomics, genetics, and brain imaging. These high-dimensional and correlated data make biomarker discovery challenging. To disentangle biomedical AD data, we propose Conditional Feature Importance (CFI), a theory-grounded framework quantifying the unique contribution of individual or grouped variables in any machine learning model while controlling false discoveries. Across ADNI, BioFINDER, and UK Biobank (nearly 48,000 participants), CFI uncovered a striking contrast between unique versus redundant biomarkers across protein and imaging signatures of AD diagnosis, onset, and progression. Age and neurofilament light chain (NfL) were important for all three outcomes, and A{beta}42 was common to diagnosis and progression. Beyond these shared predictors, in BioFINDER, markers associated with neuronal and synaptic injury, including plasma total tau, CSF -synuclein, and CSF neurogranin, contributed unique predictive information for diagnosis, whereas markers related to the amyloid cascade, CSF p-tau181 and A{beta}40, contributed unique predictive information for progression. APOE {varepsilon}4 offered no unique information once downstream proteins were accounted for, whereas contextual markers such as CSF A{beta}40 emerged only through interactions with other biomarkers. We argue that CFI increases the scientific value of machine learning by providing rigorous statistical insights on complex datasets.

items.title: Microglia target parvalbumin-expressing interneurons and tune gamma oscillations through P2Y12-dependent IL-1 receptor signaling
items.abstract: Adaptation of neuronal network activity is critical for maintaining brain homeostasis and coping with changing computational demands. Microglia, the brain's innate immune cells, are increasingly recognized to shape neuronal function in the healthy brain, yet their contribution to inhibitory circuit dynamics and network synchronization remains largely unexplored. Here, we show that microglia establish a closed-loop feedback circuit that regulates synchronized network activity in the gamma frequency range, a key feature of cognitive processes that critically depends on fast-spiking parvalbumin-positive interneurons (PVIs). This mechanism operates in ex vivo mouse hippocampal and human neocortical circuits, indicating conservation across brain regions and species. During gamma oscillations, microglia preferentially recruit their processes to PVI somata through P2Y12 receptor-dependent purinergic signaling, whereas comparable targeting is absent around pyramidal neurons. Blockade of P2Y12 enhances gamma power, as does inhibition of interleukin-1 receptor type 1 (IL-1R1), an effect absent in P2Y12-deficient mice. P2Y12-IL-1R1 signaling functionally converges on adenosine A1 receptor activation, consistent with an IL-1{beta}-adenosine-mediated neuroimmune feedback mechanism. At the cellular level, adenosine reduces excitatory synaptic input onto PVIs, whereas IL-1{beta} attenuates their fast-spiking behavior. Together, our findings establish microglia as physiological regulators of inhibitory network synchronization, linking preferential interactions with PVIs to P2Y12-coupled cytokine signaling and homeostatic gain control of gamma oscillations.

items.title: Ongoing activity in anatomically recurrent cortex is predominantly feedforward
items.abstract: The cerebral cortex is the major site of computation in the brain, and its recurrent wiring has motivated models in which repeated neuronal activation maintains information in stable attractor states. Large language models illustrate an alternative principle by transforming information layer by layer during each forward pass. A first step toward understanding what cortex and these models can teach us about each other is to establish whether feedforward dynamics can predominate in recurrent cortex. Here, we show that ongoing activity in the frontal cortex of awake mice is composed of parabolic neuronal avalanches in which activity progresses mainly through newly recruited neurons. Using two-photon calcium imaging in hundreds of simultaneously recorded layer II/III pyramidal neurons, we decomposed avalanche size into the number of participating neurons, mean activations per participant, and mean inferred spikes per activation. Avalanche size grew approximately quadratically with duration up to 0.5 s, primarily through recruitment of additional neurons. Participating neurons contributed close to one spike per avalanche on average. Newly recruited neurons also dominated the rise and fall of the average avalanche profile. An unbiased recruitment model, in which all neurons have the same selection probability, accounted for the predominance of new over repeat participation, showing that feedforward recruitment can dominate even when previously active neurons remain available for reactivation. Parabolic avalanches thus express predominantly feedforward dynamics within anatomically recurrent cortex. Cortical computation may therefore have more in common with feedforward processing in large language models than recurrent anatomy alone would suggest.

items.title: Functional balance between inhibitory and disinhibitory pathways predicts the heterogeneous effects of arousal on cortical timescales
items.abstract: Cortical activity exhibits diverse timescales that vary with behavioral state, but the underlying circuit mechanisms remain unclear. Analyzing Allen Institute Neuropixels recordings from mouse primary visual cortex, we found that the fraction of excitatory neurons activated by optogenetic stimulation of somatostatin (SST) interneurons varied across mice. Intrinsic timescales lengthened during arousal in mice with a lower fraction of activated excitatory neurons and shortened in those with a higher fraction. To investigate a possible mechanism, we trained spiking networks with cell-type-specific plasticity, producing configurations dominated by direct SST inhibition of excitatory neurons or indirect disinhibition via parvalbumin interneurons. Arousal-like input to vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) interneurons slowed assembly dynamics, lengthened intrinsic timescales, and accelerated assembly formation when direct inhibition dominated, with opposite effects when indirect disinhibition dominated. Our results suggest that the balance between these pathways can account for opposite timescale responses to arousal and shape its computational consequences.

items.title: SHANK3-actin cytoskeleton coupling regulates nanoscale remodelling of the postsynaptic density
items.abstract: Dynamic remodelling of multiprotein signalling complexes allows cells to rapidly adapt signalling strength. At synapses, neurotransmitter receptors and scaffolds concentrate in subsynaptic nanoclusters that govern synaptic signalling strength and that are dynamically remodelled by synaptic activity. However, although this distinct nanoscale organization of synaptic protein complexes is well-established, the mechanisms that control the activity-induced reorganization of these complexes remain elusive. Here, to resolve the mechanisms underlying the activity-induced spatiotemporal reorganization of the PSD, we combined CRISPR/Cas9-mediated tagging of endogenous synaptic proteins and quantitative super-resolution microscopy. We found that synaptic potentiation drives a rapid and long-lasting increase in the number and density of PSD scaffold nanoclusters. Strikingly, activity-induced reorganization of scaffold proteins originated in deep PSD layers and preceded AMPA receptor repositioning, indicating that newly recruited receptors populate preformed scaffold nanoclusters. Computational simulations support that this reorganization is sufficient to drive potentiation of synaptic responses. Mechanistically, we found that the interaction between the scaffold SHANK3 and the actin cytoskeleton is essential for activity-induced PSD nanocluster remodelling. Altogether, our findings present a novel mechanism through which cytoskeletal interactions remodel the spatial organization of the PSD, advancing our understanding of how the dynamic nanoscale reorganization of protein complexes can drive neuronal signalling.

items.title: Mechanical role of dural structures and tumor material heterogeneity in brain tumor mass effect
items.abstract: Brain tumor growth induces considerable deformation of the surrounding tissue, yet the mechanical contribution of intracranial dural structures and the influence of tumor material heterogeneity on mass effect remain poorly understood. In this study, we developed a heterogeneous finite element model of the brain to investigate the mechanical role of the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli and to determine how variations in tumor subregion stiffness influence the mechanical response of the brain. Two complementary analyses were performed. First, synthetic lesion models with and without the falx and tentorium were compared under otherwise identical conditions. Inclusion of these structures produced only minor changes in global displacement magnitude, but substantially altered the spatial distribution of stress. The dural structures acted as stiff internal partitions that limited interhemispheric and supratentorial-infratentorial deformation and modified load transmission throughout the brain. Including the dural structures led to a different pattern of ventricular volume change during tumor growth, with both lateral ventricles compressed in the dura-included model, whereas without the dura the ventricle on the tumor side expanded while the opposite ventricle was compressed. Second, a parametric analysis was performed using MRI-informed patient-specific tumors comprising necrotic tumor core (NTC), contrast-enhancing tumor core (ETC), and peritumoral edema (Ed). Variations in ETC stiffness produced the largest and most spatially distributed changes in displacement and von Mises stress, with stronger effects in ETC-dominant tumors. Edema stiffness produced weaker and more diffuse effects, whereas NTC stiffness mainly affected the principal stretch within the tumor. These findings demonstrate that intracranial dural structures alter the distribution of tumor-induced deformation and stress despite their limited influence on global displacement magnitude. In the patient-specific models, varying the tumor stiffness within its reported range changed the mechanical response by only a few percent, with the ETC having the largest influence.

items.title: Neutrophil lectin-like oxidized low-density lipoprotein receptor (LOX-1) limits inflammatory injury during bacterial pneumonia.
items.abstract: Pneumonia is an inflammatory condition that is caused by myriad microorganisms, necessitating broadly applicable therapeutics. Yet, host determinants of pneumonia severity remain poorly understood, demanding a more complete understanding of the cells and signals that control tissue homeostasis. Our group previously showed that the class E scavenger receptor lectin-like oxidized low-density lipoprotein receptor-1 (LOX-1) limits pneumonia-induced lung injury without affecting bacterial clearance, contrasting its well-established injurious effects in the setting of atherosclerosis. These findings indicate that location and cell type are key determinants of LOX-1 function, but cell-specific sources of LOX-1-mediated lung protection are unknown. Here, we show that a portion of lung-recruited neutrophils are stimulated to express LOX-1 upon entry into the airspaces of humans and mice during pneumonia. Neutrophil LOX-1 expression correlates with higher levels of chemokine and scavenger receptors, reactive oxygen species, and apoptotic markers that likely influence their phenotype and potentially those of neighboring cells. To determine whether neutrophil LOX-1 contributes to LOX-1-dependent tissue protection, we generated neutrophil-specific LOX-1 knockout mice (LOX-1{Delta}MRP8) and assessed their acute response to two models of bacterial pneumonia, Escherichia coli and Streptococcus pneumoniae. Elevated metrics of inflammation were detected in LOX-1{Delta}MRP8 mice following both challenges, including reduced survival during E. coli infection, without changes in bacterial clearance. Finally, deletion of LOX-1 on neutrophils resulted in modifications to the neutrophil phenotype that may contribute to increased recruitment and inflammatory potential in the airspace. Taken together, LOX-1 is a scavenger receptor that is induced on a population of neutrophils in the pneumonic airspaces, taming further neutrophilic inflammation to limit immunopathology.

items.title: Stk11 deficiency promotes tumor CXCL16 secretion and a CXCL16-dependent expansion of Aregpos CXCR6pos Vγ6 γδT17 in lung cancer
items.abstract: IL-17-producing gamma delta ({gamma}{delta}T17) T cells can promote tumor growth and metastasis. How the tumor microenvironment controls the activation, expansion, and function of {gamma}{delta}T17 in different cancers remains unclear. Using an autochthonous model of KrasG12D/Stk11-driven lung adenocarcinoma coupled with scRNAseq and V(D)J profiling, we found that KrasG12DStk11-loss tumors induced a rapid expansion of lung CXCR6+ V{gamma}4 and amphiregulin-expressing CXCR6+ V{gamma}6{gamma}{delta}T17 cells. Single-cell immune profiling of the KrasG12DStk11-loss tumors revealed a prominent Krt8+ alveolar epithelial cell (KAC) tumor subtype enriched in a number of immune-relevant genes, including Cxcl16 and its sheddase Adam10, and in vitro culture revealed that KACs, but not their normal epithelial cell counterparts, secreted CXCL16. Finally, we found that in vivo blockade of CXCL16 inhibited the expansion of lung V{gamma}6+ {gamma}{delta}T17 in response to KrasG12DStk11-loss tumors. Together, these data suggest that Stk11 loss promotes a CXCL16-secreting Krt8+ KAC tumor subtype, and that CXCL16-CXCR6 interactions are necessary to drive the expansion of pro-tumor {gamma}{delta}T17 cells in lung cancer.

items.title: CNS-derived SerpinA3n restricts pathogenesis during WNV encephalitis via suppression of inflammatory protease activity
items.abstract: Proteolytic activity is integral to host immune defense, yet little is known about how proteolytic homeostasis is maintained in the central nervous system (CNS) during viral infection. Here, we investigated roles for the serine protease inhibitor SerpinA3n in promoting host protection during West Nile virus (WNV) encephalitis. WNV neuroinvasion was accompanied by widespread induction of serpin expression, including SerpinA3n. Pharmacological inhibition of SerpinA3n within the CNS, but not in the periphery, exacerbated mortality, whereas CNS supplementation with recombinant SerpinA3n improved survival, preserved blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, and reduced proteolytic activity and leukocyte accumulation without altering CNS viral burden. Using cell-type-specific genetic deletion, we identified astrocytes and neurons as major sources of SerpinA3n in the infected CNS. Loss of SerpinA3n from either cell population increased mortality, BBB permeability, and gelatinase/collagenase activity. However, loss of neuronal, but not astrocytic, SerpinA3n exacerbated leukocyte accumulation and antigen-presenting cell activation, suggesting that the cellular context of SerpinA3n production influences its immunoregulatory functions. Both astrocyte- and neuron-derived SerpinA3n restrained granzyme B activity in the infected CNS, and neutralization of granzyme B reversed the excess mortality associated with pharmacological inhibition of SerpinA3n. Together, these findings identify serpin-mediated regulation of inflammatory protease activity as a mechanism of host protection during viral encephalitis and establish both neurons and astrocytes as important contributors to the maintenance of proteolytic homeostasis in the inflamed CNS.

items.title: CD33-CAR iNKT cells overcome acute myeloid leukemia heterogeneity by activating CD8+ T cells and enhancing tumor immunogenicity
items.corresponding_institution: Division of Hematology, Department of Oncology, Geneva University Hospitals
items.abstract: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) exhibits extensive inter- and intra-patient antigenic heterogeneity, representing a major obstacle for chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-based therapies. Cellular platforms that combine potent direct cytotoxicity with the ability to engage endogenous immune responses may help overcome this limitation. Invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells are particularly attractive for allogeneic immunotherapy because of their lack of alloreactivity and their capacity to promote cross-priming of conventional T cells. To exploit these properties in AML, we generated CD33-directed CAR iNKT cells and demonstrated direct antitumor activity against CD33-expressing AML cells both in vitro and in vivo. Using an in vitro mixed-tumor model composed of parental CD33-expressing and CD33-knockout MOLM-14 cells we show that CD33-CAR iNKT cells efficiently eliminated CD33-positive leukemia cells but did not directly control the growth of CD33-knockout cells. However, the addition of conventional T cells, particularly CD8 T cells, together with CD33-CAR iNKT cells resulted in robust T-cell activation and subsequent control of CD33-knockout MOLM-14 cells. Importantly, CD33-CAR iNKT cells induced marked phenotypic changes in antigen-negative leukemia cells, including upregulation of HLA class I and class II molecules, suggesting increased immunogenicity. Finally, we recapitulated both the antitumor and immunomodulatory effects of CD33-CAR iNKT cells in primary bone marrow samples from patients with newly diagnosed AML. Collectively, these findings show that CD33-CAR iNKT cells can promote CD8 T-cell immunity against AML and support a therapeutic strategy capable of extending antitumor activity beyond the targeted antigen, thereby helping to overcome antigenic heterogeneity.

items.title: Caspase Activity Affects Cell Cycle and Chromosome Integrity after Genome Editing in Human Hematopoietic Stem and Progenitor Cells
items.abstract: Therapeutic genome editing introduces DNA double-strand breaks into hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs), making chromosome integrity an important consideration for edited cell function. We investigated how caspase activity influences cellular responses to genome editing in primary human HSPCs. Caspase inhibition increased the fraction of phospho-histone H3-S10-positive cells and reduced micronucleus formation and DNA damage after editing. Genome editing was associated with reduced detection of BUB1 and H2A-T120p at centromeres, with partial restoration after caspase inhibition. Genetic disruption of BUB1 did not fully reproduce the effects of editing, and caspase inhibition continued to increase the phospho-histone H3-S10-positive fraction in BUB1-deficient cells. p53 suppression reduced micronucleus formation without increasing this fraction, distinguishing its effects from those of caspase inhibition. After xenotransplantation, recipients of HSPCs exposed to caspase inhibition in vitro had increased bone marrow cellularity and total CD34+ cell numbers. These findings identify caspase activity as a determinant of cell cycle and chromosome integrity outcomes after genome editing in human HSPCs.

items.title: A bacterial pathogen reveals a new mechanism of micron-scale nucleocytoplasmic transport
items.abstract: In addition to its canonical role as a selective barrier, the nuclear envelope is increasingly recognized as a dynamic structure, remodeled to integrate mechanical cues. Here, we discover that the bacterial pathogen Rickettsia parkeri deforms the nuclear envelope to an unprecedented degree to invade and exit human cell nuclei through large membrane protrusions. This extreme envelope remodeling is tolerated in part due to a bacterial protein that associates with the nuclear membrane and promotes nuclear infection, along with a mechanosensitive host enzyme that releases a signaling molecule from deformed nuclei. These findings establish a new mechanism of nucleocytoplasmic transport that redefines the size limits of nuclear envelope deformation cells can tolerate and resolves a long-standing question of how micron-scale cargo, such as bacteria, enter nuclei.

items.title: Limited biological identifiability of dominance-labelled variance components in polyploid genomic prediction
items.abstract: Genomic prediction models for polyploid crops often partition genetic variance into additive and dominance-labelled components, but a fitted dominance component is not necessarily identifiable as digenic dominance (D2). We combined known-truth simulations with a panel-conditioned diagnostic workflow on 11 public datasets from alfalfa, potato, blueberry, guinea grass, rose, Miscanthus, sweetpotato and sugarcane. The workflow uses kernel geometry, permutation references, structure controls, planted-D2 spike-ins, posterior uncertainty and paired prediction tests. In autotetraploid simulations, the standard additive-plus-dominance model assigned appreciable variance to the dominance kernel when true D2 was absent, and its share responded only weakly to planted D2 signal. In crop panels, additive and dominance kernels were highly collinear, and Bayesian degree-kernel decompositions did not localize non-additive variance to D2, although restricted maximum likelihood placed it on D2 in alfalfa and potato. Observed shares exceeded matched permutation references by more than the pre-set margin in two of nine autotetraploid datasets, and no dataset met the criteria for biological D2 interpretation. A large fitted share was not sufficient for cross-validated prediction gain. We recommend reporting these components with diagnostics that separate biologically supported dominance, prediction-useful kernels and unresolved model-basis contributions.

items.title: AHCY inhibition reshapes DNA methylation and transcriptional regulation in colorectal cancer cells
items.corresponding_institution: Applied Tumor Genomics Research Program, Faculty of Medicine, University of Helsinki, Finland
items.abstract: DNA methylation is an important epigenetic mechanism regulating gene expression, and its maintenance depends on cellular methyl group metabolism. Adenosylhomocysteinase (AHCY) is a key enzyme in the methionine cycle that hydrolyzes S-adenosylhomocysteine (SAH), thereby preventing its accumulation and inhibition of methyltransferase activity. Although AHCY has been implicated in cancer cell proliferation and transcriptional regulation, the effects of its inhibition on genome-wide DNA methylation and their relationship to gene expression remain poorly understood in colorectal cancer (CRC). Here, we investigated the consequences of pharmacological AHCY inhibition in GP5d colorectal cancer cells by integrating metabolomic profiling, nanopore sequencing-based DNA methylation analysis and RNA sequencing. AHCY inhibition resulted in SAH accumulation, widespread DNA hypomethylation and reduced cell proliferation, accompanied by changes in purine metabolism and gene expression. Despite the overall loss of DNA methylation, localized hypermethylation was also observed, particularly at CpG-rich regulatory regions. Transcriptomic analysis revealed changes in proliferation-associated and cell cycle checkpoint pathways, including strong upregulation of the cell cycle regulator CDKN1A. Importantly, promoter hypomethylation was significantly enriched among upregulated genes, including genes involved in cell cycle regulation, whereas gene body hypomethylation showed no comparable association with differential gene expression. Together, these findings demonstrate that AHCY inhibition induces extensive metabolic, epigenetic and transcriptional changes in CRC cells and suggest that promoter hypomethylation may contribute to the transcriptional responses associated with reduced cell proliferation.

items.title: Genotoxic stress and clonal expansion shape the somatic genome of systemic sclerosis skin
items.abstract: Background: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a life-limiting inflammatory disease characterised by skin and visceral fibrosis. We previously showed that fibrotic skin from patients with diffuse cutaneous SSc (dcSSc) accumulates a large number of somatic mutations, although the mechanisms that generate them and their disease-related consequences remain poorly understood. We investigated the burden, clonal architecture and biological significance of somatic mutations in dermal sections from patients with dcSSc ( 25 %) had a sequence linked with oxidative guanine damage (C>A), pointing to ongoing DNA damage and cellular stress. The C>A burden was higher in dcSSc than in lcSSc and correlated with the modified Rodnan skin score - a clinical measurement of skin fibrosis severity. Variant burden increased with patient age but not with disease duration. AHSCT did not change the mutational landscape. Conclusions: Fibrosis skin in SSc is characterized by a widespread somatic mosaicism generated by ongoing mutagenesis attributable to oxidative DNA damage. Persistence of mutant clones after regression of fibrosis argues against their being sufficient drivers of the fibrotic phenotype and identifies the somatic genome as a record of cellular injury.

items.title: The genome sequence of the reef-building coral Cyphastrea microphthalma from the Persian/Arabian Gulf
items.abstract: We present a genome assembly from the coral species Cyphastrea microphthalma from the southern Persian/Arabian Gulf (Cnidaria; Anthozoa; Hexacorallia; Scleractinia; Merulinidae). The assembly is 681.2 Mb in size, spanning 5,554 scaffolds with a contig N50 of 244.4 kb. The assembly has a BUSCO completeness of 94.1% (single = 85.1%, duplicated = 9%, fragmented = 1.6%, missing = 4.3%) using the metazoa_odb10 reference set (n = 954). Genome annotation identified 24,716 protein-coding genes (including 10 pseudogenes) and a high repeat content of 63.4%. The mitochondrial genome has also been assembled and is 17.9 kb in length.

items.title: A stratified benchmark reveals distinct short- and long-read performance gradients within difficult genomic regions
items.abstract: Accurate detection of small variants underpins population, functional and clinical genomics, yet short-read sequencing remains unreliable in repetitive and duplicated regions of the human genome, where long reads provide substantially greater sequence context. Although this disparity is well documented, aggregate accuracy metrics delineate where short- and long-read callsets diverge but not the mechanisms that give rise to these differences. Here, we present a region-stratified benchmark of single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) and insertion--deletion (INDEL) detection from Illumina short-read and PacBio HiFi long-read sequencing of the Genome in a Bottle reference sample HG002, evaluating multiple variant callers across genomic contexts, sequencing depths and INDEL lengths. Both platforms achieved near-complete accuracy in high-confidence regions, whereas short-read performance deteriorated in low-mappability regions and segmental duplications, a deficit that persisted with increasing sequencing depth. Within these regions, short-read recall declined toward the interiors of long tracts, with increasing sequence identity to the closest paralog and with greater distance from paralogous sequence variants, and these declines coincided with a pronounced excess of ambiguously placed reads. Together, these findings implicate ambiguous read placement as the predominant source of the short-read deficit, demonstrate that its magnitude can be anticipated from the length and paralog similarity of the surrounding sequence, and thereby delineate the genomic contexts in which long-read sequencing is most warranted.

items.title: Robust single-cell analysis through subsampling reveals hidden naive T cell states in aging
items.corresponding_institution: Division of Computational Medicine, Department of Medicine, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA
items.abstract: Single-cell genomics has been instrumental for studying the variation between cell states. Yet, the use of single-cell technologies to study variation between sample groups remains challenging, with findings often failing to replicate across cohorts. Here, we introduce a general framework for robust single-cell analysis that uses subsampling of individuals to identify statistical patterns that hold regardless of which unmeasured characteristics of those individuals covary with the condition of interest. Within this framework, a t-test for differential expression, a chi-squared test for differential composition, and a linear projection for contrastive representation learning outperform state-of-the-art alternatives in cross-cohort replicability. This identifies robustness by design, rather than refined distributional assumptions and model expressiveness, as a principal driver of reproducible discovery in single-cell studies. Applying robust contrastive learning to naive CD4 T cells from human blood, we uncover eleven replicating age-associated subpopulations, largely uncharacterized, that express programs of other states and go undetected by standard analysis. One of them is most strongly defined by CTLA4, a checkpoint receptor considered a hallmark of antigen-experienced and regulatory T cells, yet carries a naive surface phenotype and is distinct from regulatory T cells. This population is conserved in mice and increases in frequency with age in both the CD4 and CD8 compartments. Upon stimulation, these cells exhibit attenuated proliferation compared with conventional naive T cells and enrichment of regulatory phenotypes. Blocking CTLA4 signaling largely restores the downstream activation program to that of conventional naive cells, suggesting these cells may be a reversible contributor to the age-associated decline in naive T-cell responsiveness. By prioritizing robustness over richer models, our framework enables discovery of previously hidden cellular heterogeneity and offers a general strategy for improving resolution and replicability in single-cell genomics. Code is available at github.com/robust-precision-medicine.

items.title: Argonomics Explorer: an interactive database for dissecting Argonaute-RNA regulatory networks
items.abstract: Argonaute (AGO) family proteins associate with small RNAs (sRNAs) to form complexes that direct sequence-specific regulation of target RNAs. Recent studies in Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila melanogaster, and human cell lines have systematically characterized the repertoire of sRNA associations and targets for individual AGOs in these organisms; however, the lack of an accessible, searchable platform limits efficient comparison of the specificity and redundancy of Argonaute functions. Here, we present Argonomics Explorer (AE), an interactive database suite that integrates publicly available sRNA sequencing datasets to enable systematic interrogation of AGO-sRNA and AGO-target interactions across common model systems. AE combines independent AGO-IP datasets, AGO mutant-derived sRNA profiles, and systematic analyses to provide a cross-validated framework for examining AGO-RNA interactions. This database empowers users to query specific AGOs, transcripts, or sRNAs, and to compare associated sRNAs or targets across AGOs. Specifically, we recapitulate findings that certain microRNA (miRNA) star strands are uniquely loaded onto AGO-2 but not AGO-1 in flies. In addition, we report a preferential association of most members of the mir-35 family with the worm Argonaute ALG-2 and the association of the oncogenic oncomiR-1 miRNA superfamily with human AGO2. Such applications illustrate how the AE framework facilitates investigations into AGO specificity, redundancy, and the broader regulatory networks that shape gene expression. The Argonomics Explorer suite is freely available at https://cosbi10.ee.ncku.edu.tw/AE/.

items.title: Automated benchmarking with structured variant effect data
items.abstract: Protein variant effect prediction (VEP) has a wide range of applications, from describing the role of mutations in human disease to improving enzymes for industrial applications. VEP is now predominantly powered by machine learning models and high-throughput experimentation. Progress in this field depends on fair and systematic model comparison, which is complicated by the heterogeneity of VEP tasks and the diversity of model implementations. ProteinGym is the most widely used VEP benchmark, but it does not have a standard representation for datasets or models. This makes it difficult for others to run their own benchmarks with it and for the benchmark to keep up with new datasets and models. We address these shortcomings with the ProteinGym framework (PGF), which standardizes dataset representations, model interfaces, and evaluation protocols. The PGF consists of two packages: proteingym-base, which provides schemas for composing datasets and the PGDATA archive format, a standardized representation of VEP datasets, and proteingym-benchmark, which provides automated benchmarking of containerized models. As an example of a new experiment, we use the PGF to measure the ability of three supervised models to identify variants with property values that exceed those in the training set, a common objective in protein engineering. The PGF is available at https://github.com/ProteinGym.

items.title: RBAi Scholar: Semantic and Hybrid biomedical literature Search for Researchers and AI assistants
items.abstract: Motivation: A keyword search for mitochondrial dysfunction can miss a paper that says impaired mitochondrial function, so an empty result does not show that no such paper exists. Search by meaning addresses this mismatch, but it blurs exact strings such as gene symbols. Results: We present RBAi Scholar, which lets researchers and AI assistants search a growing corpus of biomedical abstracts by meaning (semantic search), by keyword, or by meaning among the papers that contain a required term (hybrid search). We tested it on a fixed version of 11.1 million records. For 500 questions worded unlike their target papers, semantic search placed the target in the top ten for 65.0%, against 18.6% for LitSense 2.0 and 0.8% for PubMed. OpenAlex semantic search, documented as using GTE-Large-EN embeddings, reached 27.8%. It reached 45.8% after OpenAlex rebuilt it with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, the model RBAi Scholar uses. Semantic search also led on the 380 held-out targets, which played no part in its design. Given one required term from the paper, hybrid search reached 93.9% on 328 held-out targets, against 42.1% for LitSense 2.0 with the same term. For 86 queries made of a paper's rarest identifier, such as a gene symbol, and two title words, keyword search reached 79.1%, against 34.9% for semantic search. When a blinded language-model judge graded the relevance of each system's top ten results, semantic search returned the most relevant results (nDCG@10 0.651 against 0.592 for OpenAlex semantic search with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B). Hybrid search ranked the target first more than twice as often as semantic search (50.0% against 23.3%). When we re-ran the searches for target papers on two cheaper index implementations and on the live service at 24.6 million records, every comparison kept its direction.

items.title: Adaptive Representations for Real-World Enzyme Optimization
items.abstract: Protein fitness landscapes are highly rugged, giving rise to complex optimization landscapes. Bayesian optimization (BO) with Gaussian processes (GPs) is widely used in protein engineering for its sample efficiency and calibrated uncertainty estimates. Here, we study a joint fine-tuning framework of a protein language model (PLM) and a GP across enzyme fitness landscapes that span various distinct mutation regimes encountered in real-world engineering campaigns. Joint fine-tuning optimizes the PLM and GP parameters together in an uncertainty-calibrated manner, providing an adaptive representation that utilizes the information from previously acquired points in addition to the existing knowledge from pretraining. Across seven combinatorial enzyme landscapes, this approach yields a median relative improvement in top-5% coverage of 45% over one-hot encoding and 120% over mean-pooled static ESM-C embeddings.
