We further explore several new pooling strategies beyond standard mean pooling within the joint fine-tuning framework and show that mutation-site pooling, which localizes the representation to mutated residues, is the most consistent performer across all landscapes, outperforming both established baselines and alternative pooling schemes. Finally, we show that the finetuned approach makes more effective use of training-split information, yielding better coverage across test-split BO rounds. These results suggest that adapting the representation during a campaign, rather than fixing it in advance, is the better design choice for BO-guided enzyme engineering.

items.title: AUTOENCODIX: powering a hub for biological representation learning models
items.corresponding_institution: Center for Scalable Data Analytics and Artificial Intelligence (ScaDS.AI) Dresden/Leipzig, Leipzig University, Germany
items.abstract: Autoencoders are a foundational architecture for biological representation learning and empower methods for denoising, multi-modal integration, explainable embeddings, and synthetic data generation. But, new architectures are scattered across isolated repositories, which hampers benchmarking, the reuse of pretrained models, and the transfer to new data modalities. Here, we present the next generation of AUTOENCODIX, a Python package and model hub for biological representation learning. Its modular, standardized API unifies preprocessing, training, hyperparameter optimization, evaluation, generation, and explanation across a growing set of architectures, now including disentangled, masked, semi-supervised, and 2D/3D image autoencoders. To demonstrate its use at scale, we tuned, trained, and benchmarked 15 large autoencoders on a balanced corpus of 3.7 million human cells from CELLxGENE, including nine ontology-based variational autoencoders whose latent dimensions represent core cellular functions and were defined by three large language models (LLMs). The biological-informed embeddings performed on par with classical Principal Component Analysis in downstream classification while being explainable by design, and in synthetic data generation they produced more biologically plausible error profiles than conventional variational autoencoders. Finally, AUTOENCODIX offers a new and unique combination of three pillars of explainability: by-design with biologically-informed latent dimensions, post-hoc gene-to-latent attribution scoring, and LLM-based knowledge integration for verbal description and hypothesis generation. AUTOENCODIX is open-source, open for community extensions and all pretrained models are available via Hugging Face for application on other single-cell gene expression data.

items.title: Resplitting LIT-PCBA with MolSCISSOR: A Memory-Efficient, Quasi-Deterministic Framework for Reducing Structural and Physicochemical Biases
items.corresponding_institution: Universite Paris Cite, CNRS UMR 8251, INSERM ERL 1133
items.abstract: Reliable training-test partitioning is essential for developing and evaluating virtual screening (VS) methods, particularly in the era of machine learning (ML). However, existing molecular dataset splitting approaches do not simultaneously address key challenges in rigorous VS evaluation: cross-partition structural bias, test-set inter-class physicochemical bias, high memory requirements, limited scalability, stochastic allocation, a lack of automated optimization and of flexible training-test similarity control. We introduce MolSCISSOR, a lightweight, memory-efficient, quasi-deterministic framework for stratified data partitioning that integrates clustering and training-test allocation through multi-objective optimization. MolSCISSOR is used to repartition LIT-PCBA, a well-established VS benchmark comprising 15 target-specific datasets of experimentally confirmed actives and inactives, exhibiting substantial class imbalance, many of which are large-scale. We show that simple baseline ML models achieve significantly above-chance screening performance on the original AVE-derived partitions, indicating residual biases. The MolSCISSOR-generated benchmark, SPLIT-PCBA, is more challenging than both the AVE variant and that obtained using a BitBIRCH-Lean clustering-based workflow, with stricter cross-partition structural separation and improved physicochemical balance between test-set actives and inactives. MolSCISSOR mitigates stochastic variability, requires less memory than AVE, Lo-Hi and DataSAIL, and supports multiple split configurations with varying cross-partition similarity. MolSCISSOR and SPLIT-PCBA are freely available at https://github.com/caominhtr/molscissor and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23942580.

items.title: Capturing human expertise for AI-assisted molecular structure annotation
items.corresponding_institution: Skaggs School of Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences, University of California San Diego, La Jolla, CA, USA
items.abstract: We developed a large language model-based tool that captures expert reasoning in bile acid structure elucidation, drawing on hand written notebooks, scientific literature, and recorded voice-to-text analytical sessions. It generates human-readable reports detailing evidence for and against candidate structures, tracing each inference to its source and identifying ambiguities. When applied to data, the tool proposes bile acid conjugates lacking reference spectra.

items.title: A Genome-Scale Virtual Escherichia coli in the L++ Language
items.abstract: A virtual organism is a computational model, mechanistic or learned from data, that predicts how a living system grows, adapts and responds to genetic edits, drugs and environments. As a first step toward such a model, we are building a virtual Escherichia coli, and here we present its first version, E. coli version 1.0, written for K-12 MG1655 in the L++ programming language. The model writes the cell as a biologist reads it, in one cell definition that compiles to 33,246 species and 41,649 reactions over 4,484 gene loci. Every gene's transcription, translation and decay are written out, for 4,196 of the 4,374 transcribed genes with the gene's own nucleotide and residue counts from the genome sequence, so the proteins that give E. coli its identity and functions, from metabolic enzymes to the machinery that replicates, divides and builds the cell, are each made from their own gene, with the promoter constants of 2,016 genes set toward measured protein abundances. The code wires 360 of 377 essential-gene candidates into processes that growth needs, among them all 293 that at least two genome-wide screens call essential; 177 of the 360 are read by gates and slowdowns written from those screens' calls, so for them the model's requirement follows the screens by construction. Twenty-eight two-component systems are written, and on development versions the two built from measured constants, for osmolarity and phosphate, reproduce the direction of their responses and the promoter order their constants were set to give. In a modified rich medium the cell divides every 1,100 to 1,400 s, at a pace set by a replication rate chosen to fit a 20-minute cycle. Of 95 metabolite pools measured in glucose minimal medium, 78 start within tenfold of measurement, 82 lie within it over t=1,000 to 3,000 s and 65 over t=10,000 to 20,000 s, and the model states where it does not yet match, among them 31 pools held at fixed values. Because the organism is code, a deletion, a retuned promoter or an added module is an edit, so one model serves both to understand the cell and to design its variants, and we hope to extend it toward a complete virtual E. coli together with scientists who bring their expertise and measurements.

items.title: HapAdapter: A Transfer Learning Protocol for DNA Foundation Models Adapted to Diploid Personal Epigenomes
items.abstract: The rapid rise of large language models (LLMs) has spurred the development of genomic language models (gLMs) that capitalize on the key features of natural language present in biological sequences. Moreover, DNA foundation models, a sub-class of gLMs, have demonstrated impressive accuracy in predicting a wide range of functional tracks from DNA sequence input. However, current DNA foundation models are exclusively trained on haploid reference genome sequences -- despite personal and graph genomes becoming the new standard for genomic analyses. This is principally because the cost to train gLMs on a personal diploid genome for a single individual is not currently practical. To help reconcile this disconnect between the current available use-cases of DNA foundation models with the modern direction of genomic sequence analysis, we present HapAdapter, a transfer-learning protocol that builds a small Siamese network on top of any pre-trained foundation model to enable inference from full diploid personal genome context. To demonstrate the utility of this method, we train a set of HapAdapter heads to predict allele-specific effects across assays on two representative foundation model backbones: DNABERT-2 and AlphaGenome. We demonstrate that our lightweight adapter more than doubles DNABERT-2's allele-specific discrimination and triples AlphaGenome's (130% and 210% gain in AUROC above chance, respectively, averaged over nine assays).

items.title: Inferring transcriptional bursting dynamics from scSLAM-seq data
items.corresponding_institution: Faculty of Informatics and Data Science, University of Regensburg, Regensburg, Germany | Institute of Virology and Immunobiology, Julius-Maximilians-Universitae
items.abstract: Transcription is a bursty, stochastic process. How transcriptional regulators reshape bursting dynamics during cellular responses remains poorly understood, largely because most single-cell RNA sequencing experiments measure only steady-state RNA abundance. Here, we present buRst, a probabilistic framework that infers burst frequency, burst size, and RNA degradation rates from metabolically labeled single-cell RNA sequencing (scSLAM-seq) during acute perturbations, without assuming steady state. It jointly models labeling measurements and RNA dynamics, propagating uncertainty from sparse labeling data into kinetic estimates. We applied buRst to acute MYC depletion in two melanoma cell lines. MYC amplified burst size in a manner scaling with its promoter occupancy, whereas it reduced burst frequency genome-wide, independently of occupancy. As a result, only strongly bound genes showed net activation, reconciling models of MYC as a selective activator and as a global amplifier of transcription.

items.title: GeneArbiter improves plant genome annotations while preserving established gene models
items.corresponding_institution: National Key Laboratory of Crop Genetic Improvement
items.abstract: As plant genome resources expand, updating established annotations requires incorporating improved gene models without disrupting correct structures or stable identifiers. We developed GeneArbiter, an evidence guided framework that treats annotation updating as a correction preservation problem. GeneArbiter uses the current annotation as a backbone, integrates alternative models with RNA splice junction and homologous protein evidence, and applies constrained language model arbitration followed by deterministic release and identifier reconciliation. In rice MH63, GeneArbiter recovered 4,701 reference loci missed by the current annotation while losing 1,890 current exact loci, yielding a net gain of 2,811 exact matches and increasing the gene level exact hit rate from 70.77% to 77.77%. It retained 97.54% of protein coding genes in the mature TAIR12 annotation and improved protein set quality metrics across 16 plant genomes. Independent transcript and protein evidence further supported GeneArbiter selected structural revisions at reference discordant loci. These results establish GeneArbiter as a conservative and traceable framework for maintaining plant genome annotations as new predictions and biological evidence accumulate.

items.title: Virtual Transcriptomics from Routine Histopathology Reveals Metastasis-Associated Programs and Molecular Risk States in Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
items.abstract: Background: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is a highly aggressive and biologically heterogeneous disease for which reliable biomarkers of metastatic progression remain limited. Although transcriptomic profiling can reveal clinically important molecular programs, its routine implementation is constrained by cost, tissue availability, and workflow complexity. We hypothesized that metastasis-associated transcriptional states are encoded within routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) histopathology and can be recovered using artificial intelligence enabled virtual transcriptomics. Methods: We applied the Path2Space foundation model to infer genome-wide gene expression from treatment-naive TNBC H&E tissue microarrays and identified virtual transcriptomic programs associated with lymph node metastasis. We systematically validated candidate genes across three independent international TNBC cohorts (TCGA-BRCA, SCAN-B, and FUSCC). Candidate genes were evaluated in three independent international TNBC cohorts using experimentally measured RNA sequencing, followed by TNBC-specific co-expression network analysis, molecular subtype characterization, and cross-cohort meta-analysis. Results: Virtual transcriptomic analysis nominated 118 candidate genes associated with nodal status at a nominal discovery threshold; these candidates were subsequently evaluated using experimentally measured transcriptomic data across three independent international TNBC cohorts. Cross-cohort validation converged on a parsimonious two-gene Virtual Metastatic Prediction Score (VMPS) composed of TMEM184A and ZNF57, the only genes that remained significantly associated with nodal metastasis across all four datasets. TMEM184A and ZNF57 represented complementary biological programs: a TMEM184A-centered epithelial remodeling network and a ZNF57-centered KRAB zinc-finger transcriptional regulatory network. These transcriptional modules were biologically coherent and demonstrated reproducible associations with established TNBC molecular subtypes. Across TCGA-BRCA, SCAN-B, and FUSCC, the TMEM184A module showed a pooled OR of 1.44 per SD (95% CI, 1.25-1.67; I2=0%), while the two-gene VMPS showed a pooled OR of 1.58 (95% CI, 1.28-1.94). Moreover, higher VMPS and TMEM184A module activity defined reproducible metastatic risk gradients and enriched for lymph node-positive disease across independent cohorts. Conclusions: AI-enabled virtual transcriptomics transforms routine H&E histopathology into a scalable platform for molecular discovery in TNBC. These findings establish virtual transcriptomics as a scalable discovery framework for recovering biologically interpretable, metastasis associated molecular programs from routine histopathology, with potential applications in precision risk stratification.

items.title: Methamphetamine acute exposure induces mitochondrial fragmentation in ventral tegmental area dopamine neurons
items.abstract: Methamphetamine (METH) is a potent psychostimulant that primarily acts on the dopaminergic system and has strong reinforcing effects. It also induces oxidative stress, impairs mitochondrial function, and causes neurotoxicity at high doses. We previously showed that long-term METH self-administration increases mitochondrial respiratory metabolism and reduces antioxidant capacity in the mesolimbic dopaminergic circuit. However, the effects of METH exposure on mitochondrial structure in dopamine neurons remained unexplored. Here, we examine the acute effects of METH on mitochondrial morphology using a methodology that combines classical immunofluorescence labeling with advanced computational clearing methods and quantitative morphometric analysis. We administered acute METH treatments to mice at doses known to produce stimulant (3 mg/kg) or neurotoxic (20 mg/kg) effects. One week later, quantitative morphological analysis showed that neurotoxic METH exposure increased mitochondrial fragmentation in tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)-positive dopaminergic neurons, significantly reducing mitochondrial size and length while increasing estimated roundness. By contrast, NeuN-labeled non-dopaminergic VTA neurons showed no changes in mitochondrial morphology, suggesting that acute susceptibility to METH-induced mitochondrial fragmentation is cell-type-specific in dopamine neurons. In addition, dopamine neuron size decreased, particularly after the neurotoxic METH dose. Our findings shed light on the lasting effects of METH exposure on mitochondrial structure and can help explain the early mechanisms underlying mitochondrial functional changes in VTA dopamine neurons.

items.title: Repeated transcranial ultrasound is associated with altered temporal organization of spontaneous wheel activity during sleep disruption in mice
items.abstract: Background: Motor-cortex-targeted transcranial ultrasound stimulation (tUS) can influence neural activity and motor responses, but its relationship to spontaneous behavior during sleep disruption (SD) remains unclear. Objective: To examine how repeated tUS during sustained SD relates to the temporal organization of spontaneous running and inactivity bouts. Methods: We recorded wheel activity in 36 mice for 17 days. On Days 13-17, mice in control (Ctrl) or wheel-confinement SD housing received bilateral motor-cortex-targeted tUS or sham. Another 32 mice followed the same treatment schedule and completed the retention phase of the novel object recognition test before open-field testing on Day 17. EEG/EMG recordings in 11 untreated mice characterized the SD sleep-wake phenotype. Hydrophone measurements in water and simulations using individual skull models characterized acoustic exposure. Results: During the final three dark phases, SD/tUS mice had lower activity-resumption probability (0.132 vs 0.224) and longer median inactivity bouts (3.81 vs 2.48 min) than SD/Sham mice. Both housing-by-treatment interactions were significant. Within SD, neither total rotations nor running intensity differed significantly. The mean discrimination index was higher with tUS, although the Holm-adjusted comparison was nonsignificant. SD/tUS mice spent longer in the open-field center than SD/Sham mice. Across all 32 behavioral-test mice, lower resumption probability and longer pauses correlated with longer center time the next day. Untreated SD mice slept more and had more frequent sleep-wake transitions. Conclusions: During ongoing SD, mice receiving repeated motor-cortex-targeted tUS were less likely than sham-treated mice to resume wheel running. Their longer pauses between runs may provide opportunities for sustained rest.

items.title: A Cross-Tissue Multi-Omics Atlas of Brain Transcriptomes and Liquid Biopsy EV Proteomes in Parkinson's Disease and Multiple System Atrophy
items.corresponding_institution: Division of Thoracic Surgery, Department of Surgery, Faculty of Medicine and Health Sciences, McGill University, Montreal, QC, Canada
items.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) and Multiple System Atrophy (MSA) are progressive synucleinopathies characterized by widespread molecular alterations across neuronal and glial populations. While brain tissue provides direct insight into disease mechanisms, liquid biopsies, particularly extracellular vesicles (EVs) in plasma, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and urine, offer a minimally invasive avenue for clinical diagnosis and monitoring. However, the extent to which cell-type-specific brain transcriptional changes translate into detectable circulating protein signatures remains unclear. Here, we present a comprehensive multi-omics meta-analysis integrating eight human post-mortem brain single-nucleus RNA-sequencing (snRNA-seq) datasets with eight circulating proteomic datasets. We uniformly reprocessed and analyzed over 1 million nuclei, spanning ~20,000 protein-coding genes across four broadly defined disease-relevant brain regions from 171 individuals alongside ~8,000 liquid biopsy proteins from over 400 individuals. We resolved cell-type-specific differentially expressed genes (DEGs) across dopaminergic neurons, microglia, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes alongside disease-specific differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) in peripheral biofluids. Mapping brain DEGs onto liquid biopsy proteomes revealed that ~25% of brain DEGs were detectable as biofluid DEPs in at least one dataset, while multi-cohort filtering prioritized 32 unique recurrent cross-omic biomarkers. These include concordantly regulated markers of complement and glial reactivity (C1QB, C3, CHI3L1), neurotrophic and neuropeptide signaling (IGFBP5, NRP1, SST), lipid metabolism (LPL, APOC1), proteostasis (HSP90B1), and cytoskeletal/extracellular matrix remodeling (MMP2, PLOD1), alongside inversely regulated chaperones and synaptic/vascular factors (HSP90AA1, CAMK2A, VWF). Furthermore, cross-omic protein-protein interaction networks converged on pathways governing chaperone-mediated protein folding, ubiquitin-proteasome degradation, mitochondrial bioenergetics, and SNARE-mediated vesicular transport. Ultimately, this integrative atlas links brain cell-type-specific transcriptomic dysregulation to accessible EV cargo, providing a scalable framework for mechanistically informed liquid biopsies in neurodegeneration.

items.title: Ultra-Fast Signals during Spreading Depolarizations
items.abstract: Spreading depolarizations (SDs) are major pathophysiological events implicated in various brain diseases. Hallmarks of SD include a negative DC shift, reflecting near-complete neuronal depolarization, and the depression of cortical activity. Using microelectrode field potential recordings from the rat cortex, we found that, in contrast to the depression of activity in conventional AC frequency bands (0.5-1000 Hz), high-potassium-induced SDs were associated with increased local field potential power at ultra-fast frequencies (4-8 kHz), which we term the Ultra-Fast Signal (UFS). UFSs were time-locked to the SD-related DC shifts, although their peaks were delayed relative to those of the DC shifts. Furthermore, UFS magnitude and duration correlated with those of the DC shift, and UFSs exhibited vertical propagation profiles across cortical depth similar to DC shifts. During partial superficial SDs, UFSs were confined to the cortical layers recruited by the SD. UFSs were also prominent in SD clusters during isoelectric SDs, occurring against a background of suppressed AC activity. We propose that the UFS could serve as an additional SD marker that is particularly useful for detecting isoelectric SDs.

items.title: Non-Ordinary Visual Spaces, Self-Motion and Sense of Agency in Near-Death Experiences
items.abstract: Near-death experiences (NDEs) are a subset of non-ordinary states consciousness in which people frequently report unusual perceptions of space and self-motion. How the occurrence of self-motion varies across the visual-field boundary configurations described in first-person accounts remains underinvestigated. Alongside a semi-structured digital questionnaire, participants represented their NDE visual spaces schematically, outlining visual-field boundaries and marking self-location and self-motion direction. Across successive reconstructions, we examined visual-field geometry and extent in relation to self-location, the subjective experience of where one feels located, and self-motion, the perceived movement of the self through visual space. In spaces with reported self-motion, we also examined whether the movement was experienced as voluntarily initiated or controlled. Self-motion predominated in conical visual fields and in fields bounded by more strongly curved elliptic arcs. Self-motion was absent in most fields bounded by flatter elliptic arcs and in most fully ellipsoidal fields. Among spaces with self-motion, passive agency predominated in conical fields. Active agency was more frequent in ellipsoidal than in conical fields and was reported in half of the fully ellipsoidal fields with self-motion. Sparse data limited these exploratory comparisons. The analysis yielded no clear evidence of an association between perceived velocity magnitude and agency. These findings suggest that visual-field geometry is associated with whether self-motion occurs during the NDE Core and, when it occurs, with whether it is experienced as voluntarily initiated or controlled. The reconstruction approach provides a framework for investigating the spatial organization of first-person experience in NDEs.

items.title: A Spatiotemporal Code for Cognitive Flexibility in the Mid-Posterior Cerebellar Cortex
items.corresponding_institution: University of Minnesota Department of Neuroscience
items.abstract: Cognitive flexibility is the critical ability to adapt behavior in changing environments. Although traditionally associated with the prefrontal cortex, behavioral, lesion, and functional imaging evidence suggests the cerebellum contributes to cognitive flexibility. To test the role of the cerebellum at the circuit level, we paired widefield calcium imaging of single-cell Purkinje cells with a cognitive flexibility task and computational behavioral model. We find mid-posterior Purkinje cells encode all reinforcement learning parameters needed to produce flexible behavior, including specific representations for contingency degradation (CD) and enhancement (CE). Comparing somatic and dendritic encoding reveals a significant bias towards integrative multi-trial CD and CE representations in somas over long timescales, while dendrites encode more single-trial reward prediction errors. Activating lobule VIa, the region with strongest CD flexibility encoding, with patterned photostimulation causally expedites CD behavior. These results establish that the cerebellum extends beyond its canonical motoric functions to act as an important coordinator of cognitive flexibility behavior.

items.title: Network size regulates the balance between reuse and reconstruction of neural dynamics during reversal learning
items.abstract: Neural system size is a fundamental quantitative property that may influence cognitive function. While larger neural systems have been associated with enhanced cognitive performance, how system size contributes to cognitive flexibility remains poorly understood. In particular, it is unclear whether size influences not only how efficiently a system learns but also how previously established neural dynamics are reorganized when learned associations must change. We addressed this question using recurrent neural networks trained on a reversal learning task. Despite reaching the same performance criterion, networks differed strikingly in how their internal dynamics changed across reversal. Some networks largely preserved prereversal population trajectories, thereby reusing previously established dynamics, whereas others substantially reorganized them, effectively reconstructing their dynamical structure. This continuum of adaptation strategies was particularly broad in small networks. Importantly, the extent of reorganization was related to network properties established before reversal: networks with larger prereversal recurrent weights tended to exhibit stronger reconstruction. We then examined whether the balance between reuse and reconstruction depended systematically on network size. As network size increased, changes in internal dynamics became progressively smaller and less variable, indicating increasing convergence toward the reuse strategy. Larger networks also learned both the initial and reversed mappings more rapidly and consistently. Thus, network size shapes not only learning efficiency but also the strategy by which previously learned population dynamics are modified during flexible adaptation, shifting the balance from diverse reuse reconstruction strategies in small networks toward consistent reuse in larger networks.

items.title: Contextual Guidance and Suppression in Visual Search: Probing Learned Attentional Settings With a Color Singleton
items.abstract: How does learning a spatial context shape the selection of a newly salient distractor? In two eye-tracking experiments (26 participants each), observers searched for a T among Ls in repeated (Old) or novel (New) configurations. A designated distractor occupied a fixed or variable location and became a red color singleton in the second session. Repeated configurations predicted a stable target location in Experiment 1 but not in Experiment 2. Familiar configurations yielded faster responses alongside an increased probability of initial saccades toward fixed-location singletons. These co-occurring effects were observed at outer singleton locations in Experiment 1 and at both inner and outer locations in Experiment 2. Contextual cueing was stronger in Experiment 1, where familiar configurations also increased initial target selection, reduced ordinary-distractor selection, and facilitated target acquisition. These findings suggest that learned context shapes both the priority assigned to individual search items and search efficiency following distractor selection. The singleton probe reveals how learned spatial contexts shape both the distribution of attentional priority across individual search items and the efficiency of search following distractor selection.

items.title: Assessing gait control from short time series using a geometric characterization of stride-by-stride corrections
items.abstract: Gait variability in healthy adults exhibits Long-Range Autocorrelations (LRA), reflecting long-term statistical dependencies between stride intervals. Previous studies have interpreted LRA within an optimal control framework, where stride length and duration are regulated in a coordinated manner to maintain a constant walking speed. Such objective offers redundancy among gait parameters that achieve success. In this context, imposing constraints on the walking cadence reduces this redundancy and leads to a loss of LRA. The model therefore predicts that during free walking, stride-by-stride adjustments should be directed toward the redundant axis, whereas during cued walking, they should be directed toward the imposed target values. Consequently, differences between conditions should be observable based on a geometric characterization of changes in length and duration. With simulations and experimental data, we show that stride-by-stride adjustments discriminate between cued and free walking conditions, supporting the geometric interpretation of the model. Moreover, this metric achieves good discrimination (Area Under the Curve = 0.74) for 50-stride series, compared with LRA estimates that typically require series of 80 strides to achieve comparable success. In sum, our study validates a novel geometric approach to quantifying gait control strategies, supporting the emergence of LRA through flexible adjustments of stride parameters.

items.title: Prior Experience Alters Exploration in Standard Behavioral Assays More Robustly Than Sex or Light/Dark Cycle in C57BL/6J Mice
items.corresponding_institution: National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences/National Institutes of Health
items.abstract: Circadian phase during testing, biological sex, and repeated exposure to the same testing apparatus are all experimental variables known to impact outcomes in neurobehavioral studies. However, the combined, interactive effects of these intrinsic and extrinsic variables on common behavioral tests are not well established, and the effect of repeated testing is particularly understudied. In this study, we examined the compounding impact of these variables by comparing male and female mice on either a standard light cycle or reversed light cycle in the elevated plus maze (EPM), elevated zero maze (EZM), open field test (OFT), Y-maze spontaneous alternation (SA), and novel object recognition (NOR). To examine the impact of repeated exposure to the same testing apparatus, mice were re-exposed to the EPM, EZM, OFT and SA 24 hours after the initial test. We found that exploratory behavior in EPM, EZM, and OFT was robustly diminished on the second exposure. Furthermore, exploration in the open arms of the EPM dropped dramatically, proportionally more than can be explained by the drop in total exploration. The only endpoint unaffected by repeated testing was percent alternation in SA. Light cycle had smaller, more inconsistent effects across assays; male mice on a reversed light-dark cycle showed increased object exploration and improved discrimination in NOR, and mice on a reversed light-dark cycle showed less time exploring the center in the OFT. The effect of sex was minimal, and behavior in EZM and Y-maze was unaffected by sex or light condition. We propose that the first test in any assay elicits an incidental learning experience which is expressed on the second test as a reduction in exploration. The robustness of this test-retest drop in exploration argues that this is a critical experimental variable that must be incorporated into experimental design and interpretation of behavioral results.

items.title: Angiostrongylus cantonensis fifth-stage larvae Excretory-Secretory Products Induce Presenilin-1-Associated Molecular Changes and Inflammatory Responses in Mouse Astrocytes
items.abstract: Background Parasite infection may cause significant effects on the immune response in the host brain. Previous studies have demonstrated that excretory-secretory products (ESPs) released by fifth-stage larvae (L5) of Angiostrongylus cantonensis induce inflammatory responses in mouse astrocytes. However, the underlying molecular mechanisms involved in ESP-induced neuroinflammation remain unclear. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the molecular mechanisms underlying inflammatory responses in mouse astrocytes following treatment with A. cantonensis L5 ESPs. Methods Mouse astrocytes were treated with A. cantonensis L5 ESPs to investigate changes in the JNK-related inflammatory signaling pathway, including Presenilin-1 (PS1), glycogen synthase kinase-3{beta} (GSK-3{beta}), {beta}-catenin, nuclear factor kappa B (NF-{kappa}B), and interleukin-6 (IL-6). Furthermore, the JNK inhibitor - SP600125 was also employed to determine the mechanism between JNK pathway and inflammation induced by A. cantonensis L5 ESPs. Results Treatment with A. cantonensis L5 ESPs showed a significant increase tenses in PS1, GSK-3{beta}, NF-{kappa}B, and IL-6, while the expression of {beta}-catenin decreased during post 12 until 24 hours treatment. Furthermore, pretreatment with SP600125 attenuated ESP-induced PS1 and GSK-3{beta} expression, which restored {beta}-catenin expression. These findings suggest that JNK-associated signaling helps regulate PS1-associated molecular responses and inflammatory signaling in astrocytes exposed to A. cantonensis L5 ESPs. Conclusions A. cantonensis L5 ESPs induce an inflammatory response in mouse astrocytes, which is accompanied by JNK-related and GSK-{beta}/{beta}-catenin signaling pathways. Inhibition of JNK signaling attenuates these molecular changes, suggesting that JNK-associated signaling may contribute to parasite-derived ESP-induced inflammation. These findings provide further insight into the molecular interactions between A. cantonensis and host astrocytes.

items.title: Hepatocyte NMD restrains inflammation and is impaired in alcohol-associated hepatitis
items.abstract: Nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) limits the abundance of transcripts containing premature termination codons (PTCs) and regulates other endogenous mRNAs. How distinct transcripts respond to reduced NMD capacity in liver disease remains poorly understood. Here, we found that hepatic UPF1 and UPF2 protein abundance was markedly reduced in human alcohol-associated hepatitis. Hepatocyte-specific Upf2 deletion in mice caused liver injury, cell death, and macrophage accumulation, with innate immune gene induction evident by day 11. Integrated intron-exon RNA-seq analysis identified 259 protein-coding candidate NMD-regulated genes, including genes involved in inflammation, stress responses, and metabolism. Canonical NMD substrates, including the PTC-containing isoforms of Tra2b, Hnrnpl, and Ptbp2, accumulated markedly following hepatocyte-specific Upf2 deletion. In contrast, partial Upf2 knockdown in primary mouse hepatocytes induced NMD-targeted inflammatory genes, including Ccl2, Ccl7, Icam1, and Ifit2 while producing only modest changes in the examined PTC-containing isoforms. Human alcohol-associated hepatitis livers likewise exhibited increased CCL2, ICAM1, and IFIT2 expression, accompanied by modest and variable changes in these canonical NMD substrates. These findings support differential transcript responsiveness to reduced NMD capacity and indicate that selected PTC-containing substrates may incompletely reflect its effects on endogenous gene regulation. Together, our results identify hepatocyte NMD as a restraint on inflammatory gene expression and suggest that its suppression may contribute to hepatic inflammation in alcohol-associated hepatitis.

items.title: A novel simultaneous RNA extraction workflow from mouse Retinal Pigmented Epithelial (RPE) and retina
items.abstract: Purpose: In Posterior Segment Eye Diseases (PSEDs), the homeostatic relation between retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and retina is disrupted. A better understanding of the transcriptomic changes occurring in different ocular cell types can help to elucidate disease mechanisms. Currently, there is no complete detailed workflow describing the process of simultaneous RNA isolation from RPE and retina separately. In this paper, our aim was to develop an easy, reproducible protocol for simultaneous isolation of RNA from both murine RPE and retina. Methods: We developed an efficient and straightforward workflow for isolating RNA from both murine RPE and retina simultaneously. We described the method in detail spanning from mouse euthanasia to downstream RNA analysis. We compared the efficiency of this isolation method between different mice strains (C57BL/6 vs BALB/c). Results: Our method provided high yield of RNA from both RPE and retina across different strains. We observed better quality of RPE RNA in terms of A260/130 ratios in C57BL/6 mice. The retinal RNA quality and yield were comparable across both strains. Beta-catenin immunofluorescent staining also validated our success of RPE removal in the choroidal flat-mounts in both strains. Conclusions: We described an improved workflow for obtaining RNA simultaneously from both RPE and retina. We compared the efficiency of our process via multitude of downstream analyses across different mice strains. Translational Relevance: This method will be beneficial to understand the RPE or retinal tissue specific mRNA transcript changes in preclinical mice models of PSEDs.

items.title: Transgene-free immortalisation of bovine satellite cells by genetic disruption of CDKN2A
items.abstract: Production of cultivated meat demands a supply of cells that differentiate into muscle, even after extended proliferation. As primary bovine satellite cells (PrimSCs) lose proliferation and differentiation capacity over prolonged culture, immortalised cell lines are necessary for rapid commercialisation. Here, we report the first evidence of a transgene-free single knockout mRNA-hit-and-run-based strategy that yields immortalised bovine satellite cells (ImmSCs). We demonstrate targeted disruption of CDKN2A alone is sufficient to immortalise SCs from three cow breeds. ImmSCs maintained a 17h doubling time over 75 population doublings, while sustaining myogenic potential in 2D and 3D differentiation. Transcriptionally, ImmSCs evade senescence and continue to resemble young primary cells. Finally, we show that ImmSCs are non-tumorigenic and proliferate even with a 90% reduction in FGF-2, HGF, and T3. By combining immortalisation with regulatory compatibility, we demonstrate a simple and generalisable single-locus disruption strategy that minimizes batch variability and enables scalable production of cultivated meat.

items.title: Comparative Metagenomic Analysis of Chondrosia and Chondrilla Sponge Microbiomes Reveals Distinct Symbiotic Communities, Functional Potential, and Contrasting Environmental Responses
items.abstract: Marine sponges frequently maintain distinct, host-specific microbial communities despite inhabiting overlapping or identical environments. In this study, we performed comparative shotgun metagenomic sequencing on two sympatric sponge taxa, Chondrilla and Chondrosia, collected from the same shallow-water habitat in the Florida Keys to examine whether differences in microbiome composition and functional potential persist under shared environmental conditions. Morphological examination and phylogenetic analyses of nuclear 18S rRNA sequences confirmed the taxonomic placement of the green specimens within Chondrilla and the black specimens within Chondrosia sp. Community-level profiling revealed taxonomic differences between the two hosts: the Chondrilla microbiome exhibited a strong enrichment of Cyanobacteriota, notably Candidatus Synechococcus spongiarum, whereas the Chondrosia microbiome was characterized by Poribacteria, Chloroflexota, Nitrosopumilales, and other sponge-associated lineages. Functional annotation of metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) identified distinct functional potential between the two microbiomes, particularly regarding pathways associated with osmoregulation, oxidative and environmental stress responses, and secondary-metabolite biosynthesis, including diverse biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) such as terpenes and RiPPs. Additionally, parallel physiological monitoring during a freshwater exposure experiment demonstrated contrasting environmental responses, with Chondrosia exhibiting long-term survival over ten months under static low-salinity conditions compared to rapid deterioration in Chondrilla. Together, our findings provide genome-resolved evidence that sympatric sponge hosts maintain distinct microbial assemblages and functional profiles, establishing a framework for future investigations linking sponge-microbe interactions, biosynthetic potential, and stress resilience.

items.title: Structural Complexity in the Maize Pangenome Graph Is Generated by Transposable Elements and Sorted by Selection
items.abstract: Pangenome graphs capture the structural variation that linear references miss, but what generates their complex regions, whether these are targets of selection and whether the structural context of a gene affects its expression is unknown. These questions were addressed with a graph of 58 chromosome level maize assemblies (57 inbred lines and a teosinte accession), a genome dominated by transposable elements (TEs). Between the segments shared by all assemblies, the conserved intervals, bubbles open where assemblies diverge; every bubble's complexity was scored by the number and length of its paths and bubbles were classified as high, medium or low complexity. TEs are 96% of the annotations in high complexity bubbles, whereas genes concentrate in low complexity bubbles and conserved intervals; genes confined to complex bubbles are enriched for transposase activity, chromatin constituents and defence responses. To test for selection, Tajima's D was computed in 10 kb windows from 38.5 million SNPs of the independent Maize 282 association panel; neutral demographic models place fewer than 2% of simulated windows in its 5% tails. The lower tail, the sweep like windows, holds as many bubbles as the rest but simpler ones, mostly large TE presence-absence variants; the upper tail, with an excess of intermediate frequency alleles, holds the most complex ones. This holds across window sizes and recombination rates and within the temperate lines, and the graph's structural variant allele frequencies agree. The structural context of a gene shows in its expression: genes confined to complex bubbles are expressed in fewer tissues than genes in conserved intervals, and 1,707 genes differ in expression between NAM founders with different structural variant alleles. Structural complexity in maize is thus TE generated standing variation, reduced by hard sweeps and preserved by maintained polymorphism, not a target of selection, and reflected in gene expression.

items.title: Benchmarking sequence-to-function models and mapping enhancer-gene interactions with E2GScore
items.corresponding_institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney), Sydney, NSW, Australia
items.abstract: Sequence-to-function models predict gene expression and chromatin features directly from DNA sequence and are increasingly used to infer enhancer-gene regulatory interactions. However, differences in attribution procedures and benchmarking datasets complicate comparisons between models, while the biological information captured by their enhancer-gene scores remains poorly understood. Here we introduce E2GScore, a unified framework for extracting and benchmarking enhancer-gene predictions from sequence-to-function models. By systematically varying scoring protocols, we identify gene-readout normalization and cell-type-matched expression tracks as important determinants of performance, whereas in silico mutagenesis offers no advantage over less computationally demanding input gradients. We compare seven sequence-to-function models and three established enhancer-gene predictors against CRISPR interference screens in K562 cells and primary human astrocytes. AlphaGenome 1 and 2 outperformed all other sequence-to-function models, and matched or outperformed experimentally informed predictors, particularly for distal enhancers, without a statistically significant difference between AlphaGenome versions after multiple-testing correction. We further show that the apparent reduction in predictive performance in astrocytes relative to K562 cells observed across models results primarily from differences in benchmarking dataset composition, particularly enhancer-TSS distance and target-gene expression. Using the open-weight AlphaGenome 1, we then generated E2GMap, a genome-wide resource of enhancer-gene regulation comprising 14.7 billion enhancer-gene attribution scores across 454 human biosamples, 45% of which are absent from existing enhancer-gene maps such as those from ENCODE-rE2G and AlphaGenome 2. E2GMap is available at e2gscore.com. Together, E2GScore and E2GMap establish a framework for rigorous evaluation of sequence-based enhancer-gene predictions and provide an extensible resource for studying gene regulation across human cell types and tissues.

items.title: Epstein-Barr Virus Load in Lymphoblastoid Cell Lines and Its Association with Schizophrenia
items.corresponding_institution: Center for Psychiatric Genetics, Endeavor Health Research Institute, Evanston, IL, USA;  Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Neuroscience, The University of
items.abstract: Background: Blood Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) DNAs are reported to have genetic determinants and correlate with prevalence of autoimmune, neurological, respiratory and cardiovascular condition. However, whether a patient is more susceptible to EBV virus infection is unknown. Lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs) are often immortalized by infecting individuals' peripheral lymphocytes by EBV in a dish, providing an ex vivo model to address this question. Here, we examined associations of EBV viral load in LCLs with schizophrenia (SCZ) diagnosis, SCZ and bipolar (BIP) polygenic risk scores, and host genetic variation. Methods: EBV viral load in LCLs from the Molecular Genetics of Schizophrenia (MGS) study was examined using univariable and multivariable linear regression. Separate multivariable models evaluated SCZ diagnosis, bipolar disorder polygenic score (BIP-PGS), and SCZ polygenic score (SCZ-PGS), adjusting for age, sex, and the first five genetic ancestry principal components. An exploratory analysis examined age at schizophrenia onset. A genome-wide association study (GWAS) was conducted in 2,000 participants using the same covariates. Results: SCZ diagnosis was not significantly associated with EBV viral load after covariate adjustment (Beta=-0.004, SE = 0.025, P = 0.868). Neither BIP-PGS (Beta=-0.009, SE = 0.013, P = 0.469) nor SCZ-PGS (Beta=-0.002, SE = 0.013, P = 0.897) was significantly associated with viral load. Univariable analyses also identified no significant association with age at SCZ onset. For GWAS of EBV loads in LCL, no variant reached genome-wide significance (P < 5 x 10e-8). The strongest association was observed at rs7188098 in the GP2 gene on chromosome 16 (P = 3.7 x 10e-7). Conclusions: These analyses did not identify statistically significant associations of LCL EBV viral load with SCZ diagnosis or the psychiatric polygenic scores examined. The GWAS identified suggestive signals of association with EBV load, which require further investigation in larger sample sizes.

items.title: Confident but misplaced: a model-free ruler for post-translational modification placement by AI structure predictors
items.corresponding_institution: Institute for Advanced Studies, New Uzbekistan University
items.abstract: AI structure predictors accept post-translationally modified (PTM) residues, but whether they place the added atoms where crystallography finds them, and whether their confidence reveals when they do not, is unknown. We first built a ruler from experiment alone: independent crystal structures of the same site reproduce the added atoms of oxidised cysteine and methionine to 0.32 [A], the closest pre-cutoff library rotamer lies at 0.41 [A] and a model-free guess at 4.17 [A]. We then predicted 176 hold-out PTM sites, released after every model's training cut-off, with RareFold, Boltz-2, Chai-1 and AlphaFold 3, using identical inputs and thresholds fixed before measurement. On oxidised Cys/Met (up to 34 sites in 25 proteins), the three all-atom models place the matching distal atoms of neighbouring canonical side chains to 0.35-0.38 [A] but the added oxygens at 1.19-1.51 [A]; 29-41 % of placements are wrong by more than 2 [A], as sterically plausible rotamers that the electron density does not support. RareFold misplaces ordinary side chains as well. Across all PTM classes, residue confidence does not flag the failure: at pLDDT [≥] 90, 24-46 % of modified-residue placements are catastrophic, 3.5-5 times the rate for matched canonical atoms. One seed rarely samples the correct rotamer; more seeds sample it more often, yet the models' own ranking does not select it. Methyllysine shows the same gap, whereas for pyridoxal-lysine the models diverge (AlphaFold 3 1.13 [A], Boltz-2 4.96 [A]). A high residue pLDDT at a modified residue therefore does not verify its side chain.

items.title: ComProg resolves spatial cell-cell communication into dynamic communication programs and receiver responses
items.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics enables cell-resolved inference of ligand-receptor (LR) signaling, but the resulting communication maps are highly redundant, sensitive to LR database choice and difficult to relate to receiver-cell transcriptional responses while accounting for cell identity and spatial context. Here we present ComProg, a framework that organizes spatially inferred cell-cell communication into communication programs representing recurrent combinations of LR pairs and identifies associated transcriptional responses in receiver cells through cell-type- and niche-matched comparisons calibrated against synthetic negative-control genes. We applied ComProg to spatial transcriptomic datasets spanning mouse kidney injury and repair, non-small-cell lung cancer profiled in two and three dimensions, and gastric cancer during immune checkpoint blockade. ComProg identified compact sets of communication programs that tracked injury and repair, localized to distinct tumor compartments, recurred across serial sections and differed between treatment response states. In injured kidney, program-associated transcriptional responses were concentrated in receiver cell types expressing the corresponding receptors, supporting the biological specificity of the inferred associations. Together, ComProg provides a framework for reducing complex LR-level communication maps into interpretable and comparable signaling programs and linking these programs to transcriptional responses in specific receiver-cell populations.

items.title: StrucMind links protein contacts and ligand environments to atoms in PyMOL
items.abstract: StrucMind provides two PyMOL plugins for comparing protein contact maps and examining the interactions around a bound ligand. A contact seen in only one structure can reflect a difference in packing or a gap in the coordinates needed for comparison. Contact Maps aligns corresponding residues, identifies retained, gained and lost contacts, and records why a comparison remains unresolved. Structure Analysis measures direct ligand-protein contacts, traces paths through individual water molecules, and characterizes aromatic packing and pocket geometry. Users can select a contact or a water-mediated path to inspect the atoms in PyMOL. Exported atom identities, distances and coordinate coverage let a colleague retrace the assignment. Keywords. Molecular recognition, Noncovalent interactions, Protein contact maps, PyMOL, Water bridges.

items.title: Tumor2Line: population-aware tumor-cell line alignment for cancer cell line selection
items.corresponding_institution: Shanghai Jiao Tong University Center for Systems Biomedicine
items.abstract: Abstract Cancer cell lines are widely used in cancer research and drug development, yet their representativeness of patient tumors varies across models and biological contexts. Here, we introduce Tumor2Line, a population-aware framework that reframes cancer cell-line selection as an alignment problem between tumor and cell-line populations using unbalanced optimal transport. Tumor2Line improved the recovery of documented tumor-cell line pairs over conventional similarity-based approaches. Systematic analysis across 22 cancer lineages revealed that tumor-cell-intrinsic programs were generally better preserved, whereas programs with greater tumor microenvironment dependence showed lower fidelity. Furthermore, Tumor2Line-selected cell lines showed drug-sensitivity patterns associated with clinical treatment outcomes and improved concordance in genetic dependency profiles with patient-derived organoids. These findings provide a basis for more informed selection of cancer cell-line models and help researchers interpret preclinical findings in the context of model-specific representational fidelity. Tumor2Line is available at https://github.com/Duan-Lab1/Tumor2Line Keywords: Cancer cell lines; Tumor-cell line alignment; Population-aware modeling; Cancer model fidelity; Optimal transport

items.title: Pretrained Decision Models in Bioinformatics: Comparable to Active-Learning Screening, Baseline-Dependent in Cell-Type Annotation, Behind a Trained Mass-Spectrometry Re-scorer
items.abstract: Much of biomedical research rests on small, repeated decisions with a fixed set of answers: whether a study belongs in a systematic review, whether two trial claims contradict each other, which type a cell is, whether a peptide-spectrum match is correct. Pretrained decision models answer such questions without training on the data at hand, but how far they can replace the methods established for each task is unknown. Here we tested two such models, Jev and d3-ultra, against an established tool or, where none exists, published benchmark results. We evaluated four tasks with known answers, ordered from text input to numeric input. On text, the models were usable without any training: in screening for 39 systematic reviews, their reading order showed no detectable difference from the active-learning screener ASReview at the ideal stopping point. In detecting contradictory drug-trial claims, they scored close to the best published model. On gene names, they helped only where a curated marker database was weak: they trailed it in pancreas and led it in heart, by a margin that depended strongly on how the database was applied. On numbers from one mass-spectrometry run they accepted 30 to 55% fewer matches at 1% estimated error than a re-scorer trained on that run. Pretrained decision models are therefore a practical first pass for text-based decisions and worth trying where curated knowledge is thin, but no substitute for a tool trained on the experiments own numbers.

items.title: rnaModScan: context-aware deep learning-based filtering of nanopore m6A and inosine calls
items.abstract: Nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS) can detect multiple RNA modifications, but falsepositive background calls complicate transcriptome-wide analysis. We developed rnaModScan,a deep learning filter that integrates Dorado scores for all eight modification types with local sequence, repeat, and per-read alignment features to distinguish N6-methyladenosine (m6A) and inosine candidates from background calls. Using public RNA004 data, we evaluated site classification by grouped five-fold cross-validation and assessed transfer to HeLa cellular RNA using model weights fitted exclusively to HEK293T cellular RNA and unmodified in vitrotranscribed controls. For m6A sites outside the canonical DRACH motif, filtering removed 92.85% of the Dorado/modkit candidates while retaining 93.34% of their original matches to the GLORI reference map. The F1 score relative to DRS-covered GLORI sites increased from 3.04% to 26.76%. For inosine, filtering removed 83.44% of the candidates while preserving 99.86% of their original Slic-seq matches, and the reference-map F1 score increased from 5.22% to 22.05%. Filtering also brought the motif, repeat, and transcript-position distributions of retained candidates closer to those in the orthogonal short-read maps generated by GLORI and Slic-seq. These results support rnaModScan as a practical complement to Dorado-based RNA004 analysis for prioritizing transcriptome-wide m6A and inosine candidates.Availability: rnaModScan is available at https://github.com/uedaLabR/rnaModScan and archived in Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24546829).Keywords: direct RNA sequencing; RNA modifications; Dorado; deep learning; inosine; m6A

items.title: L++: A Language for Programming Life
items.abstract: Living systems run on a code written in DNA or RNA, but expressing that code as a model that scientists can write, run and read remains difficult. We present L++, a holistic programming language in which life can be described, simulated and, beyond that, designed; its nouns are biological, and people and AI systems can both write it. Molecules, reactions, compartments, cells, organs and populations are written directly and nest by containment, so one grammar spans a reaction and the population around it. Quantities carry units, objects take places in space, and values can be set in time. Named kinetic parameters select one family of rate laws, from mass action to cooperative enzyme kinetics, and a few operators write complexes, states and gene products in one line. Modules compose by import, and a process can be written by its inputs, outputs and rate before its mechanism is known; the aim is that one description can model an organism or design one. lppc compiles a program and lpps runs it, and a run repeats exactly with the same build, options and seed. Ten programs written with an AI assistant, from an enzyme in a tube to a lake ecosystem and a drug therapy from molecule to patient, show the language across levels of biological organization, and a genome-scale virtual Escherichia coli, reported separately, shows it holds a whole organism. Our ultimate goal is the Human Code: the human, from molecules to the whole body, written in L++ as a mechanistic model that runs.

items.title: Reconstructing regulatory histories of cell fate decisions from single-cell lineage and multi-omics
items.corresponding_institution: School of Mathematics, Sun Yat-sen University, Guangzhou, China; Guangdong Province Key Laboratory of Computational Science, Sun Yat-sen University, Guangzhou,
items.abstract: Understanding how distinct cell identities emerge from common progenitors requires access to regulatory histories that molecular snapshots cannot directly reveal. We introduce RegArch, a probabilistic framework integrating transcriptomic profiles, chromatin-derived evidence, and time-scaled cell lineages to reconstruct terminal and unobserved ancestral gene regulatory networks (GRNs). These lineage-resolved networks enable characterization of regulatory reorganization, prioritization of differentiation-associated and branch-biased regulators, and identification of constitutive, lineage-associated, and state-restricted modules. Simulations demonstrate ancestral network recovery and improved terminal GRN inference. In Caenorhabditis elegans, inferred ancestral GRNs combined with measured regulator expression generated target-expression signatures preferentially matching their corresponding progenitor profiles. EMS lineage analyses identified a shared regulatory module and branch-enriched modules with distinct ancestral representation. In zebrafish hearts sampled after injury, developmental ancestry informed endocardial- and epicardial-associated candidate regulator prioritization. RegArch thus generates testable hypotheses about the regulatory origins of cellular diversity.

items.title: FunDLM: A Foundation DNA Language Model for Fungi
items.abstract: Background: Fungi are important pathogens and biotechnology resources, but lack a broadly applicable fungal DNA language model. Models trained on diverse fungal genomes can support functional interpretation of genomic variants and a broad range of genomic tasks. Results: We introduce FunDLM, a family of four DNA language models pre-trained on 426 fungal reference assemblies spanning 217 genera and 14.3 Gb of sequence. Without task-specific training, FunDLM-Medium-1024bp distinguished phenotype-associated missense variants of Saccharomyces cerevisiae from synonymous controls with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.875. It performed comparably to Evo 2, a generalist model with about 15 times more parameters, and better than Nucleotide Transformer v3. The model also recognized mutations that disrupt start codons or introduce premature stop codons in S. cerevisiae and the blast fungus Pyricularia oryzae. Its scores for missense variants, computed from DNA alone, correlated with those of protein language models in S. cerevisiae and two Fusarium species (Pearson correlation 0.57-0.75). After fine-tuning, FunDLM-Small-1024bp identified supernumerary chromosome sequences in four Pyricularia isolates not used for training (average precision 0.884), and FunDLM-Medium-1024bp recognized centromeres on a chromosome withheld from training (AUROC 0.908). Fine-tuned models also predicted three histone modifications in an isolate and on chromosomes not used for training (AUROC 0.910-0.996). Conclusions: FunDLM provides reusable sequence representations for assessing functional impacts of fungal variants as well as annotation of genomic and epigenomic features. The released models, data, code, and benchmarks support applications across fungal species.

items.title: Adult gut microbiomes single out individuals at population scale
items.corresponding_institution: Universite Paris-Saclay, INRAE, MaIAGE, Jouy-en-Josas, France
items.abstract: Gut microbiome DNA is shared openly under the assumption that only human host DNA poses an ethical risk. Here we show that querying all publicly available metagenomes with one stool sample recovered another sample from the same person for 94% of 483 adults. Extrapolated to the world population, recovery rates remain well above the re-identification risk threshold advised for public release.

items.title: Leukocyte content accounts for most microRNA-immune associations in cutaneous melanoma: a confounder-adjusted reassessment
items.abstract: Loss of antigen presentation allows tumours to escape T cells and resist immune checkpoint blockade. In melanoma cell lines, several microRNAs repress genes of the antigen-presentation machinery, and many microRNAs have been proposed as immune biomarkers in melanoma tissue. Most tissue evidence comes from bulk biopsies, in which both microRNA profiles and immune-gene expression depend on the immune-cell content of the sample. Following a pre-specified analysis plan, we regressed five immune-module scores on 662 mature microRNAs in 431 melanomas from The Cancer Genome Atlas (3,310 tests), with and without adjustment for tumour purity, leukocyte content, interferon tone and clinical covariates. We labelled each microRNA by its likely cell of origin, required target-level evidence for candidates, re-tested nine published microRNA sets, and examined the antigen-presentation programme in four skin-cancer single-cell datasets, three checkpoint-blockade cohorts (155 patients) and survival data. Of 1,334 associations significant before adjustment, 82.5% were lost after it, and 188 emerged only after it. Only 20 of the 127 microRNAs associated with antigen presentation after adjustment were labelled tumour-intrinsic, and none met the target-level criterion. The closest candidate, miR-361-5p (myeloid-suppression module), failed only a multiple-testing correction added after the target-level results were known. Published sets were enriched among unadjusted antigen-presentation associations (odds ratio 3.32) but not among adjusted ones (1.02), and lost significance as often as other microRNAs (83.3% versus 85.8%). In single-cell data, non-malignant cells expressed the antigen-presentation programme more strongly than malignant cells in 19 of 20 contrasts. A higher antigen-presentation score predicted longer survival after adjustment for composition (hazard ratio 0.69) but not for interferon tone (0.86), and the immunotherapy cohorts were uninformative. In melanoma tissue, most microRNA-immune associations reflect the immune-cell content of the biopsy. Showing that microRNAs control antigen presentation in tumour cells will require compartment-resolved measurements and adequately powered target-level tests.

items.title: Thin2Seg: Single-cell Segmentation of Label-free FLIM at Low Photon Counts
items.abstract: Significance: Fluorescence lifetime imaging microscopy (FLIM) of NAD(P)H can measure the metabolism of single cells without labels. However, its weak autofluorescence requires long acquisitions that can lead to phototoxicity, while shorter acquisitions leave too few photons for current cell segmentation methods. This trade-off is aggravated in 3D live-cell models, such as spheroids and organoids, and in thin, highly adherent 2D cultures. Aim: We develop Thin2Seg to adapt a generalist segmentation network to low-photon FLIM using unlabeled recordings and a single annotated training image. The method also assesses which predicted cell masks remain stable under photon loss without additional manual annotations. Approach: We use binomial photon thinning to generate low-photon views of full-photon FLIM recordings. During training, the student network uses these low-photon views to predict the features that a teacher network extracts from the corresponding full-photon images. We evaluate Thin2Seg on macrophage and small intestinal organoid datasets against three approaches: fine-tuning on full-photon images, photon augmentation, and segmentation after denoising. We also use the predicted macrophage masks to pool photons within each cell and estimate fluorescence lifetimes. Results: Thin2Seg achieved the highest mean segmentation F1 scores among the methods tested on both datasets at median budgets of 1 and 0.5 photons per cell pixel. At these budgets, 8-12% of masks accepted by label-free certification failed the overlap criterion against full-photon predictions, compared with 14-48% of masks accepted by Cellpose's flow-error check. At 1 photon per cell pixel, 92% of annotated macrophages were recovered and 53% of lifetimes estimated were within 10% of the full-photon reference. Median cell lifetimes were within 5% of the full-photon values in 95% of macrophage images, and M2a macrophages remained distinguishable from each of the other three polarization states. Conclusions: Thin2Seg enables single-cell segmentation and lifetime analysis of label-free FLIM from much shorter acquisitions. It uses a single annotated training image and segments low-photon FLIM images directly, supporting live-cell analysis at lower photon budgets without a separate image restoration step.

items.title: Deciphering the synthetic route and apoptotic mechanisms of oxime ester (UAH-4): A potent ursolic acid derivative targeting colorectal cancer
items.abstract: The study aimed to synthesize a novel derivative of ursolic acid (UA) and evaluate its anticancer efficacy against Colorectal Cancer (CRC) cells, with a focus on elucidating its mechanism of action. The derivative, UAH-4, was synthesized through a multi-step chemical process and characterized using spectroscopic techniques. In vitro cytotoxicity of UAH-4 was assessed using the SRB assay, while its impact on colony formation, cell migration, Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) generation, Mitochondrial Membrane Potential (MMP) loss, and nuclear morphology were evaluated. Western blotting was performed to investigate the induction of apoptosis by UAH-4. UAH-4 exhibited significant cytotoxicity against various cancer cell lines, with a notable impact on the HCT-116 cancer cell line. The compound disrupted colony formation and inhibited cell migration, suggesting potential anti-metastatic effects. Mechanistic investigations revealed UAH-4-induced alterations in nuclear morphology, reactive oxygen species generation, loss of mitochondrial membrane potential, and apoptosis in HCT-116 cells. The study demonstrates the potent anticancer activity of UAH-4 against colorectal cancer cells through the induction of apoptosis. These findings suggest that UAH-4 holds promise as a therapeutic agent for CRC and warrants further investigation for its clinical potential in cancer therapy.

items.title: Exposure-driven modulation of neural response to novel word forms in toddlers
items.abstract: An enhancement of an early brain signal in response to novel word forms has been associated with lexical learning in adults. Here, we measured neural responses to novel pseudowords in 24-month-olds to investigate whether a similar early modulation occurs in young children. Participants were presented with familiar French words (e.g., bateau, boat) and novel pseudowords (e.g., bamon). Event-related potentials were time-locked to the word disambiguation point (i.e., the onset of the second syllable) and analyzed across three time bins (4 minutes each) during the experiment. We observed an early positive response, P100, occurring around 100 ms after the word disambiguation point, which decreased for pseudowords over the course of repeated exposure. No such amplitude change was observed for familiar words. These results demonstrate an early reduction in neural responses to novel word forms, suggesting rapid and dynamic changes in brain activity associated with the familiarization of novel lexical items.

items.title: Target-dependent modulation of finely tuned gamma by transcranial ultrasound in Parkinson's disease
items.corresponding_institution: Division of Neurosurgery, University of Toronto Krembil Research Institute, Toronto Western Hospital Toronto, ON, Canada
items.abstract: Background: Finely tuned gamma (FTG) is a narrowband oscillation associated with dopaminergic ON states and dyskinesia in Parkinson's disease (PD), although its physiological significance remains debated. While deep brain stimulation (DBS) can entrain gamma oscillations, whether noninvasive ultrasound can modulate endogenous FTG across motor circuits remains unclear. Methods: We analyzed local field potentials recorded using sensing-enabled DBS systems in two cohorts of patients: 17 with subthalamic nucleus (STN) and 10 with globus pallidus internus (GPi) electrodes. Theta-burst transcranial ultrasound stimulation (tbTUS) targeted the primary motor cortex (M1) or GPi. FTG was assessed before, during, and up to 45 minutes after sonication. Associations with beta activity, levodopa-equivalent daily dose (LEDD), and dyskinesia were also examined. Results: FTG was detected in eight STN patients and one GPi patient, with five exhibiting reproducible peaks suitable for longitudinal analysis, broadly consistent with previous reports of intermittent FTG expression. M1 sonication reduced STN FTG in three patients, whereas GPi sonication increased STN FTG in one but did not significantly alter locally recorded GPi FTG in another. Finger-tapping-related FTG responses were heterogeneous. Resting FTG was not significantly correlated with beta activity or LEDD. However, dyskinesia was more frequent in sessions with detectable FTG than in those without (47% vs. 20%), although this association was not statistically significant (p = 0.067). Conclusions: These findings suggest that noninvasive ultrasound can modulate endogenous FTG in a circuit-dependent manner, distinct from DBS-induced gamma entrainment. FTG may provide a complementary electrophysiological biomarker alongside beta oscillations, potentially capturing additional aspects of motor-network activity and dyskinesia. Combining noninvasive TUS with intracranial DBS sensing may offer a useful approach for investigating FTG and its potential application in future adaptive DBS and individualized neuromodulation strategies.

items.title: Neuronal Culture Media Shape Protein Abundance and Turnover in Human iPSC-Derived Neurons
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry, the University of Maryland-College Park,
items.abstract: Cultured neuron models are essential for studying neuronal biology and disease, yet it remains unclear how neuronal culture media shape the global proteome and protein turnover. Here, we compared human iPSC-derived neurons cultured in four different media: BrainPhys, DMEM/F-12, Neurobasal, or a 1:1 DMEM/F-12:Neurobasal mixture using label-free and dynamic SILAC proteomics. To enable protein turnover measurements in BrainPhys, we developed an in-house SILAC-compatible BrainPhys formulation that supported comparable viability and proteome coverage to commercial BrainPhys. BrainPhys produced a proteome and turnover landscape distinct from the other three media, which closely resembled one another. BrainPhys-cultured neurons showed lower relative abundance of DNA replication- and progenitor-associated proteins and higher relative abundance of synaptic and neuronal projection proteins, consistent with a more mature neuronal proteome. BrainPhys also globally prolonged protein half-lives, yielding a turnover profile more similar to later-stage primary neurons and in vivo brain. Despite their distinct basal proteomes, neurons cultured in different media exhibited a conserved proteomic response to acute lysosomal inhibition. Bafilomycin A1 treatment increased the relative abundance and synthesis of autophagy-associated proteins while decreasing the relative abundance of lysosomal hydrolases. Together, these findings identify neuronal culture medium as a critical determinant of neuronal proteome composition and dynamics and establish a SILAC-compatible BrainPhys formulation for future studies of neuronal proteostasis.

items.title: Non-invasive Topographic Sculpting of the Mammalian Auditory Cortex with Low-intensity Focused Ultrasound: A Platform for Personalized Editing of Sensory Representations
items.abstract: Background: Topographic maps organize the mammalian cortex, and their maladaptive reorganization underlies conditions like chronic tinnitus and focal dystonia. Low-intensity focused ultrasound (FUS) produces offline neuromodulation, yet its submillimeter spatial distribution within sensory maps remains poorly understood. Objective: To determine how offline FUS-induced amplitude changes are spatially organized within the mouse primary auditory cortex (A1) tonotopic map and depend on sonication intensity. Methods: Widefield Ca2+ imaging was combined with phased-array FUS (750 kHz, <1.5 W/cm2 Isppa, no microbubbles) in Thy1-GCaMP6s x CBA/CaJ mice. Twenty-second sonication was steered to each animal's tone-evoked centroid at 0.625 or 1.2 W/cm2. Offline gain was quantified over 40 min using Euclidean distance from the focus and functional distance (first principal component, PC1, percentile brackets). Results: Modulation followed functional rather than physical geometry: effects appeared isotropic in Euclidean distance but varied spatially across functional brackets, peaking 10 min post-sonication and persisting upwards of 40 min. Both intensities carved a modulatory trough between the 50th and 70th percentiles of A1's sensory representation (~1.0-1.2 mm from target). At 0.625 W/cm2 Isppa, this trough became suppressive (gain < 1.0) and shifted relative response timing across cortical fields, an effect absent at 1.2 W/cm2. Conclusions: Offline FUS modulation in A1 is organized by functional topography rather than physical distance, demonstrating that low-intensity FUS can serve as a spatially constrained suppressant. A forward-projection model built on this profile provides a quantitative basis for personalized, coordinate-based sonication planning for focal sensory pathologies like tinnitus.

items.title: Human lipidomics guides brain-inspired lipoprotein particle approach to ameliorate Alzheimer's disease pathology
items.abstract: APOE encodes the principal lipid-transporting protein in the brain, and lipid dysregulation is increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathogenesis. The APOE4 allele, together with advanced age and female sex, are major risk factors for late-onset AD. Yet how these risk factors interact to reshape lipid composition and transport in the brain remains unclear. Herein, we characterize lipidomic profiles in the brain, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and blood of individuals with or without AD, as well as of mice expressing humanized APOE. We identify brain lipidomic shifts associated with AD in humans, including relative depletion of highly unsaturated lipids, with many changes resembling those associated with APOE4 alone. Individuals with AD show striking depletion of lipoprotein particle (LP)-associated lipid abundance in the CSF. Additionally, humanized APOE4 mice exhibit an age-dependent deficit in CSF LP-associated lipid abundance relative to APOE3 mice. Accordingly, we leverage these insights to engineer brain-inspired reconstituted LPs (rLPs) with the goal of restoring lipid transport in the brain. rLPs promote cholesterol efflux from human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived APOE4 astrocytes in vitro. In an AD mouse model (5xFAD) expressing humanized APOE4, these nanoparticles reduce lipid-droplet accumulation, facilitate amyloid-beta clearance, enhance synaptic integrity, and improve cognitive function.
