Our previous studies confirmed that Boltz-2 is classify binder non-binders effectively. Autodock Vina and GNINA are widely used docking with knowledge and CNN based scoring functions allows to screen potential small molecules. We developed in-house VS-suite (Virtual Screening Suite) multi-environment conda orchestration designed to automate the docking workflow only using FASTA and SMILES string as inputs via streamlit-based browser GUI which integrates the boltz-2 for the complex structure prediction followed docking using AutoDock Vina for Gnina. Validation on 58 antiviral nucleoside analogues screened against SARS-CoV-2 main protease (Mpro). VS-Suite is available at https://github.com/Vsubuchem-lab/Virtual-screening-suite-VS-Suite. This consensus approaches helpful in rapid screening of small molecules against selected targets. The findings and VS-suite support its utility as a rapid and reliable tool for hit identification and rational drug development.

items.title: RecurSieve: A Python Package to Detect Subtle Gene Expression Differences Across Single-Cell RNA-seq Comparisons Using Iterative Machine Learning
items.abstract: Most existing methods for performing differential expression testing using single-cell RNA-seq data evaluate genes independently and primarily detect shifts in mean RNA levels. These methods may thus miss RNAs that distinguish experimental groups jointly or through changes in the shape of genes' expression distributions. To address this limitation, we developed RecurSieve, an iterative ensemble learning method that combines shared expression classification with unsupervised clustering to recursively identify gene sets with group-based expression differences. Because experimental labels apply to heterogeneous populations of single cells within each comparative group, RecurSieve allows dynamic label reassignment during iterative training to detect subtle, non-linear expression patterns. In benchmarking experiments using simulated data with staged distributional expression differences, RecurSieve recovered more genes (2.3-3.9 of 10 staged genes) across groups as compared to standard methods (Wilcoxon, t-test, and logistic regression; 0.0-0.7 staged genes). When applied to a single nuclei RNA-seq analysis containing low and high-pathology stages of Alzheimer's disease (46 human donor brains), RecurSieve extended results from standard approaches by identifying genes including WWOX, DPP10, KCNIP4, HS6ST3, and CNTN5 which tend to exhibit stage-specific distributional expression differences accompanied by only minor changes in average expression. A subset of the genes exclusively detected in RecurSieve analysis had been previously associated with Alzheimer's disease, underscoring the potential importance resulting from the unique sensitivity of our method. These simulated and empirical single-cell RNA-seq results demonstrate how the RecurSieve framework complements standard methods for identifying genes with unique group-specific expression differences independent of changes in average expression.

items.title: Extracting generator-specific information from irregular brain field potentials: a comparative study of feature-based and deep learning approaches.
items.abstract: Brain field potentials (FPs) reflect the combined activity of multiple neural sources, challenging the accuracy of their temporal series and their spatial origin difficult to establish from waveform inspection alone. However, FP generators obtained by independent component analysis exhibit characteristic temporal patterns and unique spatial profiles that allow their identification, even during apparently irregular activity. Here, we compared feature-based machine learning (ML) and end-to-end deep learning (DL) approaches to assess how effectively this information can be extracted from short segments and whether learning directly from raw signals offers advantages over predefined signal descriptors. We analyzed irregular FP-generator activity from multiple hippocampal generators in a dataset pooled across experimenters, recording devices, and electrode types. Feature-based approaches used predefined spectral and nonlinear descriptors to construct multidimensional representations, which were classified using seven ML algorithms: bagged decision trees (BAG), light gradient boosting machine (LGBM), quadratic discriminant analysis (QDA), random forest (RF), support vector machines (SVM), extreme gradient boosting (XGB) and multilayer perceptron (MLP). In parallel, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and transformer architectures learned discriminative representations directly from raw signals. Performance was evaluated using animal-independent data partitions to assess generalization to previously unseen animals. Both approaches discriminated among FP generators from short segments of irregular activity. Raw-signal models generally achieved higher classification performance than feature-based approaches, although the latter also captured substantial generator-specific information. This suggests that discriminative information extends beyond the predefined descriptors and includes temporal patterns that can be exploited through direct signal learning. Classification across animals further supports the reproducibility of generator-related information despite variability in experimental conditions and recording procedures. These findings provide a scalable quantitative approach to identifying FP generators from irregular activity, opening new possibilities for investigating electrophysiological signals across physiological and pathological conditions.

items.title: Bile acid-mediated ileal barrier function deficits in primary sclerosing cholangitis
items.corresponding_institution: Oxford Centre for Microbiome Studies (OCMS), Kennedy Institute of Rheumatology, NDORMS, University of Oxford, Oxford, UK.
items.abstract: Background: Given a high prevalence of ulcerative colitis (UC) in primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC-UC), research into the pathophysiology of the gut-liver axis has focussed on the large intestine. However, reduced bile flow from the liver has the potential to impact on homeostatic functions of the small intestine, including the main site of bile acid reuptake - the terminal ileum. Objective: Define ileal barrier changes in PSC-UC that are future treatment targets. Design: We used a combination of single-cell RNA-sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, bulk RNA-seq, and liquid chromatography mass spectrometry (LC-MS)-based bulk proteomics in samples from patients with PSC-UC, UC and healthy controls to determine PSC-UC-associated barrier function changes in the terminal ileum. Results: Mature enterocytes of the terminal ileum are characterised by spatially organised cell states. The phase II detoxification gene, Glutathione-S-transferase alpha 1 (GSTA1), marks one state that is enriched at the base of villi and is co-expressed with detoxification genes. Genes within this co-expression module are downregulated in ileal samples from patients with PSC-UC and protein abundance is correlated with liver function in patients. We confirm that Gsta1 mRNA is decreased in the ileum in murine cholestatic liver disease and altering microbiome capacity for bile acid deconjugation regulates Gsta1 expression. Conclusion: We have identified new pathways that are disrupted in the ileum of patients with PSC-UC which represent potential new targets for microbiome-based treatments to improve barrier function.

items.title: ManualQC: A MATLAB toolbox for visual EEG quality control and rater calibration
items.abstract: ManualQC is a MATLAB toolbox for visual quality control (QC) of epoched electroencephalography (EEG) data. It provides structured QC records of each raters selections and comments on epochs, channels, and independent components (ICs). The RaterTool module combines agreement summaries with waveform replay, displaying their epoch and channel markings on the same pre-QC recording for joint review. We illustrate the QC workflow using 20 ERP CORE datasets and demonstrate rater comparison and replay functions using results from three laboratory research assistants on a separate set of EEG recordings. Together, structured QC records and waveform replay facilitate the documentation of manual QC decisions and joint review of disagreements. items.title: Multiple classes of spindle-like oscillations reveal stereotyped lifespan dynamics amid individual variability
items.corresponding_institution: Brigham and Women's Hospital/Harvard Medical School
items.abstract: Sleep spindles, 9-16 Hz transient oscillatory bursts in the sleep electroencephalogram (EEG), are linked to memory consolidation and are altered in aging and disease states. Recent work suggests that traditionally detected spindles are only a subset of a larger class of spindle-like events, and that beyond spindles exist several classes of spindle-like transient oscillatory activity. Together these classes have been shown to comprise individualized signatures of brain activity linked to disease states including schizophrenia and REM behavior disorder. While traditional spindle activity has been studied across the lifespan, the evolution of the full set of spindle-like oscillation classes as a function of age is unknown. To address this major knowledge gap, we characterize the cross-sectional dynamics of multiple classes of spindle-like oscillations in whole-night polysomnography from the Cleveland Family Study (n = 704, age: 7-89 y). Unsupervised clustering revealed five classes of spindle-like events in the delta (2-4 Hz), theta (4-6 Hz), theta-alpha (6-9 Hz), sigma-low (9-12 Hz) and sigma-high (12-16 Hz) ranges, each with separate, stereotyped cross-sectional dynamics across the lifespan. Large heterogeneity was observed even within narrow classically defined demographics. Early life ([~]10-25 years) is marked by parallel age-related increases in the frequency of the sigma-high and theta-alpha classes and a rapid shift of fast-spindle coupling toward the slow-oscillation peak -- timing thought to be critical for memory consolidation. Midlife ([~]25-50 years) marks the maximal expression of the delta and sigma-low classes together with an increasingly central-dominant distribution of fast spindles. Late life is defined by progressive uncoupling of lower frequency events from the slow oscillation as well as a leftward shift of higher frequency events away from the peak of the slow oscillation. We further uncover a developmental axis in which slow-oscillation phase coupling decreases in frequency dependence with age. Moreover, we show that the combination of expressed event classes can define phenotypes whose prevalence shifts systematically with age. Together, these provide a robust multi-modal framework for characterizing lifespan dynamics, with wide applications spanning both mechanistic and clinical studies.

items.title: Bridging the Babble: A Method to Correlate Varying Nomenclature and Surface Marker Definitions Across the Human Splenic B Cell Literature
items.abstract: IntroductionFlow cytometry-based immunophenotyping is widely used for identifying memory B cell subsets associated with disease or immune responses. For simplicity, multi-feature surface marker vectors are often reduced to a single subset label for cell sorting, functional tests, and understanding immune cell interactions. Across the literature however, the same label is often used with significantly different phenotype feature vectors. Unfortunately, this babelization of phenotype definitions, makes it difficult to compare experimental results across studies. This becomes a significant reproducibility issue when cells reside in multiple anatomical compartments, with location-dependent phenotypes and naming conventions. MethodsHere, we report a broadly applicable, rigorous computational pipeline for analyzing flow cytometry data, with a novel implementation of the Jaccard Similarity Index (JSI) to compare gating schemes. The JSI is used to map the labels assigned to each cell when two gating schemes are applied to the same dataset. We designed a human splenic B cell flow cytometry panel comprising 29 B cell surface markers representative of the major gating schemes from 27 memory B cell studies, none of which used the same classification scheme. We then generated a cytometery dataset, replicated and mapped subset labels from 7 published gating schemes to each other and unsupervised clustering output. ResultsWe found that different gating schemes produced inconsistent classifications for the same cell, and clusters from different gating methods with the same label had varying levels of similarity by JSI. Using the normalized variation of information metric, we find that the overall technical similarity between gating schemes varied from 0.16 (highly dissimilar) to 0.60 (moderately similar). We found that using JSI with unsupervised clustering, and further incorporating literature-based frameworks, can help disambiguate human splenic B cell clustering results, identifying subsets described in the literature, with additional intra-subset heterogeneity. ConclusionsCluster comparison metrics, combined with unsupervised clustering and in silico replication of published gating schema enables accurate cluster comparisons across studies, increasing rigor, reproducibility, and precision. Overall, these methods enabled detailed mapping of multiple literature-based B cell subsets onto a single classification map of human splenic B cells, harmonizing predefined definitions with in-depth immunophenotyping.

items.title: In vivo screening identifies SLC38A3 as a metabolic booster for CAR T cell therapy
authors: de Rooij, L. P. M. H.
items.corresponding_institution: CeMM Research Center for Molecular Medicine of the Austrian Academy of Sciences; Medical University of Vienna, Institute of Artificial Intelligence, Center for
items.abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells are highly effective against certain blood cancers, but struggle in the hostile tumor microenvironment (TME) of solid tumors. We developed the CARGO method for in vivo gain-of-function screening in CAR T cells and used it to equip CAR T cells with enhanced access to nutrients inside the TME, by overexpressing 452 solute carrier (SLC) transmembrane transporters. We identified SLC38A3, a sodium-coupled amino acid transporter not endogenously expressed in T cells, as an effective booster of CAR T cell performance in xenograft models of hepatocellular carcinoma (Huh7, HepG2) and ovarian adenocarcinoma (SKOV3). Ectopic expression of SLC38A3 in CAR T cells enhanced their glutamine uptake, improved metabolic fitness, and promoted a stem-like memory phenotype, which resulted in superior antitumor efficacy and durable protection upon tumor rechallenge in glutamine-restricted solid tumors. In summary, our study shows that equipping CAR T cells with non-native nutrient transporters can confer enhanced metabolic resilience, and it establishes the feasibility and utility of in vivo open reading frame (ORF) screens in CAR T cells to tackle the hostile TME of solid tumors.

items.title: The MRE11-Rad50-Nbs1 complex acts on 3 DNA-protein covalent complexes
items.corresponding_institution: The Univ. of Texas at Austin
items.abstract: DNA-protein crosslinks (DPCs) are complex lesions that block replication, transcription, and other DNA transactions. Here we investigate repair of 3 DPC lesions using the site-specific Flp tyrosine recombinase H305L mutant that forms stable covalent complexes. In human cells, removal or catalytic inhibition of MRE11 stabilizes Flp DPCs in parallel to a proteasome-dependent pathway. High levels of Flp DPCs are also observed in budding yeast, where MRE11 deletion or mutation of the nuclease domain increases covalent Flp DPC accumulation. Mass spectrometry-based identification of endogenous DPC factors in human cells identifies TOP1 covalent complexes as the primary 3 lesion that is stabilized in the absence of MRE11 nuclease function, in addition to 5 DPCs generated by TOP2 family enzymes. This work characterizes an important role for the MRE11-RAD50-NBS1 complex in processing of 3 lesions, in addition to its well-established functions at 5 DPCs and in 5 strand resection during homologous recombination.

items.title: Effects of insulin supplementation on senescence-associated markers and cellular phenotype of human dental pulp stem cell spheroids during long-term serum-free culture
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Biotechnology, Faculty of Science and Technology, Universitas Aisyiyah Yogyakarta,
items.abstract: BackgroundIn vitro expansion of human dental pulp stem cells (DPSCs) in serum-free, three-dimensional suspension culture is important for scalable, clinically relevant manufacturing. However, this approach is limited by reduced proliferative capacity and passage-dependent senescence accumulation. In this study, we evaluated whether insulin supplementation could address these limitations while maintaining mesenchymal immunophenotype and stemness-related gene expression across serial passages in a downscale model as a reference for further DPSCs upscaling. MethodsDPSCs were expanded as spheroids for five consecutive 8-day passages (40 days total) in serum-free medium (SF), serum-free medium supplemented with insulin (SF+I), or medium containing 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS). Spheroid diameter, cell-equivalent yield, and fold expansion per passage were quantified. qPCR analysis of proliferation-associated (Ki67, PCNA), senescence-associated (p16, p21), and stemness-associated (OCT4, SOX2, NANOG, KLF4) transcripts, SA-{beta}-galactosidase staining, and flow-cytometric analysis of MSC-associated surface markers were performed. ResultsSF+I increased per-passage fold expansion relative to SF and produced expansion values that were comparable from those in FBS (22.3 fold vs 25.0 fold) with larger spheroid diameters. SF showed progressive upregulation of senescence marker p16 and p21 across passages (2.7-fold increase from passage 1 to passage 5), whereas SF+I maintained lower expression of both markers and showed markedly less SA-{beta}-galactosidase positivity at passage 5, compared with SF-based medium (13.19% vs 46.81%). KLF4 and NANOG were better retained in Sf and SF+I under serum-free conditions than under FBS, although the statistical differences were marker-specific. SF and SF+I also retained high positivity for CD105, CD90, and CD73 (>90%), whereas FBS showed substantial loss of these MSC-associated markers (CD90: 31.6%; CD73: 28.4%). ConclusionsInsulin supplementation supported long-term serum-free 3D DPSC expansion and was associated with lower senescence-associated readouts. Serum-free conditions were also associated with better preservation of the measured MSC-associated surface-marker profile and selected stemness-associated transcripts than FBS conditions. These findings warrant further multi-donor and functional validation of insulin-supplemented serum-free media for DPSC manufacturing.

items.title: Distinct Associations of Gait Variability and Physical Fitness with Resting-State Dynamic Functional Connectivity in Cognitively Normal Older Adults from the AGUEDA Trial
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Physical Education and Sports, Faculty of Sport Sciences, Sport and Health University Research Institute (iMUDS), University of Granada, Granada,
items.abstract: Gait variability and physical fitness may provide accessible indicators of brain health in aging, yet their associations with resting-state dynamic functional connectivity remain unclear. We examined associations of gait variability and physical fitness with local and distant temporal consistency of resting-state dynamic functional connectivity in 86 cognitively normal older adults from the AGUEDA trial. Gait variability was assessed using coefficients of variation for stride length, gait velocity, step time, and step length, while physical fitness included muscular strength and cardiorespiratory fitness. Dynamic functional connectivity was estimated using voxel-wise stepwise connectivity analyses. Analyses targeting regions related to Alzheimers disease risk and exploratory whole-brain analyses were adjusted for age, sex, and education. Greater gait variability was associated with local, but not distant, temporal consistency of dynamic functional connectivity. Greater stride length, gait velocity, and step length variability were associated with higher local temporal consistency in the left inferior frontal gyrus ({beta} = 0.28 to 0.33; false discovery rate-corrected P = 0.024 to 0.047) and lower temporal consistency in the right insula ({beta} = -0.47 to -0.31; false discovery rate-corrected P = 0.001 to 0.028). Whole-brain analyses revealed lower local temporal consistency in the left parahippocampal gyrus with greater stride length variability ({beta} = -0.43; family-wise error-corrected P = 0.002) and in the left calcarine cortex with greater gait velocity variability ({beta} = -0.45; family-wise error-corrected P = 0.001). No statistically significant associations were observed for physical fitness. These findings suggest that gait variability may reflect aspects of local dynamic functional brain organization in cognitively normal older adults.

items.title: Genetic variants associated with 90-day survival in sepsis patients
items.corresponding_institution: Paris-Saclay University, UVSQ, INSERM U1173, Infection and Inflammation Laboratory, Montigny-le-Bretonneux, France
items.abstract: Sepsis is a highly prevalent and life-threatening syndrome resulting from an exaggerated inflammatory response to an infection. Its etiology is multifactorial and involves both environmental and genetic factors that are presently poorly understood. We conducted a genome-wide association study (GWAS) on sepsis patients survival at 90-day following admission in the ICU. We extracted genotypes of single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) from whole-genome sequencing data of 1030 patients from three cohorts, including APROCCHSS, RECORDS-Observational and TRIAL. We used a proportional hazard Cox model adjusted for age, the first two genetic principal components and the cohort. We identified 7 significant SNVs that reached genome-wide significance (P<5 x 10-8). One of them, rs1474684, maps to the last intron of the phospholipase C Beta 1 (PLCB1) gene and likely is causative, following fine-mapping. Two other SNVs map to IMPDH1P7 gene for rs146038228 and CALCRL-AS1 for rs4667156. Both genes lie in a 400 kb region showing extended linkage disequilibrium that prevented resolution of the causative variant. The other four variants were low frequency SNVs mapping to non-coding or intergenic regions near ENSG00000288587 (rs11754929), ENSG00000248172 (rs74570843), ISG20 (rs139793868), and RNU6-144P (rs78812419). Gene Set Enrichment Analysis, a sensitive nonparametric method to rank pathways associated with variants and genes, consistently highlighted terms associated with the central nervous system, synapse physiology and cardio-endocrine regulation. Altogether, our findings shed new light on genetic factors and pathways associated with survival in sepsis patients. However, further investigation in an independent cohort will be necessary for validation of the associations.

items.title: Multicentre electrophysiology reveals the limits of auditory prediction responses as biomarkers of chronic tinnitus
items.abstract: Identifying reliable neural biomarkers of chronic tinnitus remains challenging because ageing and hearing loss independently influence auditory cortical activity. Here, we investigated auditory expectation processing in 440 adults with (n = 226) and without (n = 214) chronic tinnitus using electroencephalography during a local-global auditory paradigm across six centres. Although several electrophysiological group differences emerged in unadjusted analyses, most were substantially attenuated after adjustment for demographic and audiological factors. Two clusters remained significant within the unexpected-omission-versus-sound contrast (44 to 100 ms and 356 to 476 ms), but neither survived correction across eight contrasts. Direct comparisons between expected and unexpected omissions revealed no significant group differences. Exploratory classification using selected EEG features achieved a cross-validated area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.624, increasing to 0.689 when combined with demographic and audiological predictors. However, this improvement was not reproduced in held-out validation, and EEG features showed limited predictive value for tinnitus burden or loudness. These findings highlight a fundamental distinction between electrophysiological group differences and clinically informative individual-level biomarkers, underscoring the importance of controlling for confounding factors and establishing independent predictive validity in tinnitus research.

items.title: Cerebrospinal fluid cellular dynamics following modified interval dosing natalizumab therapy in multiple sclerosis
items.corresponding_institution: Center for Translational & Computational Neuroimmunology and the Columbia Multiple Sclerosis Center, Department of Neurology, Columbia University Irving Medical
items.abstract: Background Natalizumab, an 4-integrin monoclonal antibody, a highly effective relapsing multiple sclerosis (MS) therapy, carries a small but clinically important risk of progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML). Previous studies have suggested that alternative dosing paradigms can reduce PML risk while maintaining therapeutic efficacy. Objectives Clarify how immune cell dynamics changes with the alternative dosing. Methods We investigated alternative dosing paradigms by profiling cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) immune cell dynamics across: (1) standard interval dosing (SID, every 4 weeks), (2) extended interval dosing (EID, every 6 or 8 weeks), and (3) annual 12-week gap (aGAP). Using single-cell RNA sequencing, we analyzed 46 CSF samples from participants across dosing regimens, untreated MS controls, and one non-natalizumab-related PML case. Results Compared with controls, natalizumab reduced proportions of Treg, memory T cells, B cells, and plasmacytoid dendritic cells, while increasing tissue-resident memory T and microglia-like myeloid cells. EID and aGAP were associated with higher proportions of peripheral immune populations, including CD4+ T cells with interferon response signatures (CD4+IFN+), potentially enhancing antiviral immunity. The PML case exhibited elevated CD8+ central memory T and CD56bright NK cells proportions in the CSF, suggesting their role in viral control. Conclusions These findings support that EID and aGAP allow immune reconstitution.

items.title: Concurrent chemoradiotherapy combined with immunotherapy in locally advanced cervical cancer: an evaluation of efficacy
items.corresponding_institution: Gynecology, Anyang Cancer Hospital, Anyang, Henan Province, China
items.abstract: Objective: This study examined whether adding sintilimab to standard treatment improves early tumor response and survival in locally advanced cervical cancer. We also determined how peripheral CD8+ T-cell counts and the tumor marker CA125 change from baseline to treatment completion, and whether these measures predict the benefit of combination therapy. Method: We enrolled 126 patients with locally advanced cervical cancer (LACC; FIGO 2018 stage IB3-IVA) treated at our institution between January 2023 and January 2025 in this single-center retrospective cohort. Sixty-six received standard concurrent chemoradiotherapy (CCRT), and 60 received CCRT plus sintilimab (200 mg intravenously every 3 weeks throughout the treatment course). Peripheral blood samples were obtained at baseline and at treatment completion to quantify CD4+ and CD8+ T-cell proportions and serum CA125 levels. Short-term response was assessed by RECIST version 1.1. Progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) were estimated by the Kaplan-Meier method and compared between groups with the log-rank test. Independent prognostic factors were identified using Cox proportional hazards regression, and likelihood ratio tests examined interactions between immune markers and treatment assignment. Results: The objective response rate (ORR) was 81.67% with CCRT plus sintilimab versus 65.15% with CCRT alone (P = 0.045). Median progression-free survival (PFS) was 18.6 months in the combination group and 10.0 months in the CCRT group (log-rank P < 0.001). Median overall survival (OS) was not reached in the combination group but was 27.3 months in the CCRT group (log-rank P = 0.0027). After adjustment for age and BMI, combination therapy remained an independent favorable prognostic factor for both PFS (HR = 0.443, 95% CI: 0.290-0.678, P < 0.001) and OS (HR = 0.410, 95% CI: 0.230-0.731, P = 0.002). Stratification by the median post-treatment peripheral CD8+ T-cell proportion (24.48%) gave a median PFS of 19.9 months in the high-CD8+ group versus 12.4 months in the low-CD8+ group (HR = 0.63, 95% CI: 0.42-0.94, P = 0.022). CD8+ T-cell stratification showed a significant interaction with treatment assignment for OS (P = 0.012). Using the median post-treatment CA125 level (31.25 IU/mL), median PFS was 11.9 months in the high-CA125 group versus 19.4 months in the low-CA125 group (HR = 1.89, 95% CI: 1.26-2.83, P = 0.0017); unlike CD8+ stratification, however, CA125 showed no significant interaction with treatment for either PFS (P = 0.959) or OS (P = 0.569). Conclusion: In LACC, concurrent chemoradiotherapy combined with sintilimab improves objective response and is associated with longer PFS and OS. Patients with a higher post-treatment CD8+ T-cell proportion derive greater benefit from combination therapy, supporting its use as a stratification indicator of efficacy. CA125 mainly reflects tumor burden and overall prognosis rather than treatment benefit and is therefore unsuitable for selecting patients for immunotherapy.

items.title: Unmet Needs in NSCLC Care: Insights from Temporal Routes to Treatment
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Population Health Sciences, Geisinger, Danville, PA, USA
items.abstract: Background: Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide. Analyzing the sequence and timing of clinical events before treatment can reveal barriers to early non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) diagnosis and care. Methods: We established a retrospective cohort of 3541 adult patients diagnosed between 2012 and 2022, and received all or part of their initial treatment within our health system. Sequences of pre-treatment clinical events including imaging, primary care provider (PCP) and lung specialist visits, Emergency Department (ED) presentation, diagnosis, and treatment type were encoded using 1-gram and 2-gram representations. K-means clustering, guided by the Gap Statistic method, determined the optimal pathway groups. Results: Four distinct care pathways were identified: (1) Low-Dose Computed Tomography (LDCT) Screening (n=215), with high LDCT use (98.6%) and early-stage diagnoses (67.0%), yielding the highest 5-year survival rate (72.1%). (2) Moderate Early-Stage Detection (MESD) (n=1236) showed the second-highest rate of early-stage diagnoses (53.2%) with minimal LDCT uptake (0.3%) and the lowest rate of primary care engagement (15.2%). (3) High Comorbidity Burden (HCB) (n=1200), with the highest Charlson index (5), low early-stage diagnosis (36.5%), and low LDCT referral rates (3%). (4) ED Presentation (EDP) (n=890), with frequent ED visits prior to diagnosis (65.5%), low LDCT referral (1.2%), and the lowest rate of early-stage detection (19.8%). Conclusion: Distinct routes revealed unmet needs, including limited LDCT screening, low primary care engagement in MESD, and barriers to early medical attention in the EDP group. Targeted interventions may enable early detection and improve survival.

items.title: Covariate-Adjusted Allelic Inference on the Non-Pseudoautosomal X Chromosome with Application to Sex Differences in Allele Frequency
items.corresponding_institution: Centre for Addiction and Mental Health
items.abstract: Sex differences in minor allele frequency (sdMAF) are widely used as a quality control (QC) metric for variants in the non-pseudoautosomal region (NPR) of the X chromosome. However, conventional sdMAF tests assess marginal allele-frequency differences and generally do not account for imbalances in measured covariates, such as genetic ancestry. We develop a general regression-based framework for covariate-adjusted subgroup allele-frequency inference. Using the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem, we derive adjusted subgroup mean estimators and their joint sampling covariance under a groupwise residual-variance structure, enabling both targeted one-degree-of-freedom tests and joint tests of multiple subgroup contrasts. For X-NPR sdMAF analysis, we consider a parsimonious groupwise variance estimator motivated by the distinct genotype distributions of hemizygous males and diploid females, alongside the conventional homoskedastic and heteroskedasticity-robust HC1 estimators. Simulation studies evaluate Type I error control, robustness to Hardy-Weinberg disequilibrium, and statistical power. The homoskedastic variance estimator exhibited Type I error distortion under imbalanced sex ratios, whereas HC1 and the groupwise estimator demonstrated broadly comparable Type I error control and power across the simulated scenarios. In an application to 1000 Genomes Project data, adjusted and unadjusted sdMAF estimates were highly correlated, although covariate adjustment altered effect estimates and statistical significance for individual variants. The framework also supports a theoretical extension to sex-prevalence-adjusted allelic contrasts, with groupwise variance estimation providing a parsimonious alternative to HC1 for X-NPR sdMAF analysis.

items.title: Precise In Vivo Base-Editing Therapy for Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Liver Surgery, Ren Ji Hospital, Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, 1630 Dongfang Road, Shanghai, 200127, China.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (AATD) caused by the homozygous SERPINA1 Z variant (PiZZ) is characterized by reduced circulating functional alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT) and accumulation of mutant Z-AAT. YOLT-202 is a lipid nanoparticle-delivered adenine base-editing therapy designed to precisely correct the PiZ variant (E342K) while avoiding unintended bystander editing. We evaluated the safety and pharmacodynamic effects of a single dose of YOLT-202 in patients with AATD. METHODS In this ongoing, first-in-human, single-center, open-label, single-arm, dose-escalation study, adults with genetically confirmed PiZZ AATD and a serum total AAT concentration of less than 11 M received a single intravenous dose of YOLT-202. In this interim analysis, one patient received 35 mg and three received 45 mg. The primary end point was safety. Secondary end point was changes from baseline in serum total AAT concentrations. RESULTS Serum total AAT concentrations increased rapidly in all four patients, reaching or exceeding the putative protective threshold of 11 M by week 3. At week 4, total AAT concentrations were 15.4 M in the patient who received 35 mg and a mean of 19.0 M in the 45-mg cohort, with increases sustained for up to 11 months. Circulating M-AAT concentrations increased, whereas Z-AAT concentrations decreased. At week 3, M-AAT accounted for 98.7% of total circulating AAT in the 35 mg patient and a mean of 93.4% in the 45-mg cohort. Adverse events occurred in two patients (50%), including infusion-related reactions in two and liver-enzyme elevations in two. No treatment-related adverse events of grade 3 or higher, serious adverse events, or deaths were reported. CONCLUSIONS In this small, ongoing study, a single administration of YOLT-202 was associated with sustained increases in circulating AAT concentrations and a shift from Z-AAT toward M-AAT. Preclinical findings and liver-biopsy results from one patient provided evidence of precise correction of the PiZ variant with negligible bystander editing. No serious adverse events or treatment-related adverse events of grade 3 or higher were observed. (ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT07193615.)

items.title: Genetic architecture of the human brain glycoproteome implicates glycosylation in Alzheimer's disease and related dementias
authors: The Alzheimer's Disease Functional Genomics Consortium,
items.abstract: Glycosylation is a prevalent post-translational modification in the human brain, but its genetic regulation remains poorly defined. We profiled N-linked glycosylation in 316 human prefrontal cortices and generated the first glycoproteome-wide map of glycosylation quantitative trait loci (glycoQTLs). GlycoQTLs were enriched in regulatory regions and partly independent of protein abundance. High-mannose glycopeptiforms were preferentially affected, suggesting genetic influence on early glycan processing in the endoplasmic reticulum. Integration with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD) GWAS summary statistics identified disease-associated glycoQTLs, including those at TMEM106B and ACE. At TMEM106B, the ADRD risk allele altered the glycan composition at N183 within the fibril-forming C-terminal fragment of the protein, whereas at ACE, individual glycopeptiforms showed divergent genetic effects. Targeted trans-glycoQTL analysis further identified long-range regulation, including a hotspot at the fucosidase FUCA2. These findings establish glycoQTL mapping as a complementary functional-genomics layer that reveals disease-associated molecular effects beyond conventional protein-level analyses.

items.title: Human genetic support improves the odds of drug success but poorly predicts it
items.corresponding_institution: Berlin Institute of Health (BIH) at Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin
items.abstract: Nine in ten drug programmes that enter clinical trials fail, mostly for lack of efficacy1,2. Drug targets supported by human genetic evidence are about twice as likely to reach approval3-5, which now guides target selection. Yet most of it emerged only after the drugs had been developed, the methods linking genetic variants to genes were trained in part on known drug targets6, and recent trials of genetically supported targets have both lowered a disease marker7 and failed to reduce clinical events8,9. Here we tested how far genetic support can guide drug development across almost 17,000 target-disease pairs. Its association with clinical success held when genes were assigned without knowledge of drugs, within diseases and for evidence available years before a trial. It was strongest where the evidence pointed directly to the causal gene, larger for diseases judged on a measurable trait, and absent for drugs that use their target only to reach cells, such as antibody-drug conjugates. Genetic support, however, contributed little to distinguishing successful from failed programmes. Human genetic evidence is therefore a reliable but modest guide to where to invest, not a predictor of which programme will succeed.

items.title: Incidence and outcome of intracerebral hemorrhage in a prospective cohort and healthcare data.
items.corresponding_institution: The University of Edinburgh Edinburgh Neuroscience
items.abstract: Background: The global burden of intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) remains high. Identifying trends in incidence and outcome requires resource-intensive epidemiological surveillance. Our objective was to characterise incidence, survival and functional outcome of people with ICH in a cohort study; and compare to healthcare systems data (HSD) in the same region. Methods: We conducted a prospective population-based inception cohort study in Lothian, Scotland, UK (the Lothian Audit of Treatment of ICH, LATCH). LATCH included all spontaneous non-traumatic ICH in Lothian residents [≥]16 years between 1st June 2010 - 31st May 2013 and 1st November 2018 - 31st October 2021. We identified and characterized people with ICH in HSD in the same region and period using linked primary and secondary care records, community prescriptions and death records. We calculated incidence per 100,000 person-years; 30-day survival; and sensitivity and positive predictive value of ICH detection in HSD. For functional outcome one year after ICH, we compared the modified Rankin Scale score (mRS) in LATCH to days alive and out of hospital in HSD. Results: In LATCH, from 1283 possible cases, 1021 were first-ever ICH. We identified 876 people with ICH in HSD in the same period. In LATCH, ICH incidence was 23.7 (95%CI 22.2-25.2) per 100,000 person-years (48.5% male, mean age 72 (SD 14.6) years), with no time trend (trend in crude incidence rates 0.31/year (-3.78-4.39)). ICH incidence in HSD was 23.1 (21.6-24.6) per 100,000 person-years (48.3% male, mean age 74.2 (SD 14.0) years). The positive predictive value of ICH identified in HSD versus LATCH was 78.3% (75.4%-81.0%). 30-day case fatality was 41.2% (38.1%-44.2%) in LATCH and 39.0% (35.5%-42.3%) in HSD. We found good correlation between functional outcome measures (Spearman's r=0.88, p<0.001). Conclusions: The burden of ICH remains persistently high. HSD appears accurate for assessing incidence, survival and functional outcome.

items.title: Causal Emergence of Macroscopic Stochastic Dynamics from a Multi-modal Foundation Model of Human Sleep
items.abstract: Sleep is an essential, self organizing physiological state conserved across species, yet its macroscopic coordination remains governed by unknown physical principles. For nearly sixty years, clinical medicine has classified sleep into heuristic, discrete 30 second epochs, an empirical convention that flattens continuous non-equilibrium dynamics and leaves deep subcortical neuromodulatory control fundamentally unobservable. Although emerging artificial intelligence foundation models can decode multimodal physiology with high accuracy, their high-dimensional representations remain uninterpretable black boxes, leaving the generative laws of sleep unformulated. Here we show that, across four independent multinational cohorts, causal emergence analysis of a multimodal foundation model condenses human sleep into a single continuous order parameter whose dynamics are well described by a Landau Ginzburg jump diffusion equation. This trajectory is physiologically structured: its overnight variance follows an AASM stage hierarchy (Wake, NREM, REM), and its diffusion shape tracks apnea hypopnea severity. Bidirectional clinical perturbations further support the decomposition: continuous positive airway pressure lowers baseline diffusion and apnea band spectral excess while shallowing the late-night potential well, whereas GABAergic agonism reduces the true jump rate and nocturnal awakenings without deepening the well. Length matched comparisons under dexmedetomidine sedation deepen the well and suppress jumps relative to natural sleep. By replacing empirical classification with an explicit stochastic description, our work uses a foundation model as a probe of physiological dynamics rather than only as a predictor and treats human sleep as an analytically tractable physical system. More broadly, the finding that multi-organ coordination during sleep can be summarized by a low dimensional order parameter suggests a general route from opaque artificial intelligence representations to testable macroscopic models of the subcortical dynamics that sustain human consciousness and fail in neuropsychiatric disease.

items.title: An updated open-source, large dataset of T1-weighted stroke brain MRIs and lesion segmentation masks
items.corresponding_institution: Chan Division of Occupational Science and Occupational Therapy, University of Southern California, Los Angeles, CA, USA
items.abstract: Precise delineation of stroke lesions on MRI scans provides essential quantitative information used routinely in stroke rehabilitation research. Manual annotation continues to be the gold standard for stroke lesion delineation but is subjective and labor-intensive. Our previous release of ATLAS v2.1 (N=1271) provided a large, open-source dataset of T1w stroke brain MRIs and manually segmented lesion masks, which facilitated the development of numerous lesion segmentation algorithms. However, fully automated algorithm performance is not yet adequate to replace manual protocols; existing lesion segmentation algorithms still lack accuracy and generalizability. As model architectures grow increasingly sophisticated, they demand large-scale, diverse training data. Here, we present ATLAS v3.0 (N=1815), an updated, larger dataset of T1w stroke brain MRIs with corresponding manually segmented lesion masks. ATLAS v3.0 comes with nearly 43% more data, consisting of a publicly accessible, heterogenous training (n=1453), and a hidden generalizability dataset with subjects that remain unreleased (n=362). We anticipate this updated ATLAS v3.0 release will support the growing data demands of advanced lesion segmentation algorithms.

items.title: Decreased thermal contrast sensitivity for paradoxical heat sensation in diabetic polyneuropathy
items.abstract: Paradoxical heat sensation (PHS), the perception of warmth during cooling, is typically induced by alternating warm and cold stimulation. Recent work has demonstrated that thermal contrast, defined as the difference between alternating temperatures, is a key determinant of this phenomenon in healthy individuals. However, it remains unclear whether peripheral sensory loss changes the thermal contrast required to elicit PHS and whether the experience itself remains the same after such sensory loss. We investigated PHS in individuals with probable diabetic polyneuropathy (DPN; N = 32) and healthy controls (N = 42) using a pre-registered Bayesian computational model. The model related the probability of a warm report to thermal contrast and used response times and confidence ratings as markers of perceptual uncertainty. Although prevalence was similar between groups, the thermal contrast required to elicit PHS was higher in patients with DPN, reaching the midpoint of the psychometric function at approximately 51% thermal contrast in healthy controls and 80% in patients with DPN. In both groups, warm reports were accompanied by greater uncertainty, reflected in longer response times and lower confidence. This pattern suggests that PHS does not typically reflect a clear sensation of warmth but rather an ambiguous thermal experience. These findings show that the sensation is accompanied by perceptual uncertainty in both groups, while patients with DPN require greater thermal contrast to elicit it.

items.title: Altered Auditory Network Differentiation in Multiple Sclerosis: A BROAD-NESS MEG Study
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Electrical and Information Engineering, Polytechnic University of Bari, Bari, Italy
items.abstract: The auditory P300 is widely used at the sensor level to study cognitive dysfunction in multiple sclerosis (MS), but its brain generators have rarely been investigated. The three-stimulus oddball separates task relevance from stimulus rarity, and source-level network analysis can show where and when this distinction is altered. We recorded magnetoencephalography (MEG) in 20 MS patients and 15 healthy controls during a three-stimulus auditory oddball with standard, target and non-target tones. Broadband networks were estimated from beamformer source activity with BROAD-NESS, a principal component analysis of group-averaged sources. Groups were compared with cluster-based permutation tests corrected across networks. Four networks explained 94% of the variance. Sensory (N1m) and P3 responses and task performance did not differ between groups. In a bilateral perisylvian and sensorimotor network, the difference between target and non-target responses was smaller in patients than in controls at about 370 to 500 ms (cluster p = 0.020, corrected across networks; Hedges' g = -1.11 and Bayes factor 16.1 in the localizer window). A conventional source-by-source analysis of the same contrast found no cluster surviving correction. The effect was robust to leave-one-out analysis, an alternative network estimation and excluding participants with clinical or recording characteristics, but did not survive correction across all three contrasts (p = 0.108). Network measures were not related to discrimination performance or fatigue, and no exploratory correlation with clinical or cognitive measures survived correction. In MS, task-related source-level networks were largely preserved, but one network differentiated less between task-relevant and task-irrelevant deviants, without a behavioural deficit.

items.title: Putative Causal Effects of Amyloid-β on GFAP: a Mendelian Randomization Study
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) is a marker of astrocytic activation that correlates with cerebral Alzheimer disease (AD) pathology. The causal relationship between GFAP elevation and amyloid-{beta} remains unclear. We examined whether A{beta} drives GFAP elevation and whether GFAP is independently associated with AD progression. METHODS: In the Harvard Aging Brain Study (HABS; n=329 cognitively unimpaired participants) and the Religious Orders Study and Rush Memory and Aging Project (ROSMAP; n=835 deceased participants spanning cognitively unimpaired to dementia), we performed one-sample Mendelian randomization. APOE {epsilon}4 served as the instrumental variable to estimate the causal effect of A{beta} (PET in HABS; immunohistochemistry in ROSMAP) on GFAP (plasma in HABS; brain mRNA expression in ROSMAP). Linear regression and linear mixed-effects models assessed GFAP associations with tau, hippocampal atrophy, and cognitive decline. RESULTS: In both cohorts, Mendelian randomization supported a causal effect of A{beta} on GFAP (HABS {beta} = 0.37; 95% CI, 0.11 to 0.63; P=6.1x10-3; ROSMAP {beta} = 0.35; 95% CI, 0.12 to 0.59; P=3.3x10-3). In HABS, GFAP associations with tau and cognition were no longer significant after adjusting for A{beta}, and GFAP was not associated with hippocampal atrophy. In ROSMAP, GFAP remained associated with tau and cognition after A{beta} adjustment, but not with cognition after additional adjustment for tau. DISCUSSION: Brain GFAP gene expression and plasma GFAP elevation may be downstream consequences of A{beta} accumulation. GFAP showed little independent association with cognition once core AD pathology was accounted for. These findings refine the interpretation of elevated plasma GFAP in AD.

items.title: Neurometabolite Changes Following Football Heading: A 7 T Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy Study
items.abstract: Background/Hypothesis Concern is growing around the effects of repeated non-concussive head impacts from football heading, but it is unclear whether a single bout of heading alters neurochemistry. Neurometabolite levels were measured with 7 T proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy with the primary motor cortex before and after controlled heading. Methods In a within-subject, repeated measures study, 20 participants (15 male; mean [SD] age of 25.2 [6.6]), with no reported history of head injury in the past year or any neurological conditions, performed 20 controlled rotational headers. Proton spectra were acquired at three timepoints: one before heading (Pre) and twice after heading (Post_1 and Post_2). Neurometabolite absolute molal concentrations (mol/Kg) were used as the main outcome. Results N-acetylaspartate (NAA) showed a significant effect of Time [F(2, 36.7) = 8.01, pFDR < 0.01] with elevated levels at the Post_2 timepoints compared with both Pre and Post_1 measurements. No other metabolites showed significant changes. Conclusion An acute bout of 20 headers was associated with detectable changes in NAA concentration levels. This finding from 7 T MRS provides valuable insight into the neurochemical changes resultant from repeated non-concussive head impacts, which may be suggestive of an acute neuronal response to heading. This study was registered with the German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS00029600)

items.title: Volumetric Responses in Long-term Responders to Ivosidenib in IDH Mutant Gliomas
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Neurosurgery, Oregon Health & Science University
items.abstract: Purpose/Objectives: IDH inhibitor therapy is now FDA-approved for low-grade IDH-mutated (mIDH) gliomas. Early studies with short follow-up periods have reported variable tumor volume reduction. We describe radiographic responses in long-term responders. Materials/Methods: MRIs in patients with progressive mIDH[LK1.1] gliomas treated with targeted therapy for >36 months from 2019-2024 were retrospectively reviewed. Contouring of T2/FLAIR sequences were performed to calculate tumor volumes. Results: From total 49 consecutive patients started on targeted therapy, 13 were included (11 astrocytoma, 2 oligodendroglioma). Total 157 MRI were analyzed. All were on treatment with ivosidenib. Median duration of treatment was 59.5 months (range 37.4-79.3) with 1/13 offered chemoradiation due to radiographic progression. Pretreatment tumor volume increased at the rate of 12.6 cc/year (p = 0.0007) but declined during the first year of therapy at the rate of -9.73 cc/year (p < 0.001). Afterwards, the slope was no longer significantly different from zero (p = 0.36). Conclusions: Our real-world data demonstrates a reduction in tumor volume during the first year of treatment of progressive mIDH glioma with ivosidenib followed by prolonged stabilization. The principal benefit of mutant IDH inhibition may not be prolonged tumor volume reduction but durable stable disease. Our findings can inform clinical practice using targeted therapy over an extended period which is currently unreported.

items.title: Effects of age and lesion characteristics on chronic outcomes after childhood stroke: a large-scale study of 469 childhood stroke survivors
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Pediatrics, Carver College of Medicine, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA, USA
items.abstract: The effects of stroke on the developing brain are thought to depend on age at stroke onset, but the nature of this relationship is unclear. While it has been suggested that younger age at stroke onset might facilitate recovery, there is also evidence that critical developmental periods in early childhood confer increased vulnerability to injury. Associations between age at stroke onset and childhood stroke outcomes are mixed and often inconsistent, and the roles of lesion factors such as size, laterality and location are poorly understood. We investigated how age and lesion factors relate to chronic (6+ months post-onset) sensorimotor, expressive language, receptive language, and cognitive/behavioral impairments in 469 childhood stroke survivors enrolled in the SCOUTS study (median age at stroke=9.3 years; 57% male). We used ordinal logistic regression models to characterize associations between outcomes and age at stroke onset, left and right hemispheric lesion volumes, and years to chronic assessment, and we used voxel-based lesion-symptom correlations to evaluate associations with lesion location. We also tested whether age at stroke onset moderates relationships between lesion factors and chronic outcomes. When considered in isolation, younger age at stroke onset was significantly associated with worse outcomes across all domains, but in multivariable models, statistically significant associations were observed only for language outcomes. Larger lesion volumes in each hemisphere were significantly associated with worse contralateral sensorimotor outcomes and with worse language and cognitive/behavioral outcomes. For language outcomes, associations with lesion volume were strongest for the left hemisphere, and older age at stroke onset amplified the detrimental effect of large left hemisphere lesions on expressive language outcomes. Lesion-symptom analyses mapped sensorimotor impairments to structures including the putamen, sensorimotor cortices, superior parietal cortex, and cortico-spinal projections. Expressive and receptive language impairments both mapped to mostly left-lateralized and partially overlapping frontal, temporal and parietal structures, with the strongest associations in the white matter underlying left posterior temporo-parietal areas. Cognitive/behavioral impairments mapped to bilateral regions associated with action mode and somato-cognitive action networks including right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, left inferior frontal and supramarginal gyri, and inter-effector nodes of the right pre-central gyrus. These results provide novel insights into how age at stroke onset and lesion factors contribute to childhood stroke outcomes, map domain-level impairments to specific lesion locations, and indicate that the vulnerability of left hemisphere language networks to injury may increase as language becomes more left-lateralized during development.

items.title: Predicting pediatric stroke outcomes using adult lesion-symptom models
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Pediatrics, Carver College of Medicine, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA, USA
items.abstract: Lesion location is a key predictor of post-stroke outcomes in adults, but its relevance for predicting childhood stroke outcomes is unclear. Recent developmental neuroscience work suggests that the gross spatial organization of large-scale brain systems may be generally conserved across development, raising the possibility that damage to common anatomical substrates might underlie chronic domain-level impairments after both adult-onset and childhood stroke. If so, then it should be possible to leverage adult lesion-symptom relationships to predict chronic childhood stroke outcomes. We tested the hypothesis that lesion-symptom models trained to predict sensorimotor and language impairments in patients with adult-onset brain lesions can be translated to predict chronic sensorimotor and language outcomes after childhood stroke. We trained multivariate lesion-symptom models to predict sensorimotor (Grooved Peg-Board Test: N=463; median age=53.6, IQR=17.9 years) and language (Token Test: N=379; median age=53.2, IQR=19.4 years) impairments in patients with adult-onset brain lesions. We applied the trained models to lesion segmentations from childhood stroke survivors enrolled in the SCOUTS Study (N=469; median age=9.3, IQR=11.0 years), resulting in outcome predictions that we compared against chronic (6+ month) measures of sensorimotor and language impairment derived from the Pediatric Stroke Outcome Measure and the Recurrence and Recovery Questionnaire. The adult lesion-symptom models generated outcome predictions that robustly correlated with pediatric impairment scores (sensorimotor: rho=0.43; language: rho=0.42; PFWE <0.001), enabled classification of pediatric impairment status (both AUC=0.76; PFWE=0.004), and afforded unique predictive power in multivariable pediatric outcome models (sensorimotor: adjusted OR=3.6, 95% CI=2.4-5.2; language: adjusted OR=3.0, 95% CI=1.67-5.30). Lesion-symptom models trained using pediatric lesion and outcome data captured robust lesion-symptom relationships (both rhocv=0.40, P<0.001), but yielded no advantage over the adult model predictions when compared directly via cross-validation in the pediatric cohort. Further, the adult and pediatric models made similar predictions when applied to the same lesion data even after adjusting for common effects of lesion size and laterality, suggesting a general convergence towards common anatomical signals present in both children and adults. Lesion-symptom models trained in patients with adult-onset brain lesions can be translated across outcome measures and developmental stages to predict chronic sensorimotor and language impairments after childhood stroke. These results establish lesion location as an important predictor of childhood stroke outcomes, demonstrate the feasibility of translating adult lesion-symptom models for chronic outcome prediction in children, and support the broader conclusion that the critical anatomy underlying post-stroke sensorimotor and language impairments may be generally conserved across development.

items.title: Sleepless nights: Caregiver burden among DLB patients with nighttime behaviors in the PACE-DLB Cohort
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Neurology, University of Florida College of Medicine-Jacksonville, Jacksonville, Florida, USA
items.abstract: Background Nighttime behaviors in dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) may increase caregiver burden by disrupting sleep and respite. Objective To examine associations between nighttime-behavior severity, caregiver burden, caregiving time, and caregiver well-being in moderate-to-advanced DLB. Methods We analyzed baseline data from 188 patient-caregiver dyads in the multicenter PACE-DLB cohort. Nighttime behaviors were categorized as mild/absent or moderate/severe using the Neuropsychiatric Inventory Questionnaire. Caregiver burden was assessed using the shortened Zarit Burden Interview (sZBI). Secondary outcomes included caregiving time and well-being. Group comparisons and exploratory multivariable regression were performed. Results Moderate-to-severe nighttime behaviors were reported in 117 individuals (62.2%). Caregivers in this group reported more hours on duty daily (median 24 [IQR 15-24] vs 13 [6-24]; p=0.004), more time in the same room (6 vs 3 hours/day; p=0.011), and greater burden (median sZBI 21 [13-26] vs 18 [12-21]; p=0.015). Exploratory comparisons identified differences in prioritizing care recipients' needs (p=0.046) and caregiver sleep disruption (p=0.010). After adjustment for other neuropsychiatric symptoms and patient characteristics, the nighttime-behavior association was attenuated (beta=1.5, 95% CI -0.93 to 3.9; p=0.20), whereas anxiety remained associated with greater burden (beta=3.5, 95% CI 1.2-5.9; p=0.004). Conclusions Nighttime behaviors were associated with greater caregiver burden and caregiving demands in unadjusted analyses. Although the adjusted burden association was attenuated, nighttime behaviors may impose distinct challenges through increased supervision and disrupted caregiver sleep. Further studies are needed to determine whether interventions targeting nighttime behaviors can reduce caregiving burden.
